en: Now begins the fifth chapter.

Having heard these duties of the Snātaka as they have been declared, the sages spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire: 5.1. Now begins the fifth chapter. Having heard these duties of the Snātaka as they have been declared, the sages spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire:

Having heard the duties prescribed for the student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*) across three chapters, the sages Marīci and others spoke this matter about to be described to their teacher Bhṛgu; that is, they questioned him. Now, one might object: since the term "snātaka" is heard here, what is the purpose of mentioning the "student"? It is said in reply: this is a reference to the conduct [already established]; the duties of the student have indeed already been stated.
The phrase "the high-souled one, whose origin is from Anala" is an epithet of Bhṛgu. It refers to him whose *prabhava*—that is, whose birth or origin—is from *anala*, meaning fire.
But was not Bhṛgu already stated in the first chapter to be the offspring of Manu in the verse, "Desiring to create progeny... (MDh 1.34)?

True; this is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). It was said in that manner because it is heard that Bhṛgu’s birth was from Agni, and it was spoken upon seeing that very fact. Likewise, there is an etymological derivation (*nirvacana*): "That which first blazed forth from the heated seed became yonder sun; that which was second became Bhṛgu. Or else, this is stated figuratively (*upacārataḥ*), meaning that due to the commonality of brilliance, his birth is like that of Agni. One should not be dogmatic here as to which position is more logical, for this scripture does not have that as its primary purpose. This entire sequence of questions and answers is intended to make known the gravity of the defect of food that is about to be described: namely, that food defiled by its inherent nature is more serious than food defiled by the act of acceptance (*parigraha*). A defect in the essential form (*svarūpa*) is stronger than a defect arising from a relationship (*saṃbandhi*), because it is more immediate (*antaraṅga*).

But is it not the case that previously a more extensive penance was prescribed, namely, "For unintentional [consumption], fasting for three days" (MDh 4.223)? This present rule, however, states, "In the case of the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day" (MDh 5.20). How then can this [present rule] be considered more severe? It is said: this refers to the category of garlic and similar items. For regarding those, there is the penance for an outcast, as it is stated, "Having eaten them intentionally, one falls [from caste]" (MDh 5.19). || 5.1 ||
O Lord, how does death prevail over those brahmins who, as previously described, perform their own duty and are learned in the Vedas and the Shastras? (5.2)

He now demonstrates that which was asked by the great seers (*maharṣi*). The word "thus" (*evam*) refers to the operation of the treatise (*śāstra*); "as stated" (*yathoktam*) he refers to the meaning of the treatise. By means of this composition of the treatise, such is the Dharma that has been declared; [the text speaks of] those twice-born (*dvija*) who practice it again. Since the mention of the "Brahmin" (*vipra*) is intended to be illustrative, he will say later: "This has been declared for the twice-born" (MDh 5.26). How does death prevail? [Does it occur] in the state of a *snātaka* or in the state of a student (*brahmacarya*)? For it is proper that they should live out a full lifespan, living the life of a man. A hundred years is the lifespan of men; therefore, their dying through premature death (*apamṛtyu*) before that is not proper. For it has been said: "Through right conduct one obtains long life" (MDh 4.156), and "for those who mutter prayers and offer oblations" (MDh 4.146). 5.2.
The righteous Bhṛgu, son of Manu, did not speak to those great seers; rather, he said:
"Listen to the fault by which Death seeks to slay the brahmins. (5.3)
Through the lack of study of the Vedas, the abandonment of proper conduct, laziness, and defects in food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins. (5.4)
But surely, since the question begins with "for those who perform their own duty," it is not at all appropriate for the subsequent text beginning with "by which fault" to serve as the answer.

It is said: the phrase "by lack of practice" and so forth is stated by way of illustration. Just as you accept that the lack of Vedic study and other such factors are causes of death before one's full lifespan, so too is the defect of food which is about to be described. Even when the practice of the Vedas and other virtues exist, they do not constitute one's own duty (*svadharma*) in the same way as that previously mentioned; rather, this defect of food is far more serious. And this is stated separately because it constitutes a distinct topic [5.3–4].
Garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms, as well as those things produced from impure matter, are not to be eaten by the twice-born. (5.5)

Garlic and other such substances are well known in the world. The word *kavaka* is a generic term; it is understood to refer to what is commonly known as *kṛyāku*. Mushrooms (*chatrāka*) are indeed *kavakas*. For this reason, he will prescribe an expiation for mushrooms using the word *kavaka*, stating: "Mushrooms (*chatrāka*), village-pigs... (MDh 5.19). Nor is there any other well-known substance called *chatrāka*. Furthermore, it is not logical to understand that whatever has the shape of a mushroom is a *chatrāka* merely by similarity of syllables; if that were so, it would result in a prohibition of *suvarcalā* and other plants, which contradicts established practice. Therefore, those very things which are *kavakas* are the same as *chatrākas*. Thus says the author of the *Nirukta*: "The crushed *ahicchatraka* is that which is crushed" (Nir 5.16). By this, those white-colored things that grow on unplowed ground and in succession are *kavakas*. And he will say: "Mushrooms growing from the earth" (MDh 6.14). This is also shown by the phrase "as if crushed by a foot," meaning those things which are crushed by the striking of a foot. Consequently, the prohibition applies to those things of that shape which grow from trees or shrubs. *Kukuṇḍas* are explained in medical treatises as being *kavakas*. And this explanation is not like that of words such as "cow" (*go*). The word *kavaka* is used for mushrooms both in the *Śāka* [treatise] and in common worldly usage; therefore, its meaning is determined by established practice, and that has been demonstrated. However, even those things with similar color and smell to garlic and the like are prohibited by Viṣṇu (ViDh 51.3). In the work of Pārāśara, however, the prohibition is stated by the word itself for the sake of a specific expiation: "The Cāndrāyaṇa penance" (cf. YDh 1.175). By this, the prohibition extends to *lavataka*, *karṇikāra*, and others. Those produced from impure matter, born of impurity, and those produced through contact [are also forbidden].

Others, however, say that the prohibition applies only to those things that originate entirely from impure sources, like radishes and vāstūka greens; therefore, grains, vegetables, and the like grown in impure fields which are gathered for the sake of greater nourishment are not defiled.

That is incorrect, because according to scripture [7], everything is unfit for consumption. Furthermore, even in this context, this might be so if no substance whatsoever were produced without contact with impure matter; however, since some things are born from pure sources and some from what is contaminated, this prohibition applies only to that which originates purely from impurity, not to that which is contaminated. Although meat does indeed originate from the impurity of semen and blood, this prohibition does not apply to it, because a separate section is commenced for it [in verse 5.5].
One should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by incisions, and the *śelu* fruit, cow’s milk, and colostrum. 5.6.

That which is produced externally, adhering to a tree, distinct from its roots, trunk, fruit, foliage, branches, and flowers—whether by the oozing from the hollow of a tree or by some other cause—is *vṛkṣaniryāsa* (tree-exudation). By the inclusion of the term "red," there is no prohibition against camphor and similar substances. Those whose origin or birth is from cutting or felling are likewise included; thus, there is no prohibition against non-red portions of bark that grow on trees and the like right where they are. *Śelu* is the *śleṣmātaka*, well known from medical treatises and other sciences. However, it does not refer to the cream (*santānikā*) of boiled milk, because that is not commonly recognized [in this context]. As for the argument that "cream is appropriate because of its association with *pīyūṣa* (fresh milk)," such association can serve as a specific reason only when both terms are used together; association alone cannot justify the usage of terms whose application has not been observed. And "cow's" (*gavya*): by specifying "cow's," there is no prohibition against buffalo milk and the like. *Anādyam* refers to that which has become a solid mass through contact with fire alone, yet remains unattached. The milk of a cow that has just given birth is denoted by the word *pīyūṣa*.

But will it not be stated that milk which has undergone transformation is unfit for consumption for ten days? Indeed, such milk remains in that state for three or four days. True; however, this [rule] is meaningful if, for some reason, it should remain beyond ten days for anyone.
The two words beginning with "with effort" (*prayatnena*) are for the purpose of completing the verse. The term "unfit for consumption" (*abhakṣyāṇi*) is understood to carry over. (5.6)
One should avoid kṛsara and saṃyāva prepared in vain, as well as milk-rice, cakes,
meat that has not been consecrated, food intended for the gods, and sacrificial oblations.

In this context, "kṛsarasaṃyāvam" is a collective dvandva compound. Rice cooked with sesame seeds is denoted by the word *kṛsara*. *Saṃyāva* is a specific kind of food made from ghee, molasses, sesame, and other ingredients, well known in cities.

However, for those who maintain that because the root *yu* means "to mix," the word *saṃyāva* refers to those foods prepared by mixing together ingredients such as mung beans and lentils, for them the mention of *kṛsara* would be redundant; for that too, in this manner, is indeed a *saṃyāva*. The word *vṛthā* (in vain) applies everywhere: when something is done for one's own sake, and not for the sake of the gods, ancestors, or guests, then there is the instruction regarding *kṛsara* and the rest.

That is incorrect. For householders do not cook for a single purpose alone; rather, from the pouring of the oblation onwards, there is a dedication [of the food] for that specific purpose. What then? The performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) is enjoined with respect to food prepared in general, without specifying any particular recipient. In that regard, if one eats without having performed the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, there is a transgression of what is enjoined, but there is no prohibition [against eating such food]. For indeed, two types of expiation exist: one due to the transgression of what is enjoined, and another due to the indulgence in what is prohibited. However, if dishes such as *kṛsara* are prepared without dedicating them to a specific deity or for the scope of the *vāstuyajña* and so forth, then even the daily rules (*āhnikavidhi*) are prohibited [from being applied to that food].

Furthermore, as for the injunction "one should not cook for oneself," this too is a restatement of the acquisition of food resulting from the performance of what must necessarily be done when a transgression has occurred; it is not, however, a prohibition. For if that were the case, it would entail the performance of a penance based on two grounds, as has been stated. Moreover, even if cooking is performed for another purpose, its status as being "for oneself" cannot be prohibited. For cooking is for the sake of the object being cooked, and its status as being for oneself through that medium cannot be prohibited, since one's livelihood is ordained by that very act. Indeed, the eating of the remnants [of offerings] by servants and others is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the remainder for the householder; nor is a formal intention (*saṃkalpa*) heard here, such that a mere intention at the time of cooking—"let it be cooked for my sake"—would be prohibited. And it is said that one acts "for oneself" without reflection at a later time. Furthermore, there would be the fault of a false intention (*mithyā-saṃkalpa*), namely, the application of what was intended for the deities to oneself. Therefore, this is a restatement: if one cooks, one should not consume it solely for oneself prior to the *vaiśvadeva* rite. And thus they record this rule even regarding the eating of uncooked food: "O King, whatever food a man eats, his deities eat the same" (Rām. 2.95.31). Nor is the qualification [for this rule] restricted only to one who is hungry, because it is the cause for entering the state of a householder. Consequently, on any day that he does not eat, he incurs sin by failing to perform [the rite].

This is what is meant: whether one cooks for one's own sake or for the sake of others, in every case—even those who have undertaken the vow to never bypass the *vaiśvadeva*—one does not proceed [to eat]; thus, it reiterates its obligatory nature (*nityatā*). Furthermore, he recites: "Whether in the worldly or the Vedic context, when an offering has been cast into water or upon the ground, the *vaiśvadeva* must be performed for the removal of the five slaughtering-places (*pañcasūnā*)."
By this as well, only permanence is expressed; for there is no possibility of a Vedic Vaiśvadeva [offering], nor is there any authoritative basis in a Smṛti statement.

Regarding the phrase *pāyasāpūpam* (milk-rice and cakes): *pāyasa* is rice cooked with milk, not a derivative of milk such as curds and the like; *apūpa*s are sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). These are foods for the gods, as established by traditional practice. *Havīṃṣi* (oblations) are those prescribed by the Śruti and must be offered—prior to the *graha-homa* sacrifice—since [the author] will later state that the remnants of the oblation are to be eaten. The term *anupākṛta* refers to the meat of an animal not yet consecrated, i.e., one not used in a sacrifice. *Upākaraṇa* is a specific ritual refinement of the animal, which is prescribed in the animal sacrifices (*paśuyāga*). By this, the edibility of meat that remains after being used in a sacrifice is indicated. Although the context concerns "meat not prepared for a purpose" (*vṛthāmāṃsa*), the inclusion of the word *anupākṛta* is for the purpose of prohibiting even the meat of cows, sheep, and goats that has been left over from serving guests and others. Alternatively, the word *anupākṛta* may be intended specifically to refer to the meat of cows, sheep, and goats, because it is stated that only these animals are to be slaughtered there, and that what remains is "sprinkled" (*prokṣita*) [and thus fit]. (5.7)

The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, that of a camel, that of one-hoofed animals, that of a sheep, the milk of a *saṃdhinī* cow, and the milk of a cow whose calf has been taken away—[these are forbidden]. (5.8)

If the reading here were *anirdaśāhaṃ goḥ kṣīram* ("the milk of a cow within ten days [is forbidden]"), then a prohibition lasting ten days and so forth would be suspected to apply to camels and other animals as well. In that case, because the term *anirdaśā* (feminine) would be understood by way of textual continuity (*anuvṛtti*), one would have to rely on established custom (*samācāra*) to establish an absolute prohibition. However, if the reading is the feminine form *anirdaśāyāḥ*, there is no such suspicion at all; for a grammatical connection cannot arise between the word *anirdaśāyāḥ* and masculine derivatives such as *uṣṭraḥ*. Furthermore, because of the subsequent mention of "milk" (*kṣīra*) and because of established custom, the milk of camels, single-hoofed animals, sheep, and cows within ten days of calving—along with their products—is prohibited. But in the case of a cow in heat (*saṃdhinī*) and one whose calf has died (*vivatsā*), it is only the milk itself that is prohibited.

An *anirdaśā* cow is one whose ten days since giving birth have not yet elapsed. A *saṃdhinī* is a cow that has reached the milking time for both [lactations] and is milked in either case; she is not milked in the morning but is milked in the evening. Because her milk is very scant, she is milked at only one time; such a cow is a *saṃdhinī*.

Someone says: a *saṃdhinī* is one whose own calf has died and who is milked after having been made to suckle another's calf. A *vivatsā*, however, is one whose calf is still alive but from whom the calf has been separated; she is milked by means of a specific diet such as *kuṣṭhaka*, barley, rice-husk powder, and so forth, regardless of the calf's suckling.

Regarding the phrase *vivatsāyāḥ*: by that very mention of the calf, since [the word] *goḥ* (of the cow) would already be understood—as in the expression "let a cow whose calf has not been taken be brought"—the explicit mention of the cow is for the purpose of not excluding the goat and the buffalo. This, however, does not apply to the rule concerning the *anirdaśā* (the cow within ten days of calving). Therefore, the mention of the cow there is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the goat and others. Thus Gautama says: "The milk of a cow within ten days of calving during a birth-impurity, and that of a goat and a buffalo... (GDh 17.22–23). Furthermore, the mention of *payas* (milk) [in the compound *saṃdhinīkṣīram*] is because the connection of the word *kṣīra* (milk), which occurs at the end of the compound, is not easily established [with the preceding term]. || 5.8 ||
And among all wild animals, with the exception of the buffalo, as well as the milk of females and all fermented acids, these indeed are to be avoided. (5.9)

Wild animals include cows, elephants, monkeys, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of men," there is an absence of milk [in them]. When the intention is to express the genus (*jāti*) alone—as in the expression "of all wild animals"—the use of the masculine gender has the force of implying a connection with females, just as in the expressions *mṛgakṣīram* ("wild animal's milk") and *kukkuṭāṇḍam* ("hen's egg"). This has been demonstrated by the author of the Mahābhāṣya in the rule concerning the masculine form (*puṃbhāva*) at Pāṇini 8.3.42 (Pat III: 157). The neuter designation [for milk] is used in contrast to buffalo milk (*māhiṣaṃ payaḥ*). "Woman" (*strī*) refers to a human female. Although the term is seen used in its primary sense of "possessing a dewlap and so forth" in passages such as "a cow that is a woman for the purchase of Soma" (*strī gauḥ somakrayaṇī*), nevertheless, because no other genus is under discussion here and because this meaning is more well-known, it is used in that sense. In the verse, "Women desire sweetness; women are the unsurpassed jewel," it is understood to refer specifically to noble women (*nārī*). Commentators explain the particle *eva* as serving to exclude the application of collyrium and other such things. It is not only the drinking of a woman’s milk that is forbidden, but rather [her milk is forbidden] in these and other similar activities. However, this word is properly understood as an indicator (*sūcaka*) that depends upon the customs and other Smṛti texts, rather than being a direct denoter (*vācaka*) of this specific meaning. 5.9.
Curd is to be eaten among sour substances, as is everything produced from curd;
and likewise those [fermented drinks] which are distilled from auspicious flowers, roots, and fruits.

Since all fermented liquids (*śukta*) have been prohibited without distinction, this [verse] constitutes an exception for certain ones. Those called *śukta* are those that have reached their full essence (*prāptasāra*), having become sour either through the lapse of time or by contact with other substances. For example, sweet fruits such as the *āmrātaka* and others become *śukta* after a long period because their juice has become excessively concentrated. Likewise, sweet juices, when squeezed out, turn sour over time; such are the things referred to here. However, those which are sour by nature—such as the pomegranate (*dāḍima*), the *āmalaka*, and the citron (*jambīra*)—are not *śukta* at all. Furthermore, those that have reached the stage of fermentation through the passage of time are not included, for the word *śukta* is not a synonym for merely being sour. In this context, only those things that have become sour through cooking (*pāka*) are prohibited. It is understood here that those mixed with other substances, such as flowers or roots, are also included. Thus says Gautama: "Fermented liquid alone, except for curd. (GDh 17.14)
They are fermented. Fermentation (*abhiṣava*) consists of mixing with water and allowing it to stand.
If that is so, then time alone is the cause of acidity.

True; yet these substances are also factors. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used either in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) or in connection with an accompaniment (*sahayoga*). By means of flowers and so forth, together with water, they are fermented—that is, they are blended.

However, some say: those flowers and roots that produce acidity—such as pomegranates, *āmalaka*, and so forth, which are fermented sour (*śukta*)—are edible; whereas those which are distilled or blended with sweet substances such as grapes and the like are not eaten. For "distillation" (*abhiṣava*) is said to be the production of acidity. It is by means of flowers and other ingredients that things are made sour, and grapes and the like do not themselves induce acidity; rather, it is time alone [that does so].

But this is not correct, because it is not the meaning of the word. For the statement "he presses the soma" does not convey the understanding that he is making it sour. What then? It is the very meaning previously explained:
the production of curd, whey, mastu, kilāṭa, kūrcikā, and so forth. (5.10)
One should avoid all carnivorous birds as well as those that dwell in villages; likewise, one should avoid those with uncloven hooves and the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird. (5.11)

"Meat-eaters" (*kravyāda*) refers to those that consume raw flesh, such as herons, vultures, and the like; it includes only those that eat raw meat exclusively, and not those, such as peacocks, that are fond of both [raw and cooked meat]. Even village-dwelling animals are "non-meat-eaters" (*akravyāda*). "Single-hoofed" (*ekaśapha*) refers to horses, mules, donkeys, and so forth. As for those not specifically mentioned, since they have not been declared as edible, they are not to be eaten; however, those that have been mentioned therein are indeed edible. Regarding the statement, "One who desires offspring may eat the meat of these: the camel, the mare, the bear, the cow, and the donkey," [it means he may eat their meat].

But surely, the obtainment of those [substances] as food is established by the Vedic text itself. On the contrary, if the term "specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*) were accepted, there would arise a doubt regarding the consumption elsewhere of those enjoined in the Veda; for the meaning of the sentence would be understood as: "One should avoid what is not specified, but not what is specified. Furthermore, no substances are specified as being fit for consumption in the Smṛti, such that the inclusion of the term "unspecified" could be explained as referring to things other than those. Consequently, it would follow that those which are specified in the Veda are not to be consumed.
It is replied: The purpose of that Smṛti is not in conflict with established custom (*ācāra*). The inclusion of the term "unspecified" is a mere reiteration (*anuvāda*).

The *ṭiṭṭibha* is indeed a bird, so called because it cries out "ṭiṭī. Generally, the acquisition of names for birds is based on the imitation of their sounds. As it was stated by the author of the *Nirukta*: "The word 'kāka' is an imitation of sound; this [phenomenon] is common among birds" (*Nir* 3.18). || 5.11 ||
The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāhva, the domestic cock, the sārasa, the rajjudāla, the dātyūha, the parrot, and the maina. 5.12

The *kalaviṅka* is stated in the *Nigamas* to be the village sparrow (*grāmacaṭaka*). Since its exclusion is already established by virtue of its being a village-dweller, its repeated prohibition is for the purpose of permitting the female sparrow (*caṭakā*). For this word [for male] is like the word "bull" (*vṛṣabha*).

Others, however, consider it to be for the purpose of excluding the wild [sparrow]. For they dwell in the forest during the rainy season. And because of their great numbers, they are called "village sparrows," just as wild buffaloes are [distinguished from domestic ones].

Since the prohibition of web-footed birds (*jālapāda*)—which includes the *plava*, *haṃsa*, and *cakravāka*—is already established by what will be stated later, the explicit mention [of these] here serves to make the prohibition absolute (*nitya*). Consequently, it follows that the eating of *āṭyā* and other such birds is permitted optionally (*vikalpena*). Regarding the village cock (*grāmakukkuṭa*): because of the inclusion of the word "village," the wild cock is permitted. But why might there be any doubt regarding the inedibility of the wild cock? For in another *Smṛti* it is recited: "The cock is the foremost among those that scratch for food" (*kukkuṭo vikirāṇām*, ĀpDh 1.17.32). Thus, since its inedibility would have been established without distinction, this specific statement makes known that the general prohibition applies only to particular cases.

Now, one might ask: why is there not an option (*vikalpa*) [between these two texts], since this treatise permits it and another treatise prohibits it without distinction? This is not a matter for an option. For an option arises only when there is a conflict between rules of equal force, and here no such conflict exists. Indeed, there is no difference in authority between these two *smṛtis*, because it is logical that a general rule should be restricted by a specific one; furthermore, it has been shown that even a third [text] from a different recension (*śākhā*) belongs to a single unified treatise.

If this is so, then it would also be logical that the prohibition of webbed feet applies only to specific cases such as swans and the like, rather than a general prohibition of all webbed-footed crows and others.

This would be so if this text were authorless (*apauruṣeya*). However, if it is authorless while having different authors, there is no purpose for the general statement (*sāmānya*) when it culminates merely in specific details such as the *haṃsa* birds. But if it has different authors—that is, if it is authored by persons—then ignorance regarding the particular may occur for one who perceives the general, and ignorance regarding the general may occur for one who perceives the particular. In the hypothesis that both [statements] have an authorial basis, one person’s cognition of the general is assumed to be based on the verbal testimony [of the first], and the other’s [cognition] regarding the particular is based on the verbal testimony [of the second]. Since these two belong to the Veda and are contained within different recensional branches (*śākhā*), it is logical that they constitute a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) despite the difference in the texts. Furthermore, there can be no objection against the Veda: "If it is restricted to the particular, what is the use of the general? For there is no author [to be questioned]. In that case, comprehension arises solely from what is heard, depending entirely upon the power of the word itself; one does not postulate a different meaning on the basis of some perceived purpose.
Rajjudāla and other such materials are to be obtained from fowlers. 5.12.
Pecking birds, web-footed birds, the koyaṣṭi, birds that scratch with their claws, fish-eating aquatic birds, meat from a slaughterhouse, and dried meat. (5.13)

Those who eat by pecking and striking with their beaks—this is the nature of these birds. "Peckers" refers to the *śatapatra* and others; "web-footed" refers to the *āṭya* and others. An option regarding them has been stated.

Now, it may be argued that where there is an option, activity proceeds according to one's desire in either case, and that [desire] remains present even regarding things that are not prohibited. For eating is a worldly matter, occurring only when there is a desire for it; it is not a scriptural matter, by virtue of which it would be mandatory. Therefore, we see no purpose in a prohibition of what is already optional.

It is said: This has already been answered. In cases where the comprehension of meaning arises from the word itself due to usage that is not preceded by conscious intent, this treatise is indeed human in origin; it was composed by the Teacher with a concentrated mind and great effort in order to condense the *Śatasāhasrikā*, wherein it would be impossible to employ anything meaningless. Therefore, the mention of the "Teacher" is inferred. However, [it is not the case that] when there is no prohibition of the *jālapāda* (web-footed bird), one prohibits its specific instance, the *haṃsa* (swan), by its own name. For this, too, is merely a matter of recollection (*smaraṇa*).

Others, however, read it as *anyena jālapādas tu*; this would be a careless reading. For it has been said that the intentions of the teachers are discerned through hints, gestures, or the composition of major sūtras, and a specific distinction is inferred here. By stating "one should not eat [fish] such as the *jālapāda*," he intends a general prohibition so that both [the specific and general rules] may be meaningful.

A *sūnā* is a place where animals are slaughtered for the purpose of selling their meat; some say it refers to a meat market. *Vallūra* is meat that has been dried and kept for a long time. *Nakhaviṣkira* refers to those that scatter [food] with their claws before eating, such as peacocks, cranes, and the like. However, because of the statement "in times of distress" (MDh 11.28), there is also an occasional permissibility for them to be eaten. For he (Āpastamba) recites: "Among the *vikira* birds, the cock... (ĀpDh 1.17.32). Furthermore, it cannot be said that this statement of Manu restricts itself solely to the cock, because that would result in the mention of the cock's name being rendered meaningless. (5.13)
The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, those that feed on fish, village pigs, and all kinds of fish. (5.14)

Since the prohibition [of eating] the *baka*, *balākā*, *kākolā*, and so forth is already established by the mention of "fish-eaters" (*matsyāda*), their repetition is for the purpose of providing an option regarding others. Even though they are not birds, crocodiles and the like are to be understood as inedible because they are included under the term "fish-eaters," since the word *matsyāda* is based on the action [of eating fish]. Furthermore, the *kākola* is the *śyena* (hawk/eagle), as it is well known in other regions; it is famously stated that "this is called such among the Bāhlīkas. From the prohibition of the village-pig (*viḍvarāha*), permission for the wild pig is implied. And the prohibition of the village-dweller [in the previous rule] should be understood as intended to qualify a specific type of bird within the context; for in this way, the mention of the "village-pig" here becomes meaningful. A village-dwelling boar is a *viḍvarāha*.

But surely, if by the context there the village-dwelling birds are understood, then here too it would be logical to understand only those birds that eat fish. Not so; for here there is no context concerning birds, since the purpose is to include even non-avian creatures such as village-pigs and fish. This is a general rule (*utsarga*); we shall state its exceptions (*apavāda*). (5.14)
Whoever eats the flesh of another is called an eater of that being's flesh; since an eater of fish is an eater of all flesh, one should therefore avoid fish. 5.15

This is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the preceding injunction prohibiting the eating of fish. Whoever eats the flesh belonging to a particular creature is designated by that act of eating its flesh; for example, a mongoose is called a "snake-eater" (*sarpāda*), a cat a "mouse-eater" (*mūṣakāda*), and so forth. One who eats fish, however, becomes an eater of all kinds of flesh; he is even rightly designated as a "beef-eater" (*gomāṃsāda*). Therefore, one should avoid fish because of this extreme censure. (5.15)
The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are the first two prescribed for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*);
likewise, the *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and all *saśalka* fish are permitted in every respect.

The *pāṭhīna* and *rohitā* are specific species of fish; their edibility is permitted for use in *havya* and *kavya* offerings, such as at *śrāddha* ceremonies and the like, but not in one's daily meal. Regarding the *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *saśalka* fish, there is no prohibition against eating them in any case, even apart from *havya* and *kavya*. Some maintain that *rājīva* refers to those with the color of a lotus (*padma*), while others hold that they are those which have stripes (*rājayaḥ*) or lines. *Siṃhatuṇḍas* are those whose mouths are shaped like a lion’s. *Saśalkas* are those covered in scales. (5.16)
One should not eat solitary animals or birds that are unknown, nor any five-toed creatures, even if they are among those designated as edible. (5.17)

"Moving alone" refers to snakes, owls, and others that wander by themselves. "Unknown" means unknown by name and by specific species. Regarding "wild animals and birds": wild animals (*mṛga*) and birds (*dvija*) are not to be eaten. Even among those listed as edible, those who are prohibited—provided they do not possess that [prohibited] nature—attain the status of being edible and thus become as if "listed among the edibles. However, there is no such thing as a formal listing of edible things. Rather, those who must be avoided because they are specifically unrecognizable, yet have fallen into the category of the edible, are described in this way as "listed even among the edibles. This also applies to five-toed animals such as monkeys, jackals, and so forth. The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of completing the meter. (5.17)

The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare—these they declare to be edible among five-toed animals, as well as those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel. (5.18)

Among five-toed animals, the porcupine (*śvāvit*) and others are edible; however, regarding the rhinoceros (*khaḍga*), there is an option according to another *Smṛti*. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "But regarding the rhinoceros, they disagree" (VaDh 14.47). With the exception of the camel, one-hoofed animals—such as cows, sheep, goats, and deer—are edible.

Now, since the edibility of the porcupine and other five-toed animals has been stated, the inedibility of others is established by implication; therefore, the prohibitory statement "all five-toed animals" (MDh 5.17) would be redundant.

This is not a fault. When a prohibition is made by means of the word "all," the understanding is clear. The understanding that other things are not to be eaten, which arises from the specification of particular foods that are to be eaten, is an inferential understanding; for in that way there would be prolixity. 5.18.
Having intentionally eaten a mushroom, a village pig, garlic, a village cock, an onion, or a leek, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]. (5.19)

*Chatrāka* refers to mushrooms. A *viḍvarāha* is a village pig that roams independently. Having eaten these, one becomes an outcast (*patita*); one must perform the penance for an outcast. And it will be stated: "The consumption of forbidden food and drink, along with six other acts, are equal to the drinking of liquor" (MDh 11.55). || 5.19 ||
Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance, or even the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa; for the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day.

If ministers eat six [forbidden things] unintentionally, even if they are among the six [specific items], there is no intention to imply their simultaneous consumption because the act of eating itself is the cause for the penance. Regarding the remaining forbidden foods, such as the exudations of red trees and so forth, if one eats them, one should not eat for one day and night (*ahorātra*). The word *ahaḥ* (day) is seen to be used for the night as well, as in: "The day is black and the day is white" (RV 6.9.1). Furthermore, regarding those things prohibited in this section where a specific penance will be stated elsewhere in the context of penances—such as "the carnivorous beast, the pig," etc. (MDh 11.155)—that very penance should be understood to apply there, because it is prescribed specifically for that case; whereas this fast finds its application elsewhere. (5.20)

An excellent twice-born man should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; however, for food known [to be impure], he must perform it specifically. (5.21)

This is stated regarding a Brāhmaṇa who eats in the house of a Śūdra whose food is unfit to be eaten by Brāhmaṇas. In the house of such a Śūdra, whatever foods exist that are not fit for Brāhmaṇas to eat and are not avoided from afar—if a Brāhmaṇa eats food in such a house, then, because of the suspicion of having consumed prohibited food, the performance of the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance is prescribed. We shall explain later that when there is an injunction without specific qualification, the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra is understood [to be the penance].
He speaks regarding the purification for food eaten unknowingly when there is suspicion of an unknown defect: "If he eats it while [the defect] exists, then for the sake of his purification...

Now, one might object: "But will he not state the purification for such a case later, saying: 'What is unseen is purified by water' (MDh 5.125)? We shall demonstrate its specific scope in that very place.
However, for a known defect, a specific expiation must be performed according to the particular rule prescribed for each individual case. 5.21.
"Commendable wild animals and birds may be slain by Brahmins for the sake of sacrifice, and indeed for the sustenance of their dependents; for so Agastya practiced in ancient times. (5.22)

The permission for violence is granted in connection with food. When one is excessively oppressed by hunger and no other food is available for one's dependents and others, the killing of wild animals and birds for food must be performed. "Dependents" have been explained previously. The mention of Agastya is for the sake of praise, as he acted in that manner. The first half-verse beginning with "for the sake of sacrifice" (*yajñārtham*) is merely an explanatory commendation (*arthavāda*), for in that case, killing is already established by being ordained in the direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). Those which are praised are those permitted as fit for consumption. This very same point is stated in detail in the following verse as an explanatory commendation regarding ritual action (*karmārthavāda*). (5.22)
For in ancient times, during the sacrifices of the ṛṣis and the rites of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) consisted of the edible flesh of wild animals and birds. (5.23)

The *Sattra* known as the *Ṣaṭtriṃśatsaṃvatsara* (the thirty-six-year session) prescribes the killing of wild animals and birds; this [text] reiterates that. The *Brāhmaṇa* on that subject states: "When the day has concluded, the *Gṛhapati* goes out hunting; whatever wild animals he kills there, their vital strength (*tarasa*) becomes their sacrificial portions (*puroṣāśā*)" (ĀpŚ 23.11.12–13). Because it is an *arthavāda* (explanatory passage), there is no intention to express actual factuality through the past tense (*babhūvuḥ*). Therefore, they exist even today, as do they in the *Purāṇas*. This statement regarding the *Purāṇas* is intended to show that it is not merely the case that some practice of *Sattras* exists today; however, it does not mean that if someone were to perform all of them today, this rule would not apply to them. Alternatively, for one who is personally unable to understand the meaning of the scripture and proceeds solely by the consensus of others, according to the maxim "the path is that which the great men have trodden" (MBh 3. App. 32.68), this is said: "in the *Purāṇas*. This duty is not something new; rather, it is beginningless. The ancient sages (*ṛṣis*) were certain Brahmins perfected through austerity, or perhaps beings of a different class (*jātyantara*), as described in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts. One should not insist here: "If the sages are of a different class, like the *Gandharvas* and so forth, how can they have the right to participate in sacrifices? For this is an *arthavāda* which is understood through whatever basis is appropriate. The *brahmakṣatrasavās* are the sacrifices of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas. || 5.23 ||
Whatever food, whether solid or soft, is mixed with oil or fat and is not forbidden—even if it has stood overnight—it may be eaten, as may whatever remains from an oblation. (5.24)

Whatever food is mixed with oil (*sneha*)—whether it be *bhakṣya* (food to be chewed and swallowed) such as meat, or *bhojya* (food to be eaten) such as boiled rice (*odana*)—is to be understood here as distinct from the other, even though *bhukti* and *bhuj* have the same meaning, because they are mentioned separately. It must be "unreproachable," meaning it has not turned sour. That may be eaten even if it is stale (*paryuṣita*). By "stale" is meant that which has been kept overnight; even that which was prepared on the previous day becomes stale on the following day. Regarding the phrase "mixed with oil": a doubt arises here. Does this mean that when something like a vegetable dish mixed with sauce has become stale while being combined with oil, that stale food should be eaten? Or does it mean that even for dry food that has become stale, one must add oil at the time of eating? [In other words,] even stale cakes and the like should be eaten by mixing them with oil at the time of the meal.

Regarding this, a doubt arises: "That which is mixed with oil is said to be edible, even if it has stood overnight (*paryuṣita*). Here, the phrase "mixed with oil" (*snehasaṃyukta*) is being referred to as the subject (*uddiśyamāna*), and not as that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). For its connection with the word *tat* (that) is not heard [in the text] such that [the meaning would be]: "That which has stood overnight, if it is mixed with oil, is to be eaten."

It is said: The statement regarding those remnants of sacrificial oblations (*haviḥśeṣa*) that have stood overnight and are not mixed with fat would be meaningless; for it is impossible for them to remain overnight if they are mixed with fat. Thus, the statement becomes meaningful only if their mixing with fat is not required at the time of eating. Therefore, the purposefulness of the statement lies in its reference to the time of eating itself, by way of disregarding the mixing with fat.

Even if this is so, there is still no doubt. Because the specific term is purposeful, it is logical that the word "conjoined with fat" (*snehasaṃyukta*) has the status of being the object to be enjoined. It is replied: this much is the seed of doubt here. Since the connection as it is heard [in the text] is stronger, one might think: "Let the term 'remnant of the oblation' (*haviḥśeṣa*) be a restatement (*anuvāda*); rather, let the connection with fat be made with whatever has become stale, so that it does not fall into meaninglessness. In that case, because of the resulting meaninglessness, the assumption of a remote connection would be superior. The determination is based on established practice (*samācāra*). Ghee, oil, muscle-fat, and marrow are "fats" (*sneha*). (5.24)
Even if it has been stored for a long time, all products derived from barley and wheat, as well as preparations of milk, are pure when not mixed with oil, according to the twice-born. (5.25)

"Long-stored" means kept for two nights or more. Because of the word "api" (even/also), the term "anointed with oil" (*snehākta*) should also be connected here; this refers to barley, wheat, groats, cakes, and so forth, even when anointed with oil. "Transformations of milk" (*payaso vikriyā*) refers to products such as curd, buttermilk, and the like. (5.25)
Thus has been declared, in its entirety, what is fit and unfit to be eaten by the twice-born;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.

By the first half-verse, he delimits the preceding section. The purpose of this demarcation between sections is that this section which has just been introduced applies to the twice-born and not to Śūdras, whereas what will be stated hereafter applies to Śūdras as well.

Therefore, the specific manner regarding the consumption of meat will be explained; furthermore, the fruit resulting from its avoidance accrues to the Śūdra as well. Otherwise, because the rule "these are not to be eaten by the twice-born" (MDh 5.5) would establish a qualification for the twice-born alone, the Śūdra would have the freedom to eat meat just as he does with garlic and other forbidden items.

If it is argued that, in this way, the edibility of meat remaining after the worship of gods and others will be stated—according to [Manu Smṛti] 5.32: "Having worshipped the gods and the ancestors, one does not incur sin by eating meat"—then [the answer is]: the worship of gods and others must be performed with pure meat. Those wild animals and birds that are forbidden for the twice-born are impure; therefore, since it is impossible to perform the worship of gods with their meat, and because what remains from such [forbidden] sources is inedible, there are other distinctions of context as well. For example, those wild animals and birds forbidden for Brāhmaṇas and others become forbidden for the Śūdra as well, though by a different mode. In that case, nothing is said by way of a distinction of context regarding the prohibition of garlic and the like; the prohibition of garlic and so forth does not apply to the Śūdra.

There is indeed a purpose for this distinction in the context: lest the Śūdra be entitled to the prohibition of garlic and similar items. Since even in the case of meat, the householder has the entitlement for the worship of the gods and others, whereas for the non-householder Śūdra there is freedom of choice (*yathākāmyam*).

But surely, the Śūdra’s entitlement to the *pākayajña* is already established, and eating is prescribed for householders; yet *pākayajñas* are not performed with garlic and such things. Consequently, garlic and the like would not be edible for the Śūdra at will either. What is the fault [in this]?
The mention of "twice-born" is redundant.

This has already been addressed: for one who is not a householder or for one who is away from home, there is freedom of action (*kāmacāra*). Furthermore, it is not the case that a householder must never eat what has not been offered in sacrifice (*ahuta*). The meaning of the rule "one should be an eater of remnants" (*śeṣabhuk*, MDh 3.107) is this: one should not eat unless the rite of *vaiśvadeva* has been performed. In that context, only that substance which serves as the means for the sacrifice is pure and fit to be offered. Others, however, bring food from somewhere at the time of eating or eat from the kitchen; even that, though it is not the remnant of an offering, is not prohibited. Regarding meat, however, there is a specific restriction due to the explicit statement: "that which has not been used by the gods should never be eaten."
If the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) were eligible for this [rite], then that which will be stated later in the section on the *śuddhavidhi*—namely, "of all four castes" (MDh 5.57)—would be redundant.
We shall explain its purpose in that very context.
Furthermore, if the twice-born (*dvijāti*) were not mentioned previously, it would follow that even dog-meat and the like would be permissible food for a Śūdra.

However, we shall demonstrate in the eleventh chapter that the three verses beginning with "Of the village pig, the donkey, and the camel" (MDh 11.153–55) indicate that these are not to be eaten even by a Śūdra. || 5.26 ||
One may eat meat that has been consecrated by sprinkling, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas, or when one is engaged in a rite according to the rules, or when there is a danger to one's life. (5.27)
In the context of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, the meat remaining after the oblation is figuratively called "sprinkled" (prokṣita).

But surely the word *prokṣita* is etymological (*yaugika*), based on the causal activity of washing derived from the root *ukṣ*, meaning "to sprinkle. Thus, it is used everywhere in connection with that action, as in "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters," "The clarified butter is to be sprinkled (*prokṣaṇīya*)," and "You have been agitated by the *prokṣaṇī* waters. If it refers to the instrument of sprinkling, then how could it—being based on Vedic consecration (*saṃskāra*)—apply to meat through the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of its connection to the animal? And why resort to secondary indication when bypassing the primary meaning of the word? Therefore, it is logical that it means "washed" with water and so forth.

True, this would be so if there were no other supplementary sentences or explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "meat that has not been consecrated" (YDh 1.170) and "animals not consecrated with mantras" (MDh 5.36). Therefore, by considering those [passages], this very meaning is established. If that is the case, since it is already proven by those [texts], what is the purpose of this?

Some say this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). This cannot be an injunction (*vidhi*) for eating meat at will, because such activity is already established by the desire for gain in one who seeks to counteract hunger. An injunction is defined as that which prompts activity in a person when no activity would otherwise occur due to a visible purpose—for example: "One should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice as long as one lives. In matters where scripture alone is the authority—where it is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that "when this is done, this desired result is accomplished; or, if it is not done, this harm ensues"—there scripture is sought. However, where there is no such understanding from other sources and the matter is within the exclusive domain of scripture alone, that is called an injunction (*vidhi*). In the present case, however, even infants who suckle at the breast understand without instruction that nourishment arises from eating and that suffering is thereby removed. Furthermore, this cannot be a restrictive rule (*niyama*), because its specific form is not determined. If it were a restrictive rule in the sense that "one must eat only consecrated (*prokṣita*) meat," then, due to the absence of any limitation regarding time, one would have to sit eating incessantly, even during times for food and recreation. Thus, an impossible requirement would have been taught. As it is said: "One who does not eat at a funeral feast (*śrāddha*)" and "on the very day he realizes [the fault]. Moreover, the author of the *Mahābhāṣya* has stated that a restrictive rule is a particular kind of injunction. And since an injunction is impossible here, how can there be a restrictive rule? Furthermore, what is consecrated by one person could not be obtained by another. Therefore, this interpretation is untenable. If, on the other hand, it is a preclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) meaning "only consecrated meat" (i.e., "not unconsecrated"), this is also incorrect. For a preclusive injunction is characterized by the simultaneous or successive engagement in an action after abandoning the consumption of both the consecrated and the unconsecrated, so that hunger might be relieved. Even so, the prohibition "meats not offered in sacrifice" (*anupākṛta-māṃsāni*, Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.170) already establishes this point.

Others, however, formulate this objection against that very position: if there were a prohibition of all un-consecrated [animals] without distinction, it would follow that birds (*śakuni*) are also prohibited. Yet, since there is no specific prescription for consecration regarding those [birds], and because there is an absence of any remedial measure for them, there is no authoritative basis for adopting such a specific restriction.
They consider this to be incorrect; for if that were the case, the prohibition of birds would follow by way of a distinct sequence, as that [sequence] is indicative.

Therefore, it is logical that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the rule regarding the eating of sprinkled meat as an auxiliary to the *Śruti-karman* (the ritual of hearing the Veda), serving as an illustrative example: just as in a sacrifice eating is mandatory and non-eating constitutes a transgression of the scripture, so it is with the subsequent occasions as well. If it is a restatement, let there also be a requirement for exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). By the statement, "One should not eat the unsprinkled meat of cows, sheep, or goats," this very nature of [forbidden] meat that has not been consecrated (*anupākṛta*) is restated; its purpose is to authorize even the unsprinkled meat on specific occasions such as when desired by a Brāhmaṇa.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase “even meat that is unoffered and useless” (*anarcitaṃ vṛthāmāṃsam api*, MDh 4.213), this is intended for the sake of defining what is meant by the term “useless meat” (*vṛthāmāṃsa*) occurring in the fourth verse; otherwise, it would not be understood what that “useless meat” is. Alternatively, while in one case there is an instruction for the eater, in the other case—having made a distinction—it means that the meat belonging to one who has not performed the worship of the gods and others must not be eaten even by another, such as a guest. For guests and others in another's house are entitled to the worship of the gods with that person’s meat, even if they themselves are not authorized to perform the worship of the gods and so forth. However, if [the worship] has been performed after making the offering, then he is fit to eat it. But the second prohibition, “the gods and the ancestors” (MDh 5.32), is for the purpose of forbidding the eating of meat by those who are authorized in their own homes but have failed to perform the rites. As for the statement, “animals not consecrated with mantras” (MDh 5.36), that refers to the meaning of the word *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling/sacrificial preparation). Thus, all five prohibitory statements have been shown to have distinct meanings.

"And by the desire of Brāhmaṇas. *Kāmyā* means desire or wish; the word *kāmyā* is a Vedic (archaic) form. When this permission applies even to unsprinkled [meat] for Brāhmaṇas and others, then what is the nature of this rule? Is it that there is a transgression of the scripture (*śāstra*) in not eating it, or is it merely a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*)? If it were a counter-exception, then from the statement "one should eat at a wedding" (*vivāhe punar bhoktavyam*), it would follow that the prohibition does not apply during a wedding.
However, eating is not mandatory for its own sake; rather, if the Brāhmaṇas are venerable persons, then it is not proper to disregard their word.

Others, however, following the word *brāhmaṇānām* from the verse beginning with *krītvādi* (MDh 5.32), maintain that there is even a rule for the meat of hares and other such animals. They hold that at sacrifices, weddings, and other occasions such as communal feasts (*goṣṭhī*), if Brāhmaṇas request it, then their meat is not prohibited in its essential nature when dedicated to the gods; rather, under specific circumstances, acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and worship of the deities must be performed. Only the specific [forbidden] details are prohibited. Since this is permitted on account of the desire of the Brāhmaṇas, permission is granted even for that which is subject to the prohibition beginning with "flesh-eating birds" (MDh 5.14), provided one has made the resolve that "abstinence yields great fruit" (MDh 5.11). This applies whether the meat has been sprinkled or not, and whether the worship of the deity has been performed or not.

But when one is enjoined according to the prescribed rule, even in the event of the loss of life, and when enjoined at the *madhuparka* and the *śrāddha*, one may eat even without sprinkling [with water]. For this is the injunction according to the scriptures; regarding the *śrāddha*, the rules have already been stated: "When invited according to the rule," and "If he transgresses in any way" (MDh 3.180). Having accepted the invitation, "I shall eat at the *śrāddha*," one is not permitted to say, "I will not eat this," with the exception of things that are unfit to be eaten, things that cause impurity, or things that produce disease. Since the *haviṣya* (sacrificial food) has been prescribed, whatever is fit to be eaten and is pleasing should be given, provided it is not disagreeable. Therefore, this statement applies specifically to the *madhuparka*.
Is it not the case that there is no mandatory rule regarding the *madhuparka*?

There is a restriction stating that one worthy of the *madhuparka* must eat it, but this is not an injunction (*vidhi*) for the *madhuparka* itself. For he alone is authorized in that matter, not others such as kings and so forth. Just as the restriction of the householder is seen in the rule, "He should not dwell in [the householder's] home without eating" (MDh 3.95), by this it is understood that [the guest] should not be given [food] when he does not intend to stay. As for those who hold that there is freedom of action (*kāmacāra*) in this regard—namely, that the guest eats upon receiving honor—it is not the case that the ritual act is for his sake.
But is it not true that hospitality (*ātithya*) itself is non-obligatory (*anitya*)?

True. It is observed that the performance of the rite for the sake of *dharma* produces pleasure; therefore, for the giver, it serves exclusively the purpose of *dharma* as prescribed by the rule. For indeed, in the case of the release of the cow, it is ordained: "The *madhuparka* shall not be without meat.
If it is argued that this statement also has the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) as its subject, let it be so;
this too is a restatement (*anuvāda*), as in the previous cases, regarding both the *śrāddha* and the office of the priest.

But has it not been stated regarding the office of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) that the consumption of the *iḍā* and other portions belongs to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), such that there is a rule based on scripture for him, but not for the priests? True; however, if the priests do not consume [their shares], they are censured and become joined with an unseen fault (*adṛṣṭa-doṣa*), even though it is unknown.

Now, let it be granted that for those [priests] who are authorized, there is the eating [of meat]; for they are not joined with the fruit of the ritual action. Indeed, a servant and the like, having been hired, performs the prescribed items. And it is prescribed: "The *ṛtvij*s, with the sacrificer as the fifth, eat the *iḍā*. Therefore, since their eating is established by that [text], it is logical that for those who have accepted the office of priest (*ārtvijya*), the eating is mandatory and is thus restated here. For there is no scriptural connection regarding the eating of those who eat at a *śrāddha* or of the priests. If it is asked, "For what purpose is this a restatement (anuvāda) of the sacrificer alone?", [we reply: a restatement does not require a further purpose. Rather, something already established is stated here. Here too, when the cowherd has accepted the honor of the cow-slaughter, he must necessarily eat; for the sake of favoring him, he awaits this *madhuparka* honor. Therefore, that prior rite must be performed by him. Otherwise, because of the absence of the preliminary [act], the favor would not be accomplished through an incomplete *madhuparka*; thus, even in the case of eating meat that is otherwise prohibited, the *madhuparka* honor and the office of priest must be accepted first, as well as the feeding of Brahmins. And also in the event of the loss of life: because the context refers to the worship of the gods and others, when there is no other food available due to illness or hunger, and there is a danger to one's survival, one may eat the meat of cows, goats, and sheep. For instance, the mantra says: [Mantra follows] ...so it is said. Thus, there is no fault in eating meat when life is at stake. However, this applies only to the meat of cows, goats, and sheep; the meat of other animals must never be eaten. As stated: "The meat of animals other than these three is unfit for consumption. "Those worlds called 'non-divine' are shrouded in blind darkness;
to them go after death those people who are slayers of the Self. (Īśa Upaniṣad 3)

Even for a *brahmacārin*, the consumption [of meat] is permitted when life is at risk. For that very person, there shall be an expiation prescribed by scripture (*vācanika-prāyaścitta*) on account of his state of childhood and so forth, as it is said: "But a *brahmacārin* who should ever eat honey or meat" (MDh 11.157). Vyāsa states (VeSū 3.4.28) that when there is a danger of loss of life due to hunger, even the eating of forbidden meat is permitted. By the example of the tail-tendon (*jāghanī*), this is intended to apply to a single day. However, in the case of a disease that has already passed, it is not possible to know with certainty, "He will certainly live by eating this. In such a case, the eating of forbidden meat, such as that of domestic fowl and the like, is not permitted. But because the context concerns one who is devoid of the sprinkling of water (*prokṣaṇa*) and the worship of deities, there is indeed permission. Furthermore, the eating of meat is not only intended for the purpose of curing an arisen disease; rather, for those who are emaciated, wasting away, afflicted, or weak, the eating of meat is invariably permitted at all times.
Constantly devoted to women and wine, they are wasting away, emaciated by fatigue and disease;
constantly consuming meat and broth, they are both afflicted and weak.

However, even with goat meat that has not been sprinkled [with water], the worship of the deities and others must certainly be performed by them; but if it is impossible, there is no fault on some other day. || 5.27 ||
Prajāpati ordained all this as food for the vital breath (prāṇa): both the stationary and the moving; everything is the sustenance of the vital breath. 5.28

The *prāṇa* is the air within the belly, which constitutes the seed of the living being (*jīva*). For the sake of maintaining the body, Prajāpati fashioned this entire world as food for the fivefold movement of *prāṇa*, beginning with *udāna*. Having indicated it generally by the word "this," he specifies it further as "the stationary and the moving. For this reason, everything is the food of *prāṇa*. Because the second use of the word "all" (*sarva*)—following the specific enumeration of animals, humans, reptiles, and so forth—is not redundant; since Prajāpati has ordained everything as food for *prāṇa* in times of distress, therefore all this is its food. And thus it is heard in the *Prāṇasaṃvāda Upaniṣad*: "He said, 'What shall be my food? 'Whatever there is here, down to dogs and down to worms and moths. (ChU 5.2.1) [5.28]
The immobile are the food of the mobile; those without fangs are the food of those with fangs; the handless are the food of those with hands; and the timid are the food of the brave. (5.29)

Moving creatures such as hawks, mongooses, and others, who are engaged in the exertion of seizing their prey by pouncing upon them, have non-moving creatures such as snakes and pigeons as their food. Likewise, for fanged predators like lions and tigers, deer such as the ruru and the pṛṣata, which lack fangs, serve as food. For handless beings such as snakes and fish, those with hands—such as mongooses and hunters—are food. For the brave, who possess great energy and are indifferent to life, the timid, who cling to life and possess little courage, are killed to serve as food. (5.29)
The eater is not defiled by eating the creatures that are his food, even day after day; for both the eaters and the creatures to be eaten were created by the Creator himself. (5.30)

The self (*ātman*) is the eater; [the term] *ādya* refers to those living beings that are capable of being eaten. By eating them every day, one does not incur sin; for by the Creator, Prajāpati himself, both the eaters and the edible have been created. Therefore, in the event of a life-threatening emergency, meat must certainly be consumed—this is the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for this injunction consisting of three verses (5.30).
"The eating of meat for the sake of sacrifice—this is remembered as the divine ordinance; any practice other than this is called the demonic ordinance. (5.31)

The eating of meat, such as the *piṇḍa* and *prāśitra* portions, for the sake of sacrifice is "eating"; this is the divine ordinance, ordained by the gods. However, otherwise, the inclination toward eating meat for the purpose of nourishing the body is the demonic ordinance; the persistence of *piśācas* in consuming meat is thus a matter of reproach. (5.31)
Having purchased it, or having produced it oneself, or even having received it from another, one does not incur fault by eating meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors. (5.32)

This treatise concerns the meat of wild animals and birds. There is no fault for one who eats the meat of the *ruru*, *pṛṣata*, and other deer, as well as the *śaśaka* (rabbit), *kapiñjala* (partridge), and others, provided he has performed worship of the gods and the ancestors (*pitṛs*). Just as in the home, after the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites have been performed, there is the eating of rice and other foods even without a separate *vaiśvadeva* offering, such is not the case with meat. It is for this purpose that it is stated again: "having worshipped the gods and the ancestors. Otherwise, for a householder, the meal would already take that form [by default]. "To the gods" means that the meat is to be cast into a pure place while designating it with that word. Or else, the worship of the gods must be performed by addressing: "To Agni, to Vāyu, to Sūrya, to Jātavedas. Such offerings made in the fire do not occur elsewhere than where one possesses a sacred fire (*agni*). Furthermore, the *baliharaṇa* (offering of oblations) must not be performed without an offering into the fire, because it has been established as a distinct rite and a distinct application. Let this matter rest for now.

Others, however, say that *śrāddha* is the worship (*arcana*) of the ancestors. Indeed, the practice of worship is observed in the context of *śrāddha*, and they refer to the ancestors as "gods. Consequently, all the authors of the *Smṛtis* have prescribed only the *śrāddha* rite itself, and not any other ritual action.

But how can there be the possibility of purchasing meat? For if meat were purchased from a marketplace, it would become the meat of a butchered animal (*sauna*). The meat of an animal that has died naturally and was not killed by butchers is unfit for consumption because it does not promote health.

It is said: [meat] brought by hunters, fowlers, and the like, will be purchased. And they are not known as *saunika*s (butchers), for it is when [the meat] has been brought to the house by them while wandering for the purpose of sale that a purchase is possible; indeed, that is not called *sauna* (butcher’s meat).
Or, having produced it oneself: a Brāhmaṇa by begging, a Kṣatriya by the act of hunting. (5.32)

A twice-born man who knows the rules should not eat meat contrary to the injunctions when no distress exists; for having eaten meat contrary to the injunctions, he becomes a ghost and is helplessly devoured by those very creatures. (5.33)

The "non-injunction" (*avidhi*) refers to that eating which occurs at intervals from the remnants of the worship of gods and others mentioned previously, or on account of the desires of Brahmins and so forth; one should not eat meat by such means. This is a restatement of what has already been said. [Objection: Even in times of distress when life is at risk, the worship of gods and others is not required, for this too has indeed been stated as a cause [for eating]. Therefore, this is actually an injunction (*vidhi*), not a non-injunction. [Response: True. However, because of the connection with the *prokṣita* (sprinkled/sacrificial) meat, there might be a suspicion that only the cow, sheep, and goat are intended there; thus, it is stated "not in times of distress" (*anāpadi*) in order to grant permission regarding the hare and other such animals.

[102] One who is intent upon the performance of prescribed duties is called "one who knows the rules" (*vidhijña*). Likewise, even in the case of worldly performance, the verb *jānāti* (he knows) is used figuratively; people employ it for one intent on performance, saying, "This person knows that."

Regarding this discourse on the results [of action]: having eaten [flesh] for an unscriptural motive, the deceased (preta)—meaning one who has died—is helplessly devoured by those very creatures. By whatever object [of desire] someone eats the flesh of certain beings, that person undergoes manifold suffering; this is merely the extent of the meaning. Otherwise, people generally eat the flesh of goats and the like, yet goats and such are not themselves meat-eaters. Alternatively, it is said that because of the sin committed by eating that [flesh], even while being devoured by carnivorous beasts, one is as if being devoured by them. (5.33)
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as great as that which accrues after death to one who eats meat in vain. (5.34)
The meaning of this verse is well known. || 5.34 ||
But that man who, when duly appointed according to the rule, does not eat meat, goes after death to the state of a beast for twenty-one births. (5.35)

Regarding "occasions" (saṃbhavāt), which means births: if one does not perform the worship of the gods when there is a certain risk to one's life, yet nevertheless eats meat, he certainly incurs fault. 5.35.
A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated by mantras;
however, abiding by the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated by mantras. (5.36)

In the animal sacrifice (paśubandha), purificatory rites such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and others, accompanied by mantras, are prescribed; one may eat the meat of those animals for whom these rites are performed, provided they are remnants of Vedic sacrifices. "Eternal" (śāśvata) means constant or Vedic; "established" (āsthita) means resorted to. (5.36)
In times of distress, one may perform a sacrifice with clarified butter as the victim, or likewise with a victim made of flour;
however, one should never desire to kill an animal in vain.

If they should think: "In the Sītā-yajña, Khaṇḍi-yajña, Caṇḍikā-yāga, and other such rituals where custom is the authority, the slaughter of animals is proper for one desiring a specific result, for it is observed that an abundant harvest results from making offerings involving the slaughter of animals," then, in order to refute this, he says: "In connection with"—that is, in the context of the slaughter of animals—“one should perform the ghee-animal sacrifice; indeed, one should perform only the ghee-animal sacrifice. When one ought to sacrifice with an animal, one should worship the deities in its place with ghee, for that is a sacrificial substance in general. Alternatively, having fashioned a flour-animal—an image made of flour—one should offer it to the deities, or having prepared cakes and the like from flour.
How can this animal sacrifice be in vain?

It is said: The conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭas*) is authoritative, but not that of women and *śūdras*, because they lack Vedic knowledge. In this case, it is impossible to postulate a basis in the Vedas; for they perform these acts at that time solely for the purpose of propitiating deities. Moreover, Vedic rituals do not exist for the purpose of propitiating deities, since the deity is mentioned only as a subordinate factor (*guṇatvena*). Furthermore, they maintain here that [the practice] is based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), thinking, "The attainment of results is seen through the sacrifice of animals and the making of vows. Therefore, there is no basis in the Vedas. Even positive and negative concomitance are mere illusion, due to frequent instances of deviation.
Therefore, this verse was recited by the Teacher out of kindness as a mere restatement of a meaning already established by logic. (5.37)
As many hairs as there are on the animal's body,
so many times does the one who slaughters an animal in vain undergo death after death in future births.

One who kills animals in vain—that is, one who performs the slaughter of animals not enjoined by the *Śruti* or *Smṛti*—undergoes as many returns to birth as there were such killings. And this refers to that which is performed by worldly people on occasions such as the Mahānavamī festival; for the form "paśughna" is a Vedic (chāndasa) formation using the suffix *kap*. (5.38)
"Beasts were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice; sacrifice is for the prosperity of this entire world. Therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing. (5.39)

This fault just mentioned does not apply to killing enjoined by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. That killing which constitutes a limb of the sacrifice—for the sake of its accomplishment alone were animals created and produced by the Self-born Prajāpati. "By himself" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). For this entire world, the sacrifice—such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and others—is for prosperity; "prosperity" means abundance, nourishment, and expansion. Therefore, that killing which occurs therein should be understood as non-killing. It is said thus because of the cessation of the sin born of violence. (5.39)
Herbs, animals, trees, beasts, and likewise birds—having met their end for the sake of sacrifice, they attain higher states once again. (5.40)
But how is it that there is no fault of violence in a sacrifice?

It is said: Violence is indeed a great harm to the victim, because through the loss of life—and through the loss of children, wife, wealth, power, and so forth—there arises every kind of misfortune, and because the ripening of the fruit of that evil deed, such as rebirth in hell and the like, is imminent immediately thereafter. In a sacrifice, however, there is benefit for those who are slain, not harm, because the fruit of hell and the like does not arise; for those who have met their end and undergone destruction in a sacrifice attain heights of excellence—namely, birth among the gods or *gandharvas* by caste, or birth in other continents such as *Uttarakuru*, or in other regions.

And this is a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). For no injunction (*vidhi*) is heard here, since there is a teaching in the present tense in the words “they obtain. Nor is it appropriate to derive an injunction from an explanatory statement—as in the case of the phrase “they become established”—because of the absence of another injunction and because such a derivation is impossible.

All of this is supplementary to the prohibition against eating meat not prepared according to rule. This prohibition is also established for the sake of this world: "But one should never desire to kill an animal in vain" (MDh 5.37). And as for the permission, "Animals were created for the sake of sacrifice" (MDh 5.39), all of that is understood as being within the context of the prohibition against eating [meat]. Likewise, he will state later: "Without having caused injury to living beings... (MDh 5.48), and so forth.

Furthermore, there is no possibility of an injunction in this case. No qualification for action is possible for animals, because they lack specific discernment (*viśeṣavijñāna*). Nor can one who lacks qualification be an agent. And if one is not an agent, the production of a fruit from a scriptural rite does not occur. For in this matter, the production of a fruit does not happen through the inherent nature of things (*vastusvābhāvya*) as seen in the world—for example, poison certainly produces its own effect even when drunk by one who is ignorant [of its nature]. Scriptural matters do not function in that way.

Furthermore, because plants and the like lack consciousness (*acaitanya*), the analogy of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) does not apply. Indeed, it is observed that the fruit of a certain rite accrues to the priests even when the action is instigated by another, as in the passage beginning, "He who desires: 'May I become more wicked'" (cf. *GoB* 2.3.3). In that case, since there is no status as a supplement to another injunction and because the understanding of the injunction is clear, and since the scripture concerns human eligibility, the eligibility based on the performance of the subsidiary acts is appropriate as a literal (*vācanika*) entitlement limited to that extent—just as a penance is prescribed for a Brahmin at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of another's horse sacrifice. However, it has been stated that in the present case, there is no eligibility at all.

Herbs are *darbha* grass and the like; animals are goats and the like; trees are objects of worship; and birds—though not considered animals (*apaśu*)—are nonetheless designated as "animals" (*paśu*) when enjoined as sacrificial offerings (*havis*), as in the injunction: "He sacrifices *kapiñjala* birds" (VS 24.20). Furthermore, oxen are designated as "animals" in rites such as the *vājapeya* because they carry burdens; although there is no actual slaughter (*nidhana*) of them in those cases, the term "slaughter" is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote the suffering they endure.
