Birds are *kapiñjala* and the like; although they too are spoken of as "animals," their usage in that sense is less common, as seen in the passage: "There are seven domestic animals and seven wild animals" (ŚB 9.5.2.8). Cows and the like are non-avian animals. Alternatively, the distinction between "animals" (*paśu*) and "cattle" (*go*) may be understood as being like the relationship between "cattle" and "bulls" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). 5.40.
He shows, in brief, whatever acts of violence are enjoined by the scriptures:
"In the honey-mixture (madhuparka), in a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or the gods—it is only here that animals may be slain, and nowhere else," so Manu has declared. (5.41)
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas, when killing animals for these purposes, leads both himself and the animal to the highest state. (5.42)

The *madhuparka* has been explained; therein, the slaughter of a cow is prescribed. Sacrifice refers to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and others; therein, the slaughter of animals in the *ekādaśinī* and other rites, as well as the *nirūḍhapaśubandha* and so forth, is performed independently. Regarding that which has the ancestors as its deity (*pitṛdaivata*)—meaning a rite such as the *aṣṭakā* where the ancestors are the deities—it does not refer to the *śrāddha*. For that [the *śrāddha*] is prescribed with prepared meat, and the slaughter of an animal is not enjoined there. Nor is it appropriate for this [verse] alone to be the injunction, because violence is not enjoined in the original production (*utpatti*) of the *śrāddha*, whereas this [verse] is a clear injunction; furthermore, it could be understood as referring even to the slaughter of an animal at the *aṣṭakā*, and if it were an independent injunction, it would entail the assumption of a separate source (*mūla-kalpanā*), and it will be stated later that it is a supplement to another injunction. However, according to the view of some, the rite of the ancestors and the gods refers to the *Mahāyajña* and others. The slaughter of animals—which was not previously established—for the sake of the livelihood of dependents, such as "they are to be killed by Brāhmaṇas... for the sake of the livelihood of servants" (MDh 5.22), is permitted in times of distress when life is at stake. (5.41–42)
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress. (5.43)

This is a prohibition against violence not ordained by the Veda; nor is that which is ordained by the Veda permitted here. Furthermore, for a student (*brahmacārin*) living with his teacher or for one performing austerities in the forest, there is no other form of violence [except self-neglect]. It might occur in the case of a student who has broken his vow (*avakīrṇin*), but for a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), it does not exist at all. Even for a student, the neglect of oneself is certainly not desired. Therefore, this is indeed a mandatory injunction regarding the *śrāddha*; the mention of "at home" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).

If this were a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), what would be the basis for the phrases "in the forest" and "even in times of distress"? Furthermore, there is no animal sacrifice for a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), even one who maintains the sacred fires. Some say that we shall demonstrate this under the verse beginning with "sacrificial cakes and cooked offerings" (MDh 6.11). However, the Teacher says: [the prohibition] is appropriate for the student (*brahmacārin*). But as for the forest-dweller, since the abandonment of life is even prescribed for him by the passage beginning with "or having gone to the Aparājitā [direction]" (MDh 6.31), it will be explained more clearly in that very place that for him there is no violence for the sake of livelihood.
But surely this prohibition is stated for when one has fallen into [such a situation]; so why is permission explained in that very same context?

True; otherwise, nothing would have been accomplished by this [rule]. If it is argued that it is for the sake of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), then even for an explanatory praise, a basis must be sought. Therefore, this prohibition is not applicable in times of distress, and the injunction is not contradicted when such distress exists. Because there are many varieties of distress, the engagement [in eating] with the thought that "there will be monthly or fortnightly food during a minor distress" is forbidden. However, when one has the thought, "I cannot live if I do not eat right now," or when an assailant (*ātatāyin*) with raised weapon has approached, then permission is granted in times of distress. In this way, the Vedic injunction, "One should protect oneself from all [harm]" (GDh 9.34), is upheld. 5.42–43.
One should know that the violence ordained by the Vedas, which is restricted to this world of moving and unmoving beings, is indeed non-violence; for from the Veda, dharma has shone forth.

That killing of living beings which is ordained by the Vedas is eternal and beginningless in this world of moving and unmoving things, both stationary and sentient. However, that which consists of the Tantras and similar systems is of recent origin, arising from the error of [failing to distinguish between] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Therefore, one should understand Vedic injury to be non-injury itself, because there is no transgression in the hereafter. It is called "non-injury" in terms of its result (*kāryataḥ*), not in terms of its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*). But surely it is that very same thing which has the form of injury? Since there is no difference [between them], how can there be a difference in their results?

It is said: For indeed, Dharma shone forth from the Veda. Any exposition of Dharma and Adharma originates solely from the Veda, because human-authored works lack authority. Furthermore, the Veda itself makes known in certain places that [Dharma] is the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Nor is there an identity of nature between them, because they differ in being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and because they proceed from different intentions. In the case of worldly action, one engages out of desire for meat or out of hatred; but in the case of Vedic action, one engages because it is enjoined by the scripture as being for the sake of the sacrifice.
He shone forth completely; that is to say, he attained full manifestation. || 5.44 ||
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or even dead. (5.45)

The letter "a" here should be understood as being elided for the purpose of negation. Since it is the non-violent ones who are prohibited, there is no prohibition against [the killing of] snakes, tigers, and the like. 5.45.
He who does not desire to inflict upon living beings the afflictions of bondage or death, seeking the welfare of all, enjoys ultimate happiness. (5.46)

The afflictions (*kleśa*) are indeed bondage and slaughter, or alternatively, acts such as mutilation. He who does not wish to perform these—by whom even the act of mutilation has not been committed, and whose very desire for such objects has ceased—not only refrains from inflicting pain, but desires to seek the welfare of all; he enjoys ultimate happiness. (5.46)
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and wherever one fixes one's delight—that one obtains without effort, provided that one harms nothing at all. (5.47)

Whatever he thinks of, such as a bride-price or an honorarium, and whatever object he intends and fixes his desire and longing upon, that he obtains with ease and in a very short time. But whatever action he performs through physical effort, that he attains without obstacle immediately upon the completion of the deed. (5.47)
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should avoid meat. (5.48)

He demonstrates that the entire collection of verses prohibiting violence is supplementary to the prohibition of eating meat. As long as living beings have not been killed, meat does not come into existence; furthermore, violence brings about extreme suffering. Therefore, one should avoid meat. But surely there is meat even from those who die of their own accord; why then is it said, "not without having [killed]"? This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). Moreover, the meat of those who die of their own accord is simply not obtained because it is a cause of disease. Indeed, meat is not eaten without being given [as a gift], and there is no giving of that which is a cause of disease.

Regarding the statement "it arises": because meat is the cause of violence, there is no contradiction in its being designated as the agent; thus, the state of having a common agent [with the act of killing] indeed exists. Alternatively, the phrase "it arises" does not mean that it is simply not a cause for the arising of heaven (*svarga*); rather, what is intended is that it is a cause for the suffering of hell and other such realms. (5.48)
Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and imprisonment of embodied beings, one should desist from the consumption of all meat. (5.49)

The growth of the embryo occurs in the womb, that impure place, originating from the two impurities of semen and blood. Likewise, there is the killing and binding of embodied beings caused by those [impurities]. Having thoroughly considered all this and investigated it according to reality with a discerning intellect, one should desist from eating all meat—even that which is not prohibited, let alone that which is prohibited.

This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); however, it is not to be understood as if meat were inherently impure in its very essence, for this statement is not intended as a formal injunction regarding its impurity. (5.49)
He who does not eat meat, even while disregarding the ritual rules like a Piśāca, becomes beloved in the world and is not afflicted by diseases. (5.50)

The rule is that one should eat meat after having performed the worship of the gods; he who does not eat it while disregarding that rule, but rather eats it according to the rule, attains the favor of the world. He becomes beloved by all. [This applies even] to diseases. Disease arises for one who eats the flesh of those who are emaciated or weak; therefore, even in that case, one must eat only according to the rule. Eating in such a manner, one is not afflicted by diseases. Otherwise, even while eating meat, one is indeed afflicted by diseases, like a *piśāca*. *Piśācas* are a specific class of lower beings (*tiryagjāti*) who eat meat without regard for the rule; thus, anyone else who eats in that same way is censured as being like a *piśāca*. (5.50)
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and the seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it—all these are slayers. (5.51)

If another person, for their own purpose, approves of one being killed by someone else, thinking, "Excellent, this killer is doing it," that person is the approver (*anumantṛ*). The butcher (*viśasitṛ*) is the one who performs the dismemberment of the slain body. The server (*upahartṛ*) is the one who brings the food. The eater (*khādaka*)—all these are killers (*ghātaka*).

When the status of being a killer (*ghātaka*) is superimposed upon those who do not actually kill—such as those who perform the preparation of food or its sale—there is a censure; however, in reality, these people are not killers at all. For the worldly act of killing has the result of the loss of life, and its agent is understood from the *smṛti* to be the killer. According to specific scriptural definitions such as "the independent one is the agent," he who effects the separation of life from living beings is called a slayer (*hantṛ*). But acts such as buying and selling are entirely different from that. [Objection: But is this not also a *smṛti* rule, stating that "these, beginning with the consenter, are killers"?

This is not an authoritative means of knowledge regarding the relationship between word and meaning; rather, it concerns *dharma* and *adharma*. For in that regard, the venerable Pāṇini is more highly skilled. Furthermore, Manu and others employ words according to meanings well-known in the world; they do not record a rule for the relationship between word and meaning. These individuals are users [of language], not its recorders. But is it not the case that they do record it, based on such statements as, "He asks that teacher" (MDh 2.140)?

True. In that case, there is no contradiction with the scriptures or the *smṛtis*, nor do those passages have any other purpose. Here, however, since it is possible for the statement to be an *arthavāda* even through a figurative purpose, it cannot be determined that [the eater] is the actual slayer.

As for those who say: "If there is no eater, there is no slayer; thus, the killing is prompted solely by eating, and the prompter is considered the agent. Therefore, the status of being the slayer is primary. Consequently, it is appropriate that the eater undergoes the very same penance as the slayer."
We say that this is incorrect. There is a separate expiation for those who have been killed and for the one who tastes the meat, as stated in the *Manusmṛti* (11.151): "Having eaten forbidden meat...
Furthermore, the claim that agency belongs to the instigator is also not the case; for its definition is as follows:
"He who, through commanding or requesting, impels one who is otherwise independent [is the agent]."
"He alone is both the agent and the primary cause, not another [who acts] figuratively.
For the killer proceeds by means of the eater's livelihood, thinking, "I shall live by selling meat," but he is not commissioned by the eater.

Now, "instigation" (*prayojakatva*) consists in performing what is conducive to that [action]. One who has resolved to perform an action and who intends to provide assistance therein is the instigator (*prayojaka*). This too does not exist here at all. It is appropriate that the term "provisioning" (*saṃvidhāna*) refers to such things as the placing of instruments, the rendering of the trembling animal powerless, and the bringing forward of the sword; without these, the action is not accomplished.

If it is argued that "that for whose sake an action is commenced is the instigator (*prayojaka*)," then in the case of "he causes the boy to study" (*māṇavakam adhyāpayati*), the boy would acquire the designation of agent (*kartṛ*) based on the cause of teaching; for the act of studying itself does not have "teaching" as its purpose.

Furthermore, he does not engage in killing with any specific person in mind, such that his engagement in eating for the sake of determining that [purpose] would be purposeless. All these beings strive for their own welfare; no one remains even for a moment thinking, "I must benefit another," even if they are one whose desires are fulfilled.

Now, for one who acts for his own sake, activity is purposeless without a consumer; but when such a consumer exists, the activity becomes fruitful. And the fruit is the motive; since that fruit depends upon the consumer, the consumer is indirectly the instigator.

If that were so, then one who is killed out of hatred would be the instigator (*prayojaka*) of the killer; consequently, the very person being killed would become the killer. For without hatred, the status of being a killer is not possible. Likewise, even in the case of killing a Brahmin, the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadāna*) would be the instigator of the sin. For without a recipient, the act of receiving is not possible; therefore, not only the recipient would incur guilt, but the giver as well. Furthermore, a beautiful woman, while guarding her virtue, would incur guilt when shown excessive desire by a lustful man whose heart is burning with the arrows of the God of Love.
Therefore, this is not the definition of an instigator.

For those two—the killer and the eater—act for their own sake and experience mutual assistance like the man who lost his horse and the one whose chariot was burned; they are not, however, instigators of one another. This has been determined with precision in the verse beginning, "Of Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas" (MDh 8.104). 5.51.
There is no doer of more demerit than he who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another, without having first honored the ancestors and the gods. 5.52

This censure applies to one who eats meat for the sake of excessive nourishment, and not out of apprehension regarding the onset of disease; for it says: "he who desires to increase [his strength]," etc. Even for such a person, there is no fault if he does so without having honored the ancestors and the gods; however, this is not the case for one who, due to the cause of illness, somehow finds it impossible to perform the honoring, even if he does not do so. (5.52)
He who should perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years, and he who does not eat meat—the merit and fruit of these two are equal. (5.53)

The consumption of meat from rabbits and other such animals, which remains after being offered in worship to the gods and others, is permitted. One who abstains from this obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). The fruit of the horse-sacrifice is described as "the fulfillment of all desires and the conquest of all [regions]," and so forth. Nor should it be objected here: "How can there be equality of fruit for abstaining from meat when compared to [the sacrifice], which involves great exertion and the expenditure of vast wealth? For this restraint (*saṃyama*) is also extremely difficult to perform. Furthermore, the principle that "as in the world, there may be a distinction in the fruit according to the measure [of effort]" applies here; therefore, there is no fault in the prescription of the fruit.

We, however, say: this is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise). For it is easily consistent with the *arthavāda* position that "for a hundred years"; for it is not possible for the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) to be enjoined every year, nor is it possible for one to live for a hundred years, since such a duration of time would preclude the possibility of the qualified person (*adhikārin*) remaining alive.

"Merit and fruit" (*puṇyaphalam*) is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*); for in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), there would be a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*). (5.53)
One does not obtain that fruit by subsisting on pure fruits and roots or by eating the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat. (5.54)
"Pure" means fit for the gods. "Foods of sages" refers to grains such as *nīvāra* that ripen without being ploughed. This is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). 5.54.
"He shall devour me in the hereafter, whose flesh I eat in this world"—the wise declare this to be the true nature of "meat" (māṃsa). (5.55)

The etymological explanation of the name is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). "He shall eat me"—here, the pronoun "he" (*sa*), which refers generally, is made complete by its connection with the appropriate referent: "he who eats my flesh. (5.55)
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse; this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention bears great fruit. (5.56)

Starting from the verse "The food of the vital breath" (MDh 5.28) up to this verse, it is merely a collection of explanatory statements (*arthavāda*); only two or three verses contain prescriptive matter.

There is no fault in eating meat, as in the verse: "Having purchased it, or having produced it oneself... (MDh 5.32); this verse is similar. However, what is heard here is that abstention yields great fruit. Through many expressions of censure, such a refinement has arisen that no meat whatsoever should be eaten. He speaks for the sake of the livelihood of living beings: "There is no fault in eating meat. There is no fault in cases previously mentioned, such as when it is the remnant of an offering to the gods, or when there is the desire of a Brāhmaṇa, and so forth—provided they wish to eat it. Abstention, preceded by the resolve "I shall not eat," yields great fruit. Since no specific fruit is mentioned, the Mīmāṃsakas hold that heaven is the fruit.

Thus, for Kṣatriyas and others, [the rule applies] regarding intoxicants; but regarding sexual intercourse, it applies to all castes, except on the days of the moon’s change (*divā*) and with a woman in her courses (*udakyā*), and at times other than the prescribed period. This limited engagement is the scriptural [norm]. Such engagement is for the purpose of maintaining the bodies of living beings. And so says the author of Āyurveda: "Food, celibacy, and sleep—these three are considered [the pillars]; likewise, intoxicants and women are indeed the supports of life."

But for one who is able to live even without that [activity], its cessation yields great fruit. This is stated for the sake of illustration; the same applies to the cessation of other activities that are neither enjoined nor forbidden by the cultured (*aśiṣṭa*). Where there is an injunction, the purpose is the production of an excess of pleasure for a person engaged in it, provided it is not blameworthy; or where cessation from something leads to a fruit, as in the case of eating honey, eating choice food, wearing a woolen garment, and so forth. Such is also the practice of the cultured. And the venerable Vyāsa said thus: "But those things which, though neither enjoined nor forbidden by the cultured, arise from attachment—such as laughing, scratching, and the like—cessation from them leads to merit. (5.56)
I shall now declare the purification for the deceased as well as the purification of objects, for all four castes, duly and in their proper order. (5.57)

The mention of "even for the four" is intended to make it known that the duties prescribed in general do not apply to a Śūdra without such specific effort. The term *preteṣu jīvatām* (purity among those who have died while others live) is a compound formed according to the rule *sup-supā*. Furthermore, this purity is a specific exception to the general rule regarding the attainment [of status] upon death. Therefore, although the statement of purity (*śuddhi*) is what is formally promised, nevertheless, because purity is dependent upon impurity (*aśuddhi*) and because both are established by the authority of the scriptures, impurity is mentioned first, even though it was not explicitly promised. (5.57)

When [a child] has teethed, when it has been born after [the first birth], when the tonsure ceremony has been performed, and when it has died—all relatives are impure; the same is declared regarding a birth-impurity (sūtaka).

The tradition records that one who has just emerged from the womb is even more tender than one whose teeth have just appeared. Thus, this [rule regarding the period of impurity] is merely a general statement made without such distinction; for, depending upon that [distinction], there will be a difference in the duration of the period of impurity. For example, in another Smṛti: "Until the eruption of teeth," and likewise by the rule "In the case of a child and one residing in a foreign land" (MDh 5.77), immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed. A "child" (*bāla*) should be understood as one whose teeth have not yet erupted. And thus, the one-night period of impurity mentioned in the verse "For men whose tonsure has not been performed" (MDh 5.66) is established as applying even to one whose teeth have erupted. In this way, these two Smṛti texts become non-contradictory regarding the subject of the child through a systematic allocation of their respective scopes. Furthermore, purification after one night applies until the performance of the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), since he will later state that for those whose tonsure has been completed, the period is three nights. And that three-night period applies prior to initiation (*upanayana*); beyond that, [the rule] beginning with "A Brahmin shall be purified" (MDh 5.82) applies.

However, those who describe these alternatives—"impurity on account of death lasts ten days" (MDh 5.59)—according to the divisions of age, and connect them out of their sequential order based on other Smṛtis and established practice, [state that] the impurity is ten days for one who has been initiated, four days for one who has not been initiated, three days for one whose tonsure has been performed, one day for one whose teeth have appeared, and immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*) for a younger sibling; while options such as immediate purity apply to others. Likewise, [these durations] apply to one whose *cūḍā* ceremony has been performed, [namely] three or four days.

In their view, an option based on other Smṛti texts regarding conduct (*vṛtta*) and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) would not have been established; we shall demonstrate this later. One is said to be "dead" through the cessation of all activity, because the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *sam-* is seen to indicate the stopping of activity. "Relatives" (*bāndhavāḥ*) refers to the *sapiṇḍas* and those related by water (*samānodakas*). And "at birth" (*sūtake*) refers to the birth of a son and so forth. It is thus stated that "all relatives are impure," and with this [statement], the present passage is connected.

But how, in this case, is the distinction of age understood, given that in the expression *kṛtamuṇḍa* (one whose tonsure has been performed) a connection with a sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) is perceived? And in the expression *kṛtopanayane*, it is indeed directly heard [from scripture]. For this very reason, it is not heard at all that one who has had his *caula* performed is said to be at a certain age. It is replied: because of its association with *dantajāta* (one whose teeth have appeared) and *anujāta* (one born after), *kṛtamuṇḍa* is understood to indicate a specific time. And that time here is the first and third year.

Even though the tonsure ceremony (*muṇḍīkaraṇa*) is optional in the first year, if that option is adopted, the rule "immediate [purification] until the eruption of teeth" (*ā dantajanmanaḥ sadyaḥ*) becomes sublated.

That too is incorrect. As for the limit [of the period] "one whose tonsure has been performed" (*kṛtamuṇḍa*), by the word *ca* ("and"), it is understood that this applies both to one whose tonsure has been performed and to one whose initiation (*upanayana*) has been performed, because a different designation is applied when another sacrament (*saṃskāra*) is reached. In this way, there will be syntactic unity with this Smṛti even in the passage: "Until the eruption of teeth, purification is immediate" (*ā dantajanmanaḥ sadyaḥ*). Furthermore, in the rule "For three nights until the instruction in the vows" (*trirātram ā vratādeśāt*), the mention of "instruction in the vows" is solely for the purpose of indicating a time. Nor would it be the case that for a Brāhmaṇa the time is not fixed as exactly the eighth year, nor for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; otherwise, no specific time would have been stated for a Śūdra. In that regard also, for one whose childhood has passed, the rule "for all, it is complete" (*paripūrṇaṃ sarveṣām*) applies. Therefore, from the eighth year onwards, there is full impurity (*sarvāśauca*) for all four castes, since that same time-period exists for the Śūdra as well. However, according to the view in which the initiation of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas is observed in the eleventh year, then no specific time would have been stated for the Śūdra. In that case too, for one whose childhood has passed, the impurity is complete; prior to that, it is three nights. And the cessation of childhood is stated in another Smṛti: "One is called a child (*śiśu*) before the eighth year," while others say, "One may be a boy (*bāla*) until the sixteenth. Even for those who say that childhood ceases at sixteen, the purification after the eighth year is indeed monthly (*māsikī*). Thus it is recited: "But after six years, the purification of a Śūdra is monthly. Elsewhere it is recited that for an eight-year-old, it is a month.
But surely this distinction of age-classes is obtained from the very sentences that are about to be stated; what is the purpose of this heading, "one whose teeth have appeared"?
True; it is for the sake of easy comprehension. 5.58.
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among sapinda relatives;
it lasts for three days until the collection of the bones, or for one day. (5.59)

The definition of *sāpiṇḍya* will be stated [later]. The phrase "prior to the collection of the bones" (*arvāk saṃcayanāt*) will be explained as an elliptical expression for four days, for there is a scriptural statement: "For one who maintains the sacred fires, the collection of the bones takes place on the fourth day. And this option depends either upon conduct and Vedic study (*vṛtta-svādhyāya*) or upon conduct alone (*vṛtta*). Accordingly, another *smṛti* states: "A Brāhmaṇa who maintains both the Veda and the sacred fires becomes pure after one day;
one who possesses only the Veda after three days; but one devoid of qualities after ten days."

In that regard, for one who maintains the three Vedas and possesses the sacred fires (*agnimant*), the period of impurity lasts one day; for one who maintains two Vedas, it lasts three days; and for one devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), it lasts ten days. Gautama has prescribed immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*), and that applies specifically to a Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of not interrupting his Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). Regarding other ritual activities in those cases:
for ten days in both instances, the food of the family is not eaten;
giving, receiving, burnt offerings (*homa*), and Vedic study are suspended.
Thus, these and other such activities cease. However, because the Veda of one who has studied much perishes if not recited, the private study (*svādhyāya*) does not cease.

Accordingly, an option based on livelihood is appropriate: for one living by the six duties, there is a ten-day period; for another [living by three], a four-day period; and for one [living by two], a three-day period. For if impurity lasted ten days, it would be difficult to obtain even the mere sustenance of life, since one would lack the entitlement to accept gifts and perform other such acts during that time.

As for those who claim, "There are four stages of life (*vayas*) and four periods of impurity; therefore, there is a connection [between them] according to age and in numerical order," for them it would follow that if a child dies after the eruption of teeth, the period of impurity is ten days, but if one dies after initiation (*upanīta*), it is only one day. In that case, there would be a contradiction with other *smṛtis* and established practice. Now, if, in order to avoid this contradiction, the connection is made in reverse order: "Ten days for one initiated; four days for one whose tonsure has been performed; three days for one whose teeth have erupted; and one day for one born after [the teeth]."

In this case as well, an option is appropriate due to the contradiction with the rule, "For those whose tonsure ceremony has been performed, [impurity lasts] for three nights," since a three-night period is prescribed by its own specific term; for the four-day period is established as having a different scope based on a difference in livelihood (*vṛtti*) or a difference in the accumulation of wealth. Thus, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with another Smṛti through the phrase "after one day. Otherwise, if an option were explained based on differences in age, by what means would an option be obtained in the Mānava Śāstra that depends upon one's livelihood and Vedic study?

Therefore, according to this statement of Gautama, for one who has a livelihood even without daily acceptance of gifts—such as one who possesses a granary full of grain—and who is devoted to sacred study (*svādhyāya*), there is immediate purification upon the mere recitation of the Veda. As for those ritual alternatives (*kalpa*) involving three days and so forth, even in those cases, for those who live on such [daily] means, purification occurs after that same duration when accepting gifts for the sake of a livelihood, based on this very view of Gautama. Otherwise, he would have simply said "of a Brāhmaṇa who studies the Veda," rather than saying "for the purpose of not interrupting the study of the Veda."

Therefore, although it is heard in scripture that "purification occurs after one day," and so forth, without distinction, this must nevertheless be understood as referring to specific ritual acts. For [the author] states, as if it were a constant rule, that for a Brāhmaṇa the period is ten days: "A Brāhmaṇa is purified in ten days" (MDh 5.82). Indeed, there is no purpose for a redundant statement. Consequently, this option is to be explained by a logical method. Furthermore, where immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) applies in the case of children and the like, or a three-night period in the case of those whose tonsure has been performed, there is no option; thus, purity exists for all ritual acts in those instances. (5.59)
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the state of being a samānodaka (distant kinsman) persists as long as there is knowledge of the birth and the name.

Because of the recognition of lineage (*anvaya*) and the continued application of the term "kinsman" (*bāndhava*), those born of the same lineage (*anvayaja*) are called *sapiṇḍas* up to the seventh person. According to the rule, "To those for whom one's father gives, so [should] the son [give]," even when the ancestors are living, six [generations] are eligible to be *sapiṇḍas*. Although the offering is made to the ancestors and oneself is the seventh, therefore the grandfather, great-grandfather, and others born of the preceding lineage are designated as *sapiṇḍas*. There are six *sapiṇḍas* on the prior side; likewise, there are exactly six on the subsequent side, beginning with the son. Since the designation of *sapiṇḍa* is obtained from the coexistence of a single act of offering the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), this coexistence of the son and others is also performed by the grandson and so forth. Consequently, all those to whom one gives and those with whom one will share the status of recipient (*saṃpradāna*) are designated as *sapiṇḍas*. For in that context, the offering of the rice-ball is not intended merely as a marker of a limit—as in the expression "one should come at the time of the conch-blowing" (*śaṅkhavelāyām*)—but rather as a defining characteristic. Therefore, what is effectively stated is: "Those born in the lineage of the great-grandfather’s own great-grandfather, up to the seventh degree, are *sapiṇḍas*. This should be understood in the same way regarding one's own descendants and the descendants of the father and others. Precisely because of this distinction, the counting must be performed starting from that point until the seventh degree. Thus, in every case, those who share a common grandfather are *sapiṇḍas* starting from him up to the seventh degree.

Furthermore, since "being born from that lineage" (*tadanvayajatva*) is used as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), and because the universal (*jāti*) is not relied upon [as the defining factor], even those of different classes, such as Kṣatriyas and others, become *sapiṇḍas* of Brāhmaṇas and others. For this very reason, in the case of impurity (*āśauca*) due to their birth and so forth, for a Brāhmaṇa it lasts only ten days, whereas for them [the Kṣatriyas, etc.], it lasts their own specific period, such as twelve days and so on. Therefore, for everyone, purification occurs at their own respective time when there is a cause related to a person of a different class, or a cause related to a *sapiṇḍa* of a different class, such as a birth and so on.
Among Kṣatriyas and others, the *sapiṇḍa* relationship extends to three generations (*tripuruṣa*) in relation to a Brāhmaṇa. Thus says Śaṅkha:
"If many [sons] are born of one [father], but have separate wives and separate origins..."
They share a single funeral cake but have separate purifications; however, the cake itself is repeated among three.

"Pṛthakkṣetrāḥ" means those born of women of different castes. "Pṛthagjanāḥ" refers to those who, although of the same caste as the father, have multiple mothers; both terms are employed for this reason. "Ekapiṇḍāḥ" means they are *sapiṇḍas* (share the funeral rice-ball). However, they are "pṛthakśaucāḥ," meaning their period of purification is determined solely by the occasion of their own birth-caste. For instance, in the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and so forth, the period is ten days for a Kṣatriya and others when a Brāhmaṇa is affected, whereas it is twelve days for them when a Brāhmaṇa is affected. Furthermore, there is another distinction: "The *piṇḍa* recurs among three"; that is, it exists only among three generations of males.

With respect to those of the same caste, the *sāpiṇḍya* for Kṣatriyas and others is six generations, just as for Brāhmaṇas, because of the inclusion of specific qualifiers such as “born of one [father] but from separate wombs. With respect to those of a different caste, this statement can establish a limit of three generations. This very meaning is clarified by the following Smṛti: “Those who are heirs of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, yet are kinsmen (*bāndhava*) of a Brāhmaṇa—if there is impurity (*āśauca*) among them, the purification of the Brāhmaṇa is held to occur after ten days.”
And [it is said]: "By six, by three, or by one," and so forth.

As for women of a different caste, purification occurs at the time of their husband's death while he is still living. And it is said: "In the case of birth or death, purification for slaves and for wives born in the natural order [occurs]..."
The purification shall be equal to that of the master; when the master has died, it shall be according to the paternal rules.

Others read the first quarter-verse as "of those born of women of a different caste" (*asavarṇāsutānām*). If this reading exists, then even for Śūdra sons who reside in their father's house and remain dependent on him, the period of purification is ten days and so forth, in consideration of the father's caste.
And here, "servants" (*dāsāḥ*) refers to those who work for wages; however, regarding those who are slaves from birth (*garbhadāsāḥ*), a different rule is heard:
"Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, and likewise female and male slaves..."
"Kings and royal servants are declared to be pure immediately.

Thus, their purity should be understood to apply to physical contact alone, and not to activities such as giving gifts or eating. Since these terms are based on specific functions, one must consider whether, in the absence of those functions, there is purification, or whether all activities are permitted, or only some are authorized. For when the requirement arises—"and for the sake of not obstructing the king's business"—those very activities come to mind; and such is the established practice.
But is it not the case that no prohibition against touching is heard here?
For in another Smṛti it is recited: "After the collection of the bones, the touching of the limbs is prescribed."
Likewise, it is said elsewhere:
"A Brāhmaṇa shall attain purity after three or four days;
in the case of both birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka), purification occurs on the eleventh day."

Hārīta states: "In the case of a Kṣatriya, there is contact [with the corpse] on the sixth or seventh day, and purification regarding food after twelve days; for a Vaiśya, there is contact on the eighth or ninth day, and purification regarding food after a fortnight; for a Śūdra, there is contact on the eleventh or twelfth day, and purification regarding food after a month. Likewise, there is another statement: "Upon contact with the corpses of the castes in order, a Brāhmaṇa becomes fit to eat food after three, four, five, or six days; the others [the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra] after ten, twelve, and eighteen days respectively."

These alternatives are to be established according to the requirements of the situation, depending on whether the person is virtuous or devoid of virtue. In all cases, the *bhaktadāsas* (servants by food) of a Brāhmaṇa defile him by touch after three or four days; however, the *garbhadāsas* (slaves from birth) do so immediately. The same applies to the other castes as well.

Where this immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed, bathing with one's clothes is required in every such instance. This will be made known by the rule: "Whatever purification is ordained for each specific substance" (MDh 5.109).

"For maidens as well, the sapinda relationship extends to three generations. Vasiṣṭha states: "But for women who have sons, it is understood to extend to three generations. This refers specifically to the period of impurity; however, the rule regarding marriage has already been shown.

This is established: the seventh person is the limit, and six persons are *sapiṇḍas*. Upon reaching the seventh, [the *sapiṇḍa* relationship] ceases. The state of being *samānodakas* (distant kinsmen) is the designation of *samānodaka*. [This applies] when there is no knowledge of either birth or name. Birth refers to [the thought], "He was born in our family," and name refers to [the lineage] from such-and-such a father, grandfather, and so forth. When both are unknown, the [obligation to offer water] ceases. Therefore, even if one of the two is known, it should be understood that the water offering is not performed. [The rule is: "Having descended into a river or another reservoir of water, bending down until the water reaches the navel, facing south, and using the left hand placed over the right, they should offer water without looking back and then return. (5.60)
In the case of birth as well, it should be exactly the same; however, the impurity (sūtaka) belongs to both the mother and the father.
The impurity belongs to the mother alone, while the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution.

This is so regarding the birth of sapindas. Just as the rules of ten days and so forth were established for death with respect to one's livelihood through the six duties (*ṣaṭkarman*) and the like, and with respect to the smallness or greatness of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), so too in the case of birth, the mere impurity (*āśauca*) is extended without limitation of time. By implication, since no specific distinction is grasped, the entire set of related rules is obtained. However, if there were an extension [of the rule] limited by time, then because of its primacy, the connection would be only with the ten-day period in regard to Vedic study and the rest. Or else, due to proximity in the text, it would be connected only with the single day in preference to the ten-day period and others, and because the requirement would be satisfied by that alone, there would be no connection with the other periods such as three days. In that case, this Smṛti—which prescribes the arrangement for both death and birth based on livelihood and Vedic study without distinction—would be contradicted if it were applied to birth based solely on caste (*jāti*) without regard for qualities and the like. Furthermore, established custom (*samācāra*) would be subverted.
But surely, in this way, the rules of three days, one day, and so forth would also apply to women who have given birth, which would contradict established custom.

To this it is replied: if this were an optional alternative (*vikalpa*), then it would be so; however, the rule (*kalpa*) is actually fixed (*vyavasthita*). For in that case, the word "but" (*tu*) becomes more appropriate.

Furthermore, the word *sūtaka* does not denote impurity (*āśauca*) itself; rather, by means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it points to the impurity associated with birth. Given the association with this indication, it is more appropriate for the term to indicate specifically the state of untouchability (*aspṛśyatā*). If all forms of impurity were intended, the author would have simply used the term "impurity," as in the rule: "impurity belongs to the mother alone. Consequently, since another Smṛti text speaks of three nights of untouchability, its absence here implies an option between the two: "birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) belongs to the mother alone"; or, "of both parents, it belongs to the mother alone," which implies an option for the father. The statement "having touched [the child] and bathed, one becomes pure" is merely introductory; by the verse to be cited next, even for the father, the period is indeed three days. (5.61)
But having emitted semen, a man becomes pure simply by touching water;
however, due to the connection arising from seed, he should observe impurity for three days.

By teaching that purification occurs after three days when there is a cause, he approves of the previously mentioned purification through non-contact. If one asks for what purpose this is stated, it is for the sake of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) as a descriptive rule (*sarūpavidhi*), and not as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), like the statement: "One should offer oblations with a gruel of wild sesame" (*jartilayavāgvā vā juhuyāt*).

But having discharged semen through the act of sexual intercourse, one becomes pure after touching water—that is, bathing—immediately following the emission of semen. This refers to the *bāhika* (procreative) connection; *bāhika* means caused by the seed (*bīja*), and "connection" (*abhisaṃbandha*) means the production of offspring. Therefore, how could one not follow [the rule] there? The impurity (*agha*) lasts for three days. And the impurity of one who has not bathed after discharging semen is not the same as that which occurs at birth; rather, it lasts for three days. The latter half of the preceding verse reiterates this in order to complete the three-day period. For this very reason, the term "touching water" (*upaspṛśya*) denotes bathing—not merely sipping water (*ācamana*)—because of the scriptural statement: "Bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse."

Some maintain, however, that on the day a son is born, one may indeed touch [impure things]. Thus Śaṅkha says: "Upon the birth of a son, as long as the umbilical cord is not severed, there is no fault in accepting gifts of molasses, sesame, gold, clothing, upper garments, cows, or grain; so say some regarding that day.
Therefore, that day is auspicious for the ancestors and increases their satisfaction.
By virtue of the remembrance of the ancestors, that day is not defiled.
Likewise, it is said that "some even perform the *śrāddha*. By this, there is an absolute absence of impurity (*āśauca*) for the father.

In this regard, these two traditional texts (*smṛtis*) are to be understood as optional alternatives (*vikalpyete*), depending on the presence or absence of livelihood (*vṛtti*), as previously explained. (5.62)
Those who touch a corpse are purified in one day and night, or even in three triple-nights; those who offer water for the deceased are purified after three days. (5.63)

Three periods of three nights make nine days; one day and one night constitute a full day-and-night (*ahorātra*). Thus, ten days are taught here in accordance with the meter. Regarding those who touch a corpse—that is, those who perform the bathing, decorating, and other rites for the deceased—for others, he will prescribe mere bathing, as well as for those who carry out the body. He will clarify this in the verse: "Together with those who provide food for the deceased" (MDh 5.64). This [impurity] applies to those who are *samānodaka* (sapindas beyond the seventh degree) or to those who carry the body for a fee. However, regarding the carrying out of a corpse that has no protector, another *smṛti* states: "For those who perform such auspicious acts, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any ritual impurity."
For them, purification is prescribed immediately by means of immersion in water.

As for the statement, "a twice-born who is not a *sapiṇḍa*" (MDh 5.100), we shall explain that later. Those who offer water are the *samānodaka*s; regarding them, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) will also be taught in the verse, "when the funeral cake is offered separately" (MDh 5.77). In this case, there is an option. This [rule] concerning *sapiṇḍas* is contingent upon the suspension of Vedic study and other such factors. (5.63)
But a disciple performing the funeral rites for his deceased preceptor becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who partake of the food offered to the deceased. (5.64)

The *pitṛmedha* is the final sacrifice (*carameṣṭi*). Others, however, say that it refers to all ritual action (*sarvaṃ karma*). By performing that, the student becomes pure after ten nights. This rule applies even to a religious student (*brahmacārin*); he is equal to those who carry out the funeral rites. Just as they carry out—that is, they escort—the deceased, for them there is a period of ten days; such is the meaning: it is the same for the student as well. (5.46)
In the case of a miscarriage, a woman is purified in as many nights as there were months of pregnancy;
once her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who has become soiled by it is purified by bathing. (5.65)

In the case of a miscarriage (*garbhasrāva*), it is appropriate that the purification for the woman alone lasts for as many nights as there have been months of pregnancy, because she is the one explicitly mentioned in this statement. As for the *sapiṇḍa* relatives, however, their rule must be sought from other *smṛtis* and established custom. Vasiṣṭha, however, has prescribed three days for the *sapiṇḍas*: "When a child dies before reaching two years of age, or in the event of a miscarriage, the impurity for the *sapiṇḍas* lasts three nights" (VaDh 4.34). A miscarriage (*srāva*) occurs after the third month but before the tenth month; some, however, say it occurs before the ninth month. The term "miscarriage" (*srāva*) refers to the falling out of an embryo that has not yet reached its [full] time, and not merely to something liquid in form. Likewise, Gautama states regarding the loss of an embryo: "As many nights as there have been months of pregnancy" (GDh 14.17). Furthermore, fetuses of seven months live; therefore, in the seventh month, the full period of impurity applies. This, however, is appropriate for one born alive; otherwise, it is simply "as many [days] as there have been months of pregnancy."

In this context, it is traditionally taught that a menstruating woman becomes pure by bathing once her menstrual flow has ceased; however, according to another Smṛti, this occurs after three days have passed. The settled rule regarding this is as follows: before the three-day period, there is no purity even if the flow has ceased; after the three days, purity exists even if the flow has not yet ceased. Nevertheless, the phrase "she becomes pure" [is used]. In the present case, however, because of the word "virtuous" (*sādhvī*), there is no entry into the entitlement to perform Vedic rites while the flow has not ceased, but there is no prohibition against touching her and so forth. It has been stated: "The first four days are censured" (MDh 3.47). The construction of the words is thus: a menstruating woman becomes "virtuous"—that is, pure and fit for ritual acts—once her flow has ceased and she has bathed. The mention of the word "woman" (*strī*) is intended to include women of all castes. The preceding verses were explained as referring specifically to Brāhmaṇas; therefore, the mention of "woman" is made here to remove any doubt on that account. Furthermore, wherever there is no specific authority, the rule applies to all castes alike, as in the verse: "Of men whose tonsure has not been performed" (MDh 5.66). (5.65)

For men who have not yet had their heads shaved, purification is prescribed as lasting one night; however, for those whose heads have already been shaved, purification is held to occur after three nights. 5.66.

Some explain these genitive forms as denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), according to Pāṇini 2.3.65 (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*). Thus, they state that one whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed becomes pure after one day; likewise, there is an opinion of certain authorities that this option depends upon the stage of life. These two [verses] constitute the regulatory statement for that very verse.

Others, however, say that by means of ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), they denote the relationship (*saṃbandha*): "those who are the *sapiṇḍas* of those who have died before their heads were shaved. Among these, the latter position is intended by established custom (*samācāra*).

Immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is also prescribed in another *Smṛti*. The scope for this is shown in that very same text: "Until the eruption of teeth, purification is immediate; until the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*), it lasts one night; for those whose tonsure has been completed, it lasts three nights. (5.66)
Relatives should place a deceased child who has not yet reached two years of age outside [the village], having adorned it, upon pure ground, except for the rite of collecting the bones. 5.67.

A child who has not completed two full years since birth is called *ūnadvivārṣika*. His relatives should place that deceased child outside the village, setting him in a pit dug in the ground. In another Smṛti, it is read as "he should bury him" (*nikhanet*; YDh 3.1). Having adorned him with the ornaments used for the dead—though the mention of adornment is heard even regarding a child less than two years old, it should be understood from established custom to apply also to those for whom the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) has been performed. In a clean spot where there are no bones—that is, in a place which is pure because it is devoid of accumulated bones—he should be buried and placed there. For it is in the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) that bones are normally accumulated; therefore, by this statement, burial elsewhere than there is prescribed. The meaning of the sentence is certainly not that an accumulation of bones should not be made for such a child, since such an act would not even be applicable due to the absence of the rite of cremation (*agnisaṃskāra*). (5.67)
No cremation with fire should be performed for him, nor should the water-libation rite be performed;
having abandoned him like a log in the forest, one should pass only three days in mourning. 5.68.

The phrase "like a piece of wood" expresses his state of indifference. One should not perform the *śrāddha* rite, nor the water libation (*udaka*). By the prohibition of the water rite, the prohibition of the *śrāddha* is established, because of the relationship between the subsidiary and the principal. Therefore, the prohibition of the *śrāddha*, which is well-known from traditional practice (*samācāra*), must be proven by this indicative mark (*liṅga*). Others, however, explain it as being for the purpose of prohibiting the burial seen in other Smṛtis. Consequently, there is an option: one may either let [the body] decay or cast it away; one should not perform the activity enjoined by the scriptures. (5.68)
The water-rite should not be performed for one who has not reached three years of age by his relatives;
however, they may perform it once a tooth has emerged or when the naming ceremony has been completed. (5.69)

"Up to three years" means the prohibition lasts until the third year, and not from the fourth year onwards. It is for this very purpose that some read the word "ādi" (and so forth): "The rite should not be performed for one under three years, but for those aged three and upwards. Such is also the established custom. Or, they may perform it for one whose teeth have appeared; by association with the water-rite (*udakakriyā*), the fire-consecration (*agnisaṃskāra*) is thereby permitted. But surely, in the case of an option, there is freedom of choice (*kāmacāra*). Under such circumstances, who would resort to the alternative involving great effort and the depletion of wealth? Thus, the instruction regarding it would be useless.

It is said: This entitlement of the parents is unique in every respect. This is performed for the sake of benefiting the deceased (preta). It has already been stated previously that because it is occasional (naimittika), it must necessarily be performed; however, it is determined here that there exists a prohibition regarding its mandatory performance. That it serves to benefit the deceased is made known by way of permission. Thus, in not performing it, there is no transgression of an injunction; yet, since the benefit to the deceased arises from its performance, there is no inconsistency between the injunction and the prohibition. (5.69)
If a fellow religious student has died, purification is prescribed after one day;
however, for those who offer water libations together at birth, purity is held to occur after three nights.

Fellow religious practitioners (*sabrahmacārī*) who share the same observances (*samānavarṇa*) are included here by extension as those related by water-offerings (*ekodaka*), up to the seventh generation of sapinda relations. Among them, in the case of birth or death-impurity (*sūtaka*), there is a period of three nights. However, an alternative rule of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for those who offer water should also be understood from other Smṛti texts as being optional. (5.70)
For female relatives who have not undergone the sacramental rites, the kinsmen are purified after three days;
however, those of the same lineage (sanābhayaḥ) are purified according to the rule already stated.

In the case of the death of those women who have not been formally married but are accepted by mere word, their husbands' kinsmen are purified after three nights; however, their own paternal kinsmen, the *sapiṇḍas* and *sanābhayas*, are purified according to the rule previously stated for those "whose tonsure ceremony has been performed" (*nirvṛttacauḍakānām*), because that rule applies to the entire caste (*jāti*).

But others have stated: "For uterine brothers, [impurity lasts] ten nights. Their intention is as follows: the giving away of an eight-year-old girl is prescribed; and since she has not been given away, the designation of *caula* (tonsure ceremony) has not yet occurred—just as it does not for a boy who has undergone initiation (*upanayana*)—and because no other ritual procedure is prescribed at that time, ten days alone is appropriate.

However, others have read: "But for unmarried girls and young boys, purification occurs on that very day. Regarding this, the commentators explain that even if an unmarried girl remains [unmarried] until she is nearly fifteen years of age, the impurity lasts for only that day; for there is no authority for allowing the passage of time while bypassing the primary scriptural injunction.

To this it is replied: What is the meaning of the phrase "and among children"? For it has already been stated in the grammatical analysis (*yogavibhāga*) that "until the eruption of teeth, purification is immediate. Nor is it proper for this [present rule] to annul that [previous one], because the former is general in nature while the latter is of the nature of establishing a specific regulation. Therefore, although this period of one day is mentioned separately, it is restricted to starting from the *cūḍā* ceremony onwards, since a general rule depends upon its particulars. Consequently, this half-verse is understood to be non-Vedic (*anārṣa*); it must be interpreted as having "contact" as its subject matter. For the prohibition of contact would have applied to a child just as it does to an adult in cases of death or birth impurity (*mṛtaka-sūtaka*). To that end, this might have been said: "But for those whose daughters have not been given away in marriage, and for children, purification is after one day. In this way, the locative case is taken as expressing the "object" (*viṣaya-saptamī*). And that is appropriate, as it is a case-ending denoting a factor of action (*kāraka-vibhakti*). Otherwise, one would have to supply an ellipsis and explain it as a locative denoting a condition (*bhāva-lakṣaṇā saptamī*), such as: "when children have died, purification for the living [occurs]. Furthermore, this is established by the fact that there is no impurity resulting from touching them; for that [impurity] finds its application in other contexts, because [the child] is covered by the ground, and contact is possible with what is covered by the ground.
If it is asked, "How can a specific meaning be understood when no distinction has been stated?", [the answer is:

because in the proximity of the statement "for him there exists the ritual procedure for sipping water" (Ācamanakalpa), such a specific contact is what is perceived. Furthermore, people do not desire the touch of a child who has been touched by a menstruating woman. Thus, this must be a qualification. Accordingly, Gautama stated that in his own Smṛti (GDh 14.44): "It is indeed proper to establish the sacred fires for him. Therefore, the definition of the time for establishing the fires is entirely appropriate. 5.71.
They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, and they should immerse themselves in water for three days;
they should not eat meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground. (5.72)

Regarding *kṣāralavaṇam*: *kṣāra* refers to alkaline substances such as barley-ash (*yavakṣāra*), and *lavaṇa* refers to salts such as rock salt (*saindhava*). They shall not consume these. Alternatively, the term *kṣāra* may serve as a qualifier for *lavaṇa*, whereby the prohibition applies specifically to [alkaline] salts, thus excluding *saindhava*. Furthermore, *nimajjana* refers to bathing in rivers, ponds, and so forth, provided it is not at a formal bathing place (*atīrtha*); it also implies the avoidance of rubbing the limbs with unguents and the like. The consumption of meat is also prohibited throughout the period of impurity according to other *Smṛtis*. Thus it is recited: "They shall not approach women, they shall not perform ritual purification, and they shall not eat meat. However, the author of the *Gṛhyasūtra* says: "For three days they should remain fasting, or subsist on what is purchased or obtained [by others]" (cf. ĀśG 4.4.15). They should sleep on the bare ground, avoiding contact with others. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) during the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) is also demonstrated in another *Smṛti*. (5.72)
This rule for impurity due to death has indeed been proclaimed for when one is present;
this procedure is to be understood as applicable by relatives and kinsmen when one is absent. (5.73)

It is placed there where he died, provided that [the relatives] were present; others, however, say that this rule applies only to those who were present at the time of departure. "Relatives" (saṃbandhin) refers to those entitled to offer water (samānodaka); "kinsmen" (bāndhava) refers to the sapinda relations.
Others, however, consider "absence" (asaṃnidhāna) to mean residing in another village or another city. || 5.73 ||
And among them,
if one hears that someone who has gone abroad has died within ten days [of the initial impurity],
he shall remain impure only for as long as remains of those ten nights. (5.74)

"A foreign land" (videśa) refers to another village and so forth, as previously explained. "Passed away" (vigata) means dead. "Within ten days" (anirdaśa) is an illustrative term; for whomever there is a period of impurity, the remainder of that period constitutes his impurity. The repeated mention of "ten nights" is for the purpose of completing the meter. With respect to the occurrence [of the event], the duration of impurity for birth and death must necessarily be determined according to the specific rule; when the birth or death has occurred, the calculation begins from that point for the ten-day period and so on, and not from the moment it is known by the *sapiṇḍas*. Therefore, even if the guest learns of the birth or death while the householder does not, the food is still unfit to be eaten. Likewise, in both cases, this [period] is merely the cause of the occurrence. For those who are impure for ten days, [the purification occurs] after that; but for those who are impure for three nights or one day, they become pure immediately upon bathing with their clothes on. (5.74)
If ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights;
but when a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water.

For whomever the period of impurity has been prescribed as ten days and so forth, for him there is a three-night [period] after that; but for whomever it is three days, one day, and so on, for him there is merely a bath with one's clothes after that. Thus, as he will state later: "with one's clothes" (MDh 5.76), etc. When a year has passed—meaning elapsed—one becomes pure simply by touching water and bathing; this is the meaning. Because of the statement beginning with "with the hand and the foot," the touching of all limbs is understood, and that is indeed the bath itself. (5.75)
Upon hearing of the death of a kinsman or the birth of a son after the ten-day period has passed, a person becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes. || 5.76 ||

This rule applies to those related by water (samānodaka). It also applies to sapinda relatives in the case of the three-day or one-day period of impurity. "With his clothes" means together with his garment; "having plunged into the water" means having bathed. (5.76)

If a child, one residing in another country, or a kinsman of a separate funeral offering (pṛthakpiṇḍa) has died, one becomes pure immediately by plunging into water along with one's clothes. || 5.77 ||

"In the case of a young son who has not yet cut his teeth," "in the case of one who has gone to another country," and "in the case of one who has died as a separate *piṇḍa* (pṛthakpiṇḍa)"—these phrases have the same meaning. A "separate *piṇḍa*" refers to one for whom the *samānodaka* relationship ceases. When such a person has died while residing in another country, purification is immediate (*sadyaḥ*). Regarding death in the presence [of the relatives], it has been stated: "But for those who offer water, purification occurs after three days" (MDh 5.63). || 5.77 ||
If death or birth should occur again within ten days, the Brāhmaṇa shall remain impure for as long as that [second period] has not yet passed its ten-day limit. (6.78)

Here too, the mention of "ten days" (*daśāha*) is intended as an illustration for the period of impurity (*āśauca*). If another cause for impurity arises while the period of impurity belonging to a particular person has not yet expired, purification occurs through the remainder of the first [period] alone; one must not, however, count ten days or the like starting from the day that the intervening [impurity] occurred. Thus says Gautama: "If that [impurity] should occur again within [the first], they shall be purified by the remainder of that" (GDh 14.6). Since no specific order is understood from the compound *maraṇajanmanī* ("death and birth") without further effort, and since an intervening occurrence could theoretically apply to either, it should be understood—based on established practice—that this refers only to [impurities] of the same kind. Furthermore, the word "again" (*punar*) is more effective when referring to things of the same kind. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is also intended as an illustration for all those subject to impurity. However, another Smṛti prescribes: "If [the period] remains for one night, [purification is] by two [days]; if at dawn, by three" (GDh 14.7–8). Having introduced the rule, "For this Brāhmaṇa, upon touching a corpse, there is ten-day impurity," the Smṛti continues: "If, in the interim, another death or birth should occur, he shall be purified by the remaining days alone. This Smṛti does not admit a distinction between those of the same kind and those of a different kind. (5.78)
When an Ācārya has passed away, they say that impurity lasts for three nights;
likewise for his son and his wife, it lasts for a day and a night—this is the settled rule. (5.79)

The teacher is the one who initiates [the student]. Upon his death, the student must observe impurity for three nights. Upon the death of that teacher’s son or wife, it lasts for a day and a night. (5.79)

Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has been initiated, one remains impure for three nights; for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, one remains impure for a night with its two flanks (a pakṣiṇī rātri).

A *śrotriya* is one who studies a branch of the Veda. An *upasaṃpanna* is one who has become associated with another through friendship or some other purpose, or one endowed with virtuous conduct. Previously, however, in the case of a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) who has not yet mastered the Veda, a period of one day was prescribed (MDh 5.70). In the lexicons, on the other hand, *upasaṃpanna* is a synonym for "dead. Because the period of impurity lasts for a long time, the former explanation is superior. Others, however, connect [the rule] as "three nights for a *śrotriya* maternal uncle," while [others] connect it as "a *pakṣiṇī* night" for disciples and so forth.

Relatives (*bāndhavāḥ*) include the brother-in-law, the maternal uncle’s son, and so forth. However, when there is a connection such as "for a maternal uncle, [one should observe] a *pakṣiṇī* [period]," then for the maternal uncle, the *pakṣiṇī* period is already established by virtue of his being a relative; the repetition [of this rule] is for the sake of making it obligatory. Therefore, in the case of other relatives, [the observance] is according to one's discretion. (5.80)
When the king has died, one who resides within his realm remains impure for as long as the light [of the sun] lasts;
but if the king is not learned in the Vedas, the impurity lasts for a full day, as does that for a teacher who is well-versed in the scriptures.

The word *rājan* (king) here functions by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote the mere social class (*varṇa*) that possesses qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*). For it says: "for whom [the king] resides in his domain. If it were to denote the lord of a domain delimited by a specific caste (*jāti*), there would be secondary indication, and that would not be the primary meaning of the word. *Sajyotiḥ*: it exists together with light (*jyotis*). If one dies during the day, [the offering is made] at that very time; however, at night, that [light] is absent. Likewise, at night, it is only night and not day. This itself is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in other instances, even when only "night" or "day" is mentioned, both day and night are understood—as in "by nights equal to months" (MDh 5.65) and "three days or one day" (MDh 5.59). But in the case of "and by one day" (MDh 5.63), the mention of "night" is for the purpose of completing the meter. At night, fire is the light. For thus it is said in the *Agnihotra-brāhmaṇa*: "By fire indeed, she is radiant with brilliance; by the sun, she is not [radiant with brilliance]" (cf. AitB 25.4).

In the case of one who is not a *śrotriya*—that is, one who does not study the Veda—the [impurity lasts] for the entire day; it does not occur at all during the night, even if the occasion (*nimitta*) arises during the night. But how can one be both a non-*śrotriya* and an *anūcāna*? For it is traditionally recorded in the Smṛti: "One who has studied the *Pravacana* along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*). True, a teacher (*pravaktṛ*) is also called *anūcāna*. Therefore, this rule regarding the day applies to one who somehow expounds the texts and meanings of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and so forth. And when the Guru is present—in his capacity as the primary object of honor—or in the case of the *Ācārya*, because there is no other rule [applying to them].

Some, however, connect the negative particle (*nañ*) with the word "non-Vedic scholar" (*aśrotriya*) in that rule; here, by the elision of the negative particle, they do not prescribe this rule for anyone who is the teacher of others. (5.81)
A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month. (5.82)

This [rule] is intended to exclude the alternatives of three or four days and so forth, which depend on the previously mentioned modes of livelihood (*vṛtta*) and other factors for Kṣatriyas and the rest. As for the ten-day period for a Brāhmaṇa, it is merely restated here. However, the following must be addressed: by what means is the attainment of a fixed time [of impurity] for Kṣatriyas and others precluded, such that this [text] is understood to serve the purpose of excluding other alternatives? For this very [text] is the source that establishes such a duration of time for them. Since this exists, the ten-day period therein is understood to be for the purpose of indicating that specific duration of impurity.

Nor, even though this [text] exists, does it serve merely as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*). For even when there is a general application to the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), those other options apply only to that for whom the ten-day period has been specifically stated. Furthermore, in another *Smṛti*, it is stated with the specific intention of referring to a Brāhmaṇa: "The Vedic study of a Brāhmaṇa may resume after one day," and so forth. However, regarding those other options prescribed in other *Smṛtis*, they are to be treated as alternatives (*vikalpyante*). Regarding the time of impurity on the eleventh day, a certain commentator says: "A Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after ten days. In this context, the mention of "days" (*ahar*) is intended to be significant; therefore, there is no impurity on the tenth night. Consequently, it is appropriate to perform the invitation (*nimantraṇa*) and other rites on the preceding day. Furthermore, for one who intends to establish the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), the impurity will have already commenced through the morning vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) and other such acts.

That is incorrect. If the intention were [merely] for the day, there would be no period of impurity even during the initial nights. If it is argued that [impurity] will apply there on account of the rule "impurity for ten days due to death" (MDh 5.59), what is the authority for the claim that this [rule] does not intend [the full period]? Therefore, it has been demonstrated that this word "day" (ahar) denotes a full day-and-night (ahorātra). And likewise, in the preceding verse, the inclusion of the word "entire" (kṛtsnam) in the phrase "an entire day" (MDh 5.81) was for the purpose of excluding the night. || 5.82 ||
One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one interrupt the rites performed with the sacred fires; furthermore, while performing that rite, even a kinsman does not become impure. (5.83)

For one who holds the view: "The ritual options (*kalpa*) such as the three-day period and others that have been mentioned are optional alternatives (*vikalpyante*) to the ten-day period, not according to a fixed rule based on conduct (*vṛtta*) and so forth; therefore, since another [longer period] is possible for a longer duration of time, why should I adopt the one-day option which causes hardship to one's daily Vedic study (*nityasvādhyāya*), when I shall instead resort to the ten-day period and remain in the ease of being free from ritual duties (*niṣkarmasukha*)?"—for him, out of kindness, that fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) is clarified: these are not equal, but are indeed fixed. And the fixed rule has already been shown previously. Otherwise, for one for whom a specific period of impurity (*āśauca*) is ordained, how could there be an increase beyond that time-limit, by virtue of which this [rule] would be meaningful? What fault is there in its meaning being clear?

Others, however, say that even regarding past days, as long as the acts such as bathing have not been performed, there is no purification at all. As he will state later: "A Brahmin is purified by water" (MDh 5.98). In that state, because of his impurity, one might think, "I shall not incur fault by not performing [the rites]," and thus fail to engage in bathing and other acts for the sake of purification. Regarding this, it is said: "One should not let them increase"—one must not delay when external impurity has persisted over past days.

As for those who claim that there is no impurity on the night belonging to the tenth day, it has been stated that they do not understand correctly. Thus Gautama, having stated (GDh 14.6) that when another period of impurity arises during the midst of an existing one, purification occurs by the remainder of the first, says (GDh 14.7)—considering that purification occurs by that same [remaining] night when only one night remains—"If a night remains, [one is purified] after two [days]."

"One should not suspend rites performed with the sacred fires (*agniṣu*). Since impurity would otherwise entail the cessation of all Śrauta and Smārta rites, this is stated: those rites performed with the fires, such as the evening *homa* and others, one should not suspend (*pratyūhet*)—that is, one should not omit them. *Pratyūha* means omission or non-performance. Nor should one perform them oneself, because it is said: "Nor [should] even a blood relative (*sanābhya*) perform that rite while being impure. If even a blood relative should not be impure, how much less so anyone else? Thus says the *Gṛhya-sūtra*: having stated, "The obligatory (*nitya*) rites should be suspended, except for those involving the *vaitāna* fires; some say also those in the domestic fire (*śālāgni*)," it adds, "Others should perform these" (PārG 3.1032–34). Furthermore, the establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) is not merely the performance of the *homa*; rather, it is the entire ritual procedure (*sāṅgaprayoga*), since it is only there that a human agent is possible. However, because the principal *homa* consists of the renunciation of a substance (*dravyatyāga*), it must be performed by oneself alone. Therefore, the *homa*, the *vaiśvadeva*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and similar rites are suspended. But for other rites, such as silent recitation (*japa*), the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), and so forth, suspension is not indicated. These are indeed obligatory (*nitya*). Therefore, permission is granted only for these others, since it is prohibited in another *Smṛti*: "The *homa* and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) are suspended" (ViPu 3.13.18).
