Thus, the determination is based on the distinction between what is obligatory and what is optional (*kāmya*). As for the optional, it must certainly not be performed due to impurity, as the qualification (*adhikāra*) to perform it has ceased.
But surely, even regarding obligatory rites (*nitya*), there is no entitlement for one who is impure;

nor is ritual purity (*śauca*) a constituent part [of the rite]. If it is argued that when an obligatory rite is performed with deficient qualities, it is not considered optional (*kāmya*), then [the answer is] that this occurs on account of this very scriptural statement.

Not so. Here, even though there is a means of knowledge [to the contrary], the possibility of another person performing these [rites] is permitted by the statement, "others might perform these for him. And that [permission] is appropriate in the case of obligatory (*nitya*) rites because they are deficient [in quality], but not in the case of optional (*kāmya*) rites.
However, regarding the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, authorities disagree; they cite another *smṛti*:
"In that case, one should not perform the oblation even with dry grain or fruits."
In this way, one should not perform the ritual of sacrifice during death or birth.

Therefore, the twilight oblations (*saṃdhyāhoma*), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and the annual rites beginning with that of the month of Āśvayuja must be performed. However, the commencement of the Vedic study (*upākaraṇa*) depends solely upon the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), not upon the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). 5.83.
Having touched a divākīrti, a woman in her courses, an outcaste, a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse, or one who has touched such a person, one becomes pure by bathing. (5.84)
The *divākīrti* is a *caṇḍāla*, because of his association with extreme impurity and because he is seen used in that sense in the *Mārjāramūṣika-saṃvāda* of the *Mahābhārata*:
"And even at that time, there was a *divākīrti* afflicted by fear" (*MBh* 12.136.106).

It is not the barber [who must bathe], because he is touchable and his food is fit to be eaten. As for the claim that this bathing is for him [the barber] when performing the work of shaving, that too need not be stated, because it is already established. When one necessarily causes the work of shaving to be done, the hairs touch the limbs; since those [hairs] have fallen from the body, they are impure, and thus bathing is established [as necessary]. "Tatspṛṣṭin" means one who has been touched by that which was touched by him (*tasya spṛṣṭam* = *tatspṛṣṭam*; one who has that is *tatspṛṣṭī*). That by which these [hairs] were touched must also be bathed indeed.

In this context, because everything is equally unrelated [to the impurity], some say that the connection with the phrase "one who has touched him" refers only to the corpse and not to those such as the *divākīrti* and others.

Others, however, maintain that because they occur within a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*), and because they are heard at the end [of the list], all of them are present in the intellect; therefore, they are referred to by the pronoun *tat* (in the compound *tatspṛṣṭi*). For here, having formed a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of everything up to "the corpse" (*śava*), there is a connection with the word *spṛṣṭi*. In that case, since the meaning of the compound as a whole is present in the intellect, it is grasped by the pronoun *tat*. Indeed, a connection of the word "corpse" alone with the word *spṛṣṭi* is not perceived, because it is mutually connected with "the outcast" (*patita*) and the others. Rather, the word "corpse" alone has a connection with the subsequent word [of the compound]. For in a copulative compound, each individual word denotes the entire sense. Consequently, all [the members] are proximate [to the pronoun]. Alternatively, even if one were to first connect the term *śavaspṛṣṭi* with the word *tatspṛṣṭi*, and subsequently connect it with the others, in that case, the outcasts and the rest would have no connection with the word *spṛṣṭi*. Therefore, the determination [of the meaning] is based solely on established usage (*samācāra*). (5.84)
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always recite, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to his enthusiasm and the *pāvamānī* verses according to his ability. (5.85)

The aforementioned [substances] are impure by virtue of their proximity. The *saura* mantras are those dedicated to the Sun, such as "ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam" (RV 1.50.1) and others. The *pāvamānyaḥ* are those recited in the ninth maṇḍala of the ten books, beginning with "svādiṣṭhayā" (RV 9.1.1). "According to one's enthusiasm" and "according to one's capacity" have the same meaning; two words are used here for metrical reasons. Because of the use of the plural number, the count of three must necessarily be observed. However, beyond that, if there is no lapse in more important duties, then the recitation (*japa*) must indeed be performed. By the mention of "mantras" and specifically "the *pāvamānyaḥ*," which refers to the Ṛgvedic verses, purification occurs even if the hymn (*sūkta*) is not completed, provided it exceeds three [verses]. A dog should also be included here; it too is indeed impure. And it is stated in Gautama’s work within this very section: "And [in the case] of a dog; some say [this applies] if it should strike [him]" (GDh 14.32–33). "Purified" (*prayataḥ*) means single-minded, intent on meditating upon the deity of the mantra and so forth. Alternatively, "purified" means when one is engaged in the worship of deities and the like, if one sees [an impurity], one should act at that very moment and not otherwise. 5.85.
Having touched a human corpse that is still moist with fat, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is no longer moist, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun.

A *nara* is a human being; thus, *nāra* refers to that which belongs to him—flesh, marrow, and so forth, smeared with moisture. The *ālambhana* of a cow is its touching. The seeing of the *arka* plant and the touching of the cow are presented as alternatives [for the ritual]. 5.86.
One who has been initiated shall not offer water libations until the completion of his vow;
but when it is completed, having offered the water libation, he becomes pure after three nights alone. (5.87)

*Ādeśa* means "instruction. Because of his connection with the instruction for the observance (*vratādeśana*), he is called a *brahmacārin* by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). For him who is established in the stage of studentship (*brahmacaryāśrama*), this is a prohibition against the offering of water for those sapinda-relations who have died [before him]. However, regarding those who died earlier, one should perform the daily libation (*anvāhika*) to the gods and ancestors, as it has been prescribed. The phrase "until the observance" (*ā vratasya*) means until the completion of the student's return home (*samāvartana*); it does not mean until an intermediate period of negligence or transgression. Upon the completion of the performance of the observances, having returned home, he should offer water for each of all [the deceased] on a single day and observe impurity (*āśauca*) for three nights. However, the offering of water for his mother is desired even for one under the vow; and there is no lapse of the vow in that case. They cite another Smṛti text: "One who has received instruction, though he has committed an offense, does not [offer] water. (5.87)
The water-libation rite shall be withheld for those born of illicit unions, for those who have failed in their religious vows, and for those who commit suicide. (5.88)

The word *jāta* is connected with each term individually: one who is born in vain (*vṛthājāta*) is he who does not worship the gods, the ancestors, or human beings. Regarding those who possess the entitlement [to Vedic rites] but belong to no stage of life (*anāśramī*), having abandoned both the offered and unoffered oblations—since great faults are heard of in scripture regarding remaining for a long time in such a state, as in the passage, "having remained without a stage of life for a year," and so forth—the status of subsisting on the food of others (*parapākarati*) applies to anyone other than the student (*brahmacārin*) and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). However, cooking for one's own sake is forbidden. Those of mixed birth (*saṃkarajāta*) are the Āyogavas and others born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) through the intermixture of different castes; they are included here because they are censured and because they are associated with those born in vain. Those born in the natural order (*anuloma*), however, although their origin is mixed, are not included here because they belong to the caste of their mother and possess the entitlement [to Vedic rites]. Furthermore, the designation "mixed origin" is not applied to those born in the natural order. As stated: "These of mixed origin are born from the inverse and the natural orders" (MDh 10.25). The sons of unauthorized women (*aniyuktā-suta*) and others are those born from association with multiple men, as are those born of prostitutes (*veśyājāta*). But the sons of other men’s wives (*pārastraiṇeya*) are considered born of mixed origin even in the absence of association with multiple men.

Some maintain that this prohibition applies to the sapindas and not to their sons; however, others hold that it applies even to the sons of those who have committed suicide. That is incorrect, because no such distinction is heard in the scriptures. Regarding those who have gone forth into external ascetic orders—such as the Bhagalas, the red-robed ones (Raktapatas), and so forth—they are ineligible [for inheritance], as indicated by the use of the plural number. These are called "external" due to the diversity of their vows, observances, and philosophical views. Men who commit suicide voluntarily abandon their bodies before the exhaustion of their lifespan. This is indeed permitted in the case of the elderly or those suffering from incurable, great diseases for whom medical treatment has been abandoned, as it has been said: [The text continues with the cited verse: "One should not cause the death of one who is ill, nor should one abandon a dying person. One should not give poison or a weapon to another. But one should assist the aged, the sick, and those afflicted by incurable diseases to cast off the body. Thus, while suicide is generally forbidden, it is accepted under these specific conditions. Furthermore, the rule regarding the sapindas does not extend to their sons. As stated: "The son of a woman who has been expelled, the son of one who has died while pregnant, the son of one who has committed suicide, and the son of one who has gone forth into an ascetic order—these four do not inherit property; rather, they shall receive maintenance. Therefore, the sons of those who have committed suicide do inherit, provided they are not themselves excluded by other rules. However, the sons of those who have entered external ascetic orders are not entitled to inheritance, as they have renounced worldly life. Thus, the prohibition against the sapindas of suicides does not apply to their sons, except in the case of those who have joined external sects. It is also established that for those who have been rejected by physicians and suffer from incurable diseases, voluntary death is permissible. Therefore, the sons of such individuals do inherit. (Note: The bracketed numbers [200] and [201] appear to be citation markers from the source text.)
An elder who, having lost the memory of purity and having rejected medical treatment,
puts an end to his own life by means of a precipice, fire, fasting, or water;
"For him, there is impurity for three nights; on the second day, the collection of bones [is performed];
on the third, having offered water, one should perform the *śrāddha* on the fourth.
This applies even to one afflicted by disease such as leprosy, as it is indeed intended for "one whose activities have ceased," even while in the state of a householder.
Those who have set out on the Great Departure (mahāprasthāna) do not wish to live in vain.

One whose activities are suspended is said to be incapable of performing purification rites and the like, as well as the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana) and so forth. Or, as it is said: "Whether his body is not yet decayed, he might bring about his own destruction, or whether his activities are not yet suspended. Therefore, permission is granted for the opposite case. In other Smṛtis, the prohibition of water-libations (udakakriyā) is prescribed for others as well. As it has been stated: "And for those slain by kings, or by horned animals, fanged beasts, or reptiles..."
One should not perform a śrāddha for those who have abandoned their own selves.
Whatever water, food offerings, and other gifts are given to the departed spirits, none of it reaches them; it perishes in mid-air.
Out of fear of public reproach, men should perform the Nārāyaṇabali;
therefore, food accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā) must be given even to these [outcastes].
Likewise, elsewhere it is said: "Death from a Caṇḍāla, from water, from a serpent, from a Brāhmaṇa, from lightning,
and from fanged beasts— these are the modes of death for those who have performed the acts of purification."
And so it has been said:
"For men who set fire [to the pyre], those who perform the bathing and adornment,
and for the followers who shed tears, purification occurs through two *taptakṛcchra* penances."
Therefore, his funeral rites must not be performed by others,
nor should even the name of his lineage be used by them.
For that most wicked one dwelling in the ultimate hell, the cause is even greater:
the mere mention of his name brings terror to all.

In these very rites, Saṃvarta has prescribed the Sāntapana penance, Parāśara the Taptakṛcchra, and Vasiṣṭha the Cāndrāyaṇa together with the Taptakṛcchra; in this regard, distinctions such as whether the act is unprecedented (apūrva) and so forth may be disregarded.

Regarding what was stated, beginning with "from a Caṇḍāla, from water," and concluding with "death [is the fate] of those who perform evil deeds"—therein this doubt arises: Does this rule concerning the non-performance of funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) and the performance of penance (*prāyaścitta*) apply to one such as a Caṇḍāla who intentionally causes his own death, or rather to one who has fallen into it through negligence and does not desire it? Why the doubt? Here, Gautama states: "If they [die] by means of fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [down a precipice], provided they are desirous [of death]" (GDh 14.12). Yet here, it is heard without qualification: "from a Caṇḍāla, from water. Since there is a single scriptural authority (*ekaśāstra*) due to another Smṛti, the term "desirous" (*icchatām*) must necessarily be connected to the phrase "from water. Because of their association, the suspicion arises that the same applies elsewhere as well. Furthermore, it is heard: "of those who perform evil deeds" (*pāpakarmaṇām*). An "evil deed" (*pāpa-karman*) is a prohibited act. It is logical that one who performs a prohibited act is an "evil-doer. And the status of being a performer occurs either through one's own action or by instigating another. In this context, lightning, fanged beasts, horned animals, and the like are not meant; for these do not instigate, nor are they like pits, water, or swords where one might be an independent agent (*svatantra-kartṛ*) by entering them to kill oneself. Rather, the scripture makes known that he to whom such a death has befallen was an evildoer in a previous birth, just as those with black teeth and others are. But even so, what is the point of making this known? It would imply that those with missing limbs and the like are connected to past sins, and thus penance must be performed as stated by Vasiṣṭha—some performing two *kṛcchra* penances, some even more. However, since the agency of connection with death has been taken away [by the scripture itself], there is no purpose in this. Or, if it were determined that he was an evildoer, then anyone who had entered into matrimonial, domestic, or sacrificial relations (*yauna-maukha-srauva*) with him would also become an evildoer. Yet such is not the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭas*); for those who have formed such a relationship are not troubled by anyone, nor do they perform penance. Therefore, it is inferred that [the rule applies] to those who are desirous [of death].
However, since some read "of those killed by cows or Brahmins" in another Smṛti text and then read "of those who abandon themselves" separately, it appears that this is a specific case.

Therefore, a doubt arises: what is appropriate here? [The answer is: "of those who desire [it]. Why? Because of the mention of "evil-doers. He who, by his own will, engages in an activity that causes his own death has transgressed the scriptural injunction: "Therefore, one who desires heaven should not depart before the end of his natural lifespan" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.2.6.7). And he is rightly designated as an evil-doer.
But has it not been said that they are not like swords and such, whereby their killing could occur by mere wish?

It is said: he who does not guard against negligence has indeed committed that [transgression]. Therefore, even if a man traveling alone through a forest teeming with *caṇḍālas* and bandits has no desire such as "May the *caṇḍālas* kill me," nevertheless, because he has not avoided negligence by engaging in conduct appropriate for that situation, there is certainly a transgression of the scripture (*śāstra*). Likewise, if one crosses a river with one's arms or boards a doubtful boat steered by an unskilled helmsman, if he perishes—whether due to the loss of momentum or from the overturning of the boat—he is rightly considered an evildoer. Furthermore, if bathers were carried away after failing to recognize the depth or the presence of crocodiles and sharks by means of a pole or other means, they would not be culpable. Similarly, if one has boarded a boat with firm mooring-ropes, a sturdy rudder, and is being propelled by a skillful, attentive, and capable steersman, and should suddenly encounter a thick mass of water due to a swift, rising wind or a whirlwind, and perish by drowning, he would not transgress the scripture. Likewise, if one is bitten and perishes without avoiding a place infested by snakes, he would certainly incur demerit, and not otherwise. Similarly, if one sees a cow with sharp horns or an elephant and does not flee far away, and is killed, a transgression is appropriate in this case. Likewise, if lightning is flashing in the forest during the rains and one does not enter a village or city, there is certainly wickedness; but if lightning should somehow strike someone staying within a village, then he commits no fault. Therefore, it is proper to perform actions exactly as prescribed.
In that context, the prohibition of water-libations is intended to indicate the exclusion of all post-mortem rites (aurdhvadehika), since this has been cited in another Smṛti. || 5.88 ||
And for women who have resorted to heresy, those who act according to their lust, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor. || 5.89 ||

Heresy (*pāṣaṇḍa*) consists in abandoning the scriptures and resorting to external doctrines, such as wearing human skulls, red garments, and so forth. Those who rely on that [heresy] are those who have adopted its specific marks and are subject to its doctrines. "Acting according to desire" (*kāmacāra*) refers to the sexual union with one or many other men by following mere whim, through the abandonment of proper conduct and family standing. "Malice" (*droha*) consists in giving poison, [deadly] herbs, and so forth to her husband, or causing an abortion. "Drinking liquor" (*surāpya*) refers to the consumption of that which is prohibited, according to the specific prohibition.

On this point, someone says: "A Brahmin shall not drink *surā*. Even though there is no distinction in the meaning of the genus (*jāti*), because of the gender (*liṅga*), the prohibition applies only to the male Brahmin and not to the female. Although the genus is one and the same for both male and female, nevertheless the genders of "femaleness" (*strītva*) and "maleness" (*puṃstva*) differ. And here, since the word "Brahmin" is heard as having the masculine gender, what occasion is there for the unmentioned [female]? Just as in the case of "One should have a Brahmin woman drink [the mixture] for the sake of a son," one does not have a man drink it; likewise, when the masculine gender is heard, females are not included. In some cases, however, the gender is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). For example, in "A Brahmin must not be killed," the prohibition is understood to apply to the female as well. In that case, because the Brahmin is the object most desired (*īpsitatama*) by virtue of the accusative case ending, he possesses primacy (*prādhānya*). And in the case of the primary element, nothing other than the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—such as gender or number—is intended to be significant. For example, in "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), the cleansing does not apply to only one cup. But here, in the case of "Wine must not be drunk by a Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇena surā na peyā*), because [the Brahmin] is designated with respect to the action as an instrument by way of being the agent (*kartṛtā*), even though he is expressed by the verb (*ākhyāta*) in the form "A Brahmin shall not drink wine," the meaning of the nominal stem is established through the occurrence [of the agent] within the function of those [verbal meanings]. Thus, the nominative case is consistent with the instrumental, and [the Brahmin] becomes a subordinate factor (*guṇībhāva*). And regarding a subordinate factor, everything that is explicitly stated (*śruta*) is intended to be significant. For example, in "One should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), a male animal is sacrificed, and it is one.

To this it is replied: In this context, the second and third [cases] are not the cause for non-intention (*avivakṣā*) and intention (*vivakṣā*) based on the status of subordinate (*guṇa*) and primary (*pradhāna*); rather, they are based on what is already established (*prāpti*) and what is not yet established (*aprāpti*). That which is not already established and is logically possible as the object of an injunction (*vidhi*) is intended, because it is understood through words that do not have another purpose. However, when something else already known from another source is taken up for the sake of an injunction, it is presented by the word precisely as it was understood through that other means of knowledge, in its capacity as being connected to another enjoined action. In the sentence "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," the injunction culminates in the prohibition itself; whatever else there is, that has been understood from another source. As for the intention regarding the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is due to the consequence of the scriptural statement becoming meaningless (*śruti-ānarthakya-prasaṅga*). But regarding gender, number, and so forth—which are the meanings of the suffix—it is possible for them to be mentioned even as incidental (*nāntarīyakatvena*); thus, intention and non-intention are spoken of in their case. In this matter, a person is not to be impelled toward an action by an injunction on account of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, because such a person would act spontaneously out of aversion (*dveṣa*), and because everyone here is already spontaneously engaged in that [act]. Indeed, a prohibition that is not itself enjoined cannot in any way be syntactically connected. Since it is not established from another source, since it is not a factor of action (*kāraka*), and since it is not a qualifier of a factor of action, it does not obtain a connection even by entering into the nature [of the action] (*svabhāvānupraveśena*). Therefore, for the sake of establishing its syntactic connection (*anvaya*), its status as the object (*viṣaya*) of the injunction must be sought. And once that [prohibition] has been made the object by the injunction, the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*) is required as the object. Since the verbal root-meaning has already had its objective portion grasped by the prohibition, it has fallen away from that [objective role]; and since its performance is already established through worldly activity (*laukikī pravṛtti*), it does not even desire entry for the sake of establishing its own injunction. Rather, while requiring only the qualification of the person entitled (*adhikāra*), it establishes the person—who has been understood through another means of knowledge to be the agent of killing—as the one entitled, and thus attains connection by way of those qualifiers. Thus, the theory of "expression of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*) is established. Therefore, because the verbal root-meaning along with its qualifiers is not the object of an injunction, worldly activity must be accepted. And there exists activity characterized by passion (*rāga*); in that case, there is no restriction of gender or number, whether due to passion or aversion. Consequently, a word whose meaning is not the object of an injunction, having abandoned its denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) because it refers to a meaning already understood from another source, indicates (*lakṣayati*) the object exactly as its nature has been determined by another means of knowledge. In that regard, since gender and number are not denoted by the word through its primary intention (*tātparya*), how could there be intention? Gender and number are mentioned merely for the sake of pointing out the nominal stem; some form of expression must be used, for a bare root (*prakṛti*) is not to be employed—this is the reason for the inclusion of gender and number.

Therefore, this is the understanding here: one who has resolved upon the state of being the agent (*kartṛbhāva*) with respect to killing is enjoined to the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). Consequently, in a prohibitive sentence, the hearing of the accusative case-ending is not a factor when it is not intended to be significant. For even where the instrumental or nominative case is heard—as in "A Brāhmaṇa should not drink" (*brāhmaṇena na pātavyā*) or "A Brāhmaṇa should not drink" (*brāhmaṇo na pibet*)—there too, that [agent] is restated (*anūdyate*) because its meaning is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), since it is already established from another source. In those cases, the instrumental and nominative are connected precisely as qualifiers of the qualification (*adhikāraviśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, even when the accusative is heard, that which is not already established is intended to be significant because it is something to be enjoined, as in "One should approach one's wife" (*bhāryām upagacchet*) or "One should procreate offspring" (*apatyam utpādayet*). For the purpose of a wife is not worldly, since that is accomplished by the very act of marriage (*upayamana*).

Nor is it taken up by an injunction in another sentence such that it could be referred to according to its perception, as in the cases: "He takes the Āśvina cup" (TB 2.6.1.5), "He takes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup" (TS 6.4.8), and "The Adhvaryu takes these ten" (ŚāṅB 14.2), where the cups are indeed taken up as qualified by a specific number. Therefore, because their number is already determined, they are referred to in the injunction for wiping according to the perceived number. But here, since there is no other sentence and this very [sentence] is the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*), there is no authority for abandoning the number heard in the text; thus, the abandonment of the single [cup] presented by the independent expressive power of the word would arise solely from human intellect. Similarly, in the case of "One should sacrifice with an animal" (KS 8.1), because the injunction has the sacrifice as its object and because that [sacrifice], being of the nature of something to be accomplished, requires a means, when the thing to be enjoined is presented together with its qualifiers and the ritual action, if the operation of the injunction is not completed by the mere object, why would those things required by the meaning expressed by words intent on their own meanings not be brought forward?

Those who know the science of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-śāstra*), however, state the injunction themselves and merely immerse themselves in what has been said by others. But that which has been stated by us is easy to grasp through simple means; no extensive scholarly proficiency is required here. This much alone is its essence. That much is the knowledge useful for the practice [of the rite]; anything beyond that is mere boastfulness and is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). For it is from an explanatory praise that a specific understanding arises where the requirement of the injunction remains unfulfilled. As it has been said: when there are many means of food, such as ghee, oil, salt, and so on, and it is not determined by the injunction "he places [it]" as to which one, it is understood that it is "with ghee. However, since the performance [of the rite] during the nights is not heard of, when there is a requirement, the explanatory praise "they find firm standing" leads to the understanding that it is "for one desiring firm standing. Here, moreover, because the meaning of the word "Brāhmaṇas" is complete, the requirement is satisfied; thus, the explanatory praise is intended merely as a eulogy. Now, if this is presented merely as an observation of a sign (*liṅga-darśana*), namely, "eating the sacrificial oblation of the gods" (MDh 11.94), then—just like the statement "the inferior follows the superior"—that too is based on a partial restatement since eating is prohibited for men, and thus it has no foundation. Furthermore, women indeed do consume the remnants of the gods' food, such as clarified butter and other offerings. And there is a Vedic citation in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites: "Thou art the deed of the knower" (ĀśŚ 1.11.1). Nor is their drinking inferred from the injunction "one should have the performer of the Śrāddha drink liquor," for that refers only to the taking of [liquor] in cases such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, the negation applies to mere birth; this is the conclusion regarding this point of contention. || 5.89 ||
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or guru who has passed away, the observer of a vow is not deprived of his vow. (5.90)

He considers the word *sva* (one's own) to be an epithet of the teacher (*ācārya*), because the rule "when the teacher’s teacher is present" (MDh 2.205) extends [the status of the teacher] to that [teacher's teacher] as well; thus, this prohibition applies even to such a teacher.

Others, however, explain the word *sva* as referring to a kinsman (*bāndhava*). In that case, however, it would not be necessary to mention "the father and the mother"; rather, their mention is for the sake of establishing a constant rule (*nityārtha*).

The teacher [is the one] referred to by the statement, "Whether little or much" (MDh 2.149). By the force of what is heard [in the text], he shows that there is no loss of the vow for one who carries these [bodies] out; the established meaning of the words is that one is separated from this [vow] only after carrying out others. 5.90.
One should carry out a deceased Śūdra through the southern city gate;
however, for the twice-born, one should do so through the western, northern, or eastern gates as appropriate.

Regarding the phrase "through the city gate," the mention of the "city" (*pura*) is intended as an illustration for villages and other settlements as well. This rule applies where there is the possibility of multiple gates. This instruction is given according to the preference of each individual. Furthermore, because it is inauspicious, the sequence of castes is taught beginning with the Śūdra; therefore, the Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa should be connected respectively with the western and subsequent directions as appropriate. (5.91)
There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those performing sacrifices;
for they always abide in the station of Indra, having become one with Brahman.

Although the word *rājan* refers to the Kṣatriya caste, nevertheless, because the reason is provided here—namely, "those who occupy the station of Indra"—it is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as denoting the lords of territories. We shall explain this more precisely in the following verse. The term *vratinaḥ* refers to those practicing vows, such as those engaged in the *Cāndrāyaṇa* and other penances. The term *satriṇaḥ* refers to those performing the *Gavāmayana* sacrifice or consecrated (*dīkṣita*) for another sacrifice. Thus says Gautama: "For those who are not officiating priests, for the consecrated, and for celibates" (GDh 14.1). Here is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): Kings who have attained the status of *brahman*—that is, those who occupy the station of Indra, the position of sovereignty, and the lordship over subjects—and who are practitioners of vows and performers of sacrificial sessions (*sattra*), [are exempt from] the fault of sin (*agha*), that is, impurity (*āśauca*).
Others, however, consider "satrin" to refer to those constantly engaged in giving;
yet, according to its primary application, it denotes a specific type of sacrifice. (5.92)
Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his position of high authority;
the reason for this is his seat [of power], intended for the protection of his subjects. (5.93)

That place whose nature is great is "māhātmaka. That state in which a man resides and protects his subjects is called *māhātmya*, and that is sovereignty over the subjects. As it has been said: "And the seat (*āsana*) is the cause here. Thus it is stated: it is not merely birth [that qualifies one], but rather the authority to protect the subjects. Furthermore, the word *āsana* (seat) here does not refer to a physical chair or bed; rather, it refers to the duties of one who has attained that position. Therefore, even if a non-Kṣatriya is capable of protecting the subjects, the ancient commentators have explained that for him too there is indeed an absence of ritual impurity (*āśauca*). "For the sake of protecting the subjects" means that there is not a total cessation of all impurity for everyone; rather, that maintenance of impurity which is an obstacle to protecting the subjects is what ceases. For example, in times of famine and the like, the support of the subjects through the distribution of food from one's own treasury, as well as the performance of pacification rites (*śānti*) during celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial portents—these must be performed by the king, even if he is suddenly occupied with other matters. Alternatively, when doubts regarding Dharma arise among the twice-born in the various stages of life (*āśrama*), there is also the duty of being an expounder at the first sacrifice and so forth; that too is a purpose [for the exemption]. (5.93)
And for those killed in a riot or in battle, by lightning or by a king, or for the sake of a cow or a Brahmin, or for whomever the king so desires. || 5.94 ||

*Ḍimba* refers to a tumultuous crowd or a quarrel involving many people without weapons; *āhava*, *saṃgrāma*, and *yuddha* all mean battle. In these cases, there is immediate purification for those who have been killed. *Vidyut* (lightning) and *aśani* (thunderbolt)—this has already been explained. A *pārthiva* is anyone who is a lord of the earth or of the four castes. For one killed for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow, even outside of battle, as well as for one killed by water, fire, or fanged creatures, there is immediate purification. And for whomever the king desires [to be purified immediately], such as one authorized to carry out his own affairs or for the sake of protection. (5.94)

Whence is this [conclusion]? Because for kings, the cessation of impurity occurs only through the act of protection; how then could there be a cessation for anyone else, without distinction, merely by his will?
"The king bears the body of the eight guardians of the world: Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vittapati, and Yama. (5.95)
Vapu is a portion of Tejas; Vaiśravaṇa is the lord of wealth; Varuṇa is the lord of the waters. || 5.95 ||
Right here follows a second explanatory statement (arthavāda):
"A king presided over by Lokeśa is not subject to impurity;
for the purity and impurity of mortals arise from and dissolve back into the worlds. (5.96)

The king is presided over by these lords of the worlds; he has neither purity nor impurity, because mortals—that is, human beings—have authority over these two. Furthermore, the origin and dissolution, the engagement and withdrawal of those two, belong to mortals in relation to the worlds, but not to the lords of the worlds themselves. (5.96)

For one whose hand is engaged in the duty of a Kshatriya with weapons raised in battle, the sacrifice is immediately completed and so too is the period of impurity; such is the established rule. (5.97)

That by which one is praised or slain is a weapon (*śastra*). Therefore, even when one is killed by means of stones, clubs, and the like, the sacrificial rite (*yajñasaṃsthā*) is completed; it is not only by weapons such as swords and so forth. A battle (*saṃgrāma*) is called *āvaha* where those competing with one another are summoned for combat. The duty of a Kṣatriya (*kṣatradharma*) consists of not turning one's back [in battle] and being employed by a lord for the sake of the subjects. It concludes—that is, reaches its end—immediately (*sadyaḥ*). The sacrifice (*yajña*), such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, is joined with its merit; that is to say, [the sacrificer] is endowed with its merit. Impurity (*āśauca*) likewise lasts only immediately [after death].

On this point, some connect the word "immediately" (*sadyaḥ*) with the phrase "one slain according to the duty of a Kṣatriya. Consequently, they maintain that this rule applies only to one who has died on the battlefield, and not to one who dies on another day or elsewhere.
This, however, must be examined. 5.97.
A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya, his mount or weapon;
a Vaiśya, his goad or reins; and a Śūdra who has performed his duties, his staff. (5.98)

When the period of impurity (*āśauca*) for ten days or other such durations has been completed, this further duty must be performed. It was explained previously that "having touched water" (*apaḥ spṛṣṭvā*) prescribes bathing. The phrase "having performed the rite" (*kṛtakriyaḥ*) refers to Kṣatriyas and the other castes; and since no other rite is mentioned, the "rite" here is specifically bathing. Having bathed, they may touch vehicles and other such items. Others, however, say it refers to the performance of the *śrāddha* rite. By performing the *śrāddha* and so forth, everyone becomes pure. In that case as well, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by touching water with his hand, while Kṣatriyas and others do so by means of vehicles and the like. (5.98)
This purification regarding sapinda relatives has been declared to you, O best of the twice-born; now learn the rules for the purification after death concerning all those who are not sapindas. 5.99.
The first and second halves of the verse serve the purpose of introducing and stating the connection between the preceding and subsequent subjects. (5.99)

Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as if for a kinsman; the same applies to the maternal relatives of his mother. (5.100)

"Like a kinsman" means according to the law of dharma, not by means of a purchase price. "And those who are related to the mother": the inclusion of the word *āpta* (related) is for the purpose of including close kinsmen such as maternal uncles and others. From this it is inferred that one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* or not a *samānodaka* is not anyone other than a *sapiṇḍa*. (5.100)
If he eats their food, however, he becomes pure in ten days;
if he does not eat their food, he is purified in a single day, provided he does not dwell in that house.

For one who does not eat but remains [in the village], it is exactly three nights as previously stated; for one who does not eat but does not remain [in the village], it is exactly one day; and for one who both eats and remains [in the village], it is exactly ten days. || 5.101 ||
If one follows a deceased person out of desire, whether they be a relative or a stranger, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. 5.102.

Following after [a corpse] means following it with conscious intent; if one follows it by any other means, there is no requirement for bathing with one's clothes on. Touching fire and consuming clarified butter are prescribed as the causes of purification for such a person. 5.102.
While his own kinsmen are present, he must not have a deceased Brahmin carried by a Śūdra;
for that oblation, defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven. (5.103)

One should not cause [the body] to be carried away nor have it removed while members of one's own kin of the same caste are present; because of the mention of the *āhuti* (oblation), one should not burn [the body]. The mention of the *vipra* (Brahmin) is not restrictive; for even in the case of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, the touch of a Śūdra is indeed a fault, as the prohibition is understood from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). 5.103.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, smearing [with clay], wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the agents of purification for embodied beings. (5.104)

Knowledge and the other [factors] are cited as examples for the purification of time; likewise, these are the causes of purification with respect to their own respective objects. In this same way, time also should not be suspected here. The fact that each of these serves as a cause of purification in a particular instance will be stated right here in this section, while for others, it will be stated in their respective places.

In this context, *jñāna* is that which is taught through Sāṃkhya and Yoga. For by means of it, through the removal of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of ignorance, one attains faultless knowledge upon the destruction of passion and other defects. And it will be stated: "The intellect is purified by knowledge" (MDh 5.108). *Tapaḥ* refers to penances such as the *Kṛcchra* and *Cāndrāyaṇa*. That is the cause of purification for major and minor sins (*pātaka* and *upapātaka*). Fire [is the purifier] in the case of earthenware and similar objects, according to the rule: "by re-baking" (MDh 5.121). Food consists of pure substances such as milk and roots; that too, like austerity, purifies. The fact that earth and water are causes of purification is well known. Regarding the mind, it will be stated: "the mind [is purified] by truth" (MDh 5.108). *Upāñjana* is the smearing of monasteries and the like with lime, cow dung, and so forth, as well as sweeping and anointing. Wind [is the purifier] in the case of grass, wood, and the like touched by outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) and others when they have fallen from a chariot. *Karma* refers to rites such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). And it has been said: "Standing and reciting the morning twilight prayer, one removes the sin of the night" (MDh 2.102). This has been explained in the second book.

Although austerity is indeed an action (*karman*), it is taught separately for the purpose of indicating its preeminence; moreover, in the scriptures, austerity is generally specified as distinct from action, as in the passage: "Those devoted to action, those devoted to austerity" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.219). || 5.104 ||
Of all forms of purity, purity in respect to wealth is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure in respect to wealth is truly pure, not he who is purified by clay and water. (5.105)
What is the relevance of this?

Just as one who has voided excrement in earth, water, or a clean place proceeds without delay, so too, when one stumbles through negligence by stealing another's property or the like, a means of purification (*prāyaścitta*) must be resorted to immediately for the sake of cleansing. This will be explained in the eleventh [chapter]. (5.105)
The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts, by charity;
those whose sins are concealed, by the recitation of prayers; and those most learned in the Vedas, by austerity. (5.106)

Those who are wise are purified by forbearance alone; for they are not afflicted by hatred, envy, or avarice. Thus, even when evil deeds have been committed, they remain eternally pure. Forbearance is a quality of the mind, consisting of equanimity toward all things. Even regarding the gift, its efficacy in removing the stain of killing has been stated in such passages as, "By giving, one washes away the slaughter" (MDh 11.138). Furthermore, for those whose sins are concealed, the recitation of mantras (*japa*) has indeed been prescribed in the section on secret penances. For those learned in the Vedas, austerity consists of the study of the Vedas and knowledge itself, as it is said: "For a Brāhmaṇa, austerity is knowledge" (MDh 11.234). However, penances such as the *kṛcchra* are the cause of purification for everyone, not only for those learned in the Vedas. (5.106)
That which requires cleansing is purified by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.

In the case of rivers whose waters have diminished on both banks and are defiled by impurity, the water of that very river becomes pure through its own current when it has reached its full force and is eroding its banks. This is not like other ground, for regarding the purification of such ground, there is no such understanding as there is for riverbanks—namely, that "ground is purified by five means" (MDh 5.122).

Alternatively, this statement—"by the current of the river"—is made because of the suspicion of impurity arising from contact with an impure flow in a fast-moving stream. It should not be thought that a river does not become pure even if it is touched by impure flows from this side and that side.
When no physical transgression is observed, a woman whose mind is corrupted by contemplating the beauty and virtues of another man is purified by the flow of menstrual blood during her season.

Renunciation will be described in the sixth chapter; by that, the best of the twice-born become pure. This does not apply in any way to mental misconduct. Whatever was thought by the ignorant—such as the killing of minute living beings—is removed from them. (5.107)
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the elemental self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom. 5.108

The qualified agent is precisely this: the person who is the inner self (*antarātman*); the internal organ, which is the mind (*manas*); the intellect (*buddhi*); and the body, which is the locus of experience. Since the sense organs are composed of the elements (*bhautika*), they are not counted separately. In this context, one thing is purified by another. The statement, "But everything [is purified] by time," is intended as a praise.

By the word "limbs" (*gātrāṇi*), he indicates the whole by means of its parts. Through water—that is, through bathing—the body is purified. But the mind consists of both the real and the unreal; its impurity arises from improper intention (*asat-saṃkalpa*), and that is removed by truth, which is to say, by a virtuous intention (*sat-saṃkalpa*). Although the mind was previously stated to be the cause of purification [in verse 5.104], this statement regarding speech does not imply that speech effects the purification of the mind. Thus says the Śruti: "Speech speaks only when impelled by the mind; for the speech of one whose mind is elsewhere is indeed demonic (*asuryā*), not pleasing to the Vedas" (AitB 9.4).

The elemental self (*bhūtātmā*) becomes purified when endowed with knowledge—arising from the study of Sāṅkhya and Vedānta—and with austerity, such as the *kṛcchra* penance. The word "elemental" (*bhūta*) here refers to the ultimate reality (*tattva*). This is the absolute Self, which is known through the non-reified notion of "I," and it should not be understood as the elemental self consisting of the body. The intellect (*buddhi*) becomes defiled by perceiving the forms of objects that do not exist, as in dreams and the like, through an attachment to objects imagined according to false doctrines; thus, it errs by determining a false distinction between the real nature of the object and its form. Alternatively, that intellect which is born of unexhausted evil karma from previous births, or produced by each individual misdeed—the innate ignorance of the Self characterized by the grasping of non-difference, or characterized by the lack of discrimination between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the Self, taking the form of attachment to wealth, children, and so forth, and being the cause of excessive craving—is purified by knowledge. This knowledge consists of the cultivation of valid means of cognition based upon the self-luminous [Self]. The purification of the intellect occurs through the ascertainment of its changelessness, established by the fact that there is a distinction between the intellect and its objects, that the object possesses form, and that the transformation of the intellect into the form of the object is not proven [to be real].
And in the preceding [verse], *vidyā* is indeed the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas; its status as a cause is like that in the verse, "As fire by its heat [consumes] fuel" (MDh 11.245).

Thus, being pure and purified, one attains the world of Brahman—this is that fourfold purification. This is a praise [of the practice of *brahmacarya*], stating that just as these purifications are causes for the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), so too is this [practice] in the acts of procreation and so forth. 5.108.
This decision regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you;
now hear the decision concerning the purification of various kinds of substances.

[This refers to] various kinds of substances of many types—substances that serve as implements, distinguished by being fiery, earthen, liquid, solid, separate, combined, functional, and so forth. By this [verse], he states the distinction from the previous form of purity. In that [previous case], purity consisted in the predominance of the intellect (buddhi) over the self; for substances, however, it arose from their being appropriated by that [intellect]. Here, however, it is the reverse. Listen to the definitive conclusion. This verse is intended to show that the purpose is not identical to that of the preceding one. 5.109.
The purification of luminous gems, as well as of all stone-made objects,
has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth.

"Metallic substances" (*taijasa*) are those which become liquid through contact with fire, such as silver, gold, copper, iron, tin, lead, and so forth. "Jewels" (*maṇi*) are those resembling crystal. "Stone" (*aśman*) is a rock; a vessel made from it is "made of stone" (*aśmamaya*). The word "of all" (*sarvasya*) is for the purpose of completing the meter. The objects of meditation (*ālambana*) are stones from mountains and those found in rivers. Since they share the same function as ash, clay and ash are treated as alternatives (*vikalpyete*); water, however, is to be combined with them. But what, then, is the function here?

The removal of stains and odors. It has been stated: "Purification from impurity consists in the removal of stains and odors" (GDh 1.42), and here too it is said: "As long as [the stain] does not depart from that which is smeared with impurity" (MDh 5.124). In this regard, the coarseness of the substance is the same for both earth and ash; purification occurs through the difference in the effect caused by oiliness. The rendering of the impure into a state of purity is the fitness for social interaction resulting from the removal of transgression.
If this is so, then impurity must be defined: "This thing, being in contact with that, is impure.
But surely, worldly objects will be understood in that matter by the world itself.

It is not so; only the general [notion] is known from common worldly usage. That which is loathsome due to contact with urine, feces, or blood is called "impure" (*aśuci*) in the world. That which is unfit for actions such as touching is impure. And how that unfitness arises must be discerned from the scripture (*śāstra*) alone. Furthermore, one who does not stumble over the property of others and so forth is called "pure. Therefore, nothing is established here by this worldly consensus regarding the nature of things. Even if it were established that "that which is struck down is impure," the fact that "this is struck down by that" cannot be established without a specific scripture.

But how, then, can there be a determination of specific categories of things from the treatise (*śāstra*), given that the treatise is an authority only with respect to what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) and not for the establishment of existing entities, as is the case with Pāṇini? This is because the *smṛtis* of Manu and others are accepted as being rooted in the Veda.

It is said: there certainly exists an inference based on a positive injunction (*vidhi*) to the effect that "one should not engage in transaction with that which is defiled by this substance. There is no contradiction in understanding that whatever causes the prohibition of transaction through contact is the cause of the corruption (*upaghāta*). Likewise, regarding purification (*śuddhi*), one can establish its basis in a positive injunction as follows: "One should engage in transaction with a substance that has been corrupted, provided that the prescribed acts such as washing have been performed. Furthermore, the meaning of the injunction is not that "purification must be performed"; for if that were the case, one would incur sin by failing to do so. Rather, since in a worldly transaction aimed at a visible purpose one might naturally proceed with any vessel—whether pure or otherwise—due to one's desire, the scriptural rule (*niyama*) is established: "When there is a need, one should transact using a vessel of this kind, and not one that is not of this kind."

But surely, under the view that [the rule] is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), only one who seeks spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*) has the entitlement; for anyone else, there would be the contingency of [incurring] desire-driven action (*kāmaprasaṅga*). As it is said in the discussion on correct and incorrect words: "Even though there is no difference in their capacity to denote meaning, there is a restriction regarding merit and demerit" (*Vākyapadīya* 3.3.30). True, provided there were no prohibition against an impure recipient. But since there is a prohibition, how could there be any transaction with one whose purification has not been performed? The injunction for purification is merely a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). In the case of a counter-exception, how can there be spiritual merit? There is simply no transgression of the prohibition.

Or let it be that this recollection is solely intent upon the comprehension of the meaning of words, like the discrimination between what is correct and incorrect, or like a very slight memory. But as for the claim that the statements of Manu and others are rooted in action—who has said this? In whatever case a certain kind of source can be understood, that alone is accepted. In the case of the *Aṣṭakā* and similar rites, which are of the nature of action (*kārya*), a statement of that same nature serves as the source; but regarding an established fact (*siddha-artha*), the source must likewise concern an established fact. In the determination of word-meanings, the root is first of all linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), and never a human act (*kṛti*). Here, however, it is not possible in any way for usage to be the root. And as for purification accomplished by Vedic mantras, how could it possibly have a basis in worldly usage? Furthermore, the injunction would be rendered purposeless.

But is there not also a rule for Pāṇini stating, "One should speak with correct words, not with incorrect ones"? This is not a *smṛti* (traditional legal/grammatical authority) of Pāṇini; for that [work] concludes merely with this: "This word is correct, this one is not. However, although there is indeed such a recollection (*smaraṇa*) by the authors of the *Dharmasūtras*, this must be understood precisely from the *Abhidhānasāra*.

But surely, even in the case of those [Vedic] recollections (*smṛti*), an injunction is heard: "The heirs shall divide in this manner," "the eldest shall take four shares" (MDh 9.153), and "the eldest alone shall take" (MDh 9.105). Is it then that the injunctive sense (*liṅ*) is remembered in other forms such as the imperative (*praiṣa*) and so on? If you argue that the word-meanings themselves are of the nature of injunctions, and that the imperatives and the like—which are supplements to the injunction—are everywhere understood as instigation (*pravartanā*), then what instigation is there in the cases of cause and effect, benediction, or the expression of appropriate time? Furthermore, the act of taking (*grahaṇa*) cannot be enjoined, because it is already established by one's own desire.

If it is argued that the injunction is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) since the desire for property is common to both oneself and others, this is not so; for a restrictive injunction is untenable when there is no excess over what is already prescribed by means of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). If it is argued that this is an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) termed a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), that may be correct. However, at the very time of partition, if anyone were to take an additional share with the consent of his brothers, he would incur sin even if there were such permission, and ownership (*svatva*) would not be made known regarding a portion of a single object. For in the injunction regarding taking [the share], the acquisition of ownership is implied. That which is other than that is understood to be "not one's own" (*asva*); thus it is a prohibition. Yet, if one were to take possession even by transgressing that [prohibition], ownership would indeed arise. And for that reason, ownership is even accepted through theft and the like. At that time, apart from actual possession (*parigraha*), it cannot be determined whether "this is his own" or "this is not."

Therefore, since injunction (*vidhi*), restriction (*niyama*), and exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) are impossible here, the purpose of this division is merely this much: "this one [is the owner] in this portion, and this one in that portion. Consequently, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the phrase "they should divide" (*liṅ bhajeran*) refers to the appropriateness of the time (*prāptakālatā*). In cases such as "they should take" (*hareyuḥ*), there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of worldly practice, just as in "one who is hungry should eat" or "one should approach the Lord for the sake of security and prosperity" (GDh 9.63). And Gautama states quite explicitly: "Inheritance, purchase," and so forth (GDh 10.39).

Therefore, regarding the Smṛti concerning the Aṣṭakā and other rites, the statement on purity and impurity remains as nothing other than an injunction for a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra-vidhi*); since it is rooted in an injunction, it is indeed enjoined by an injunction. Consequently, both purity and impurity are to be understood through scripture. Thus, purity must also be stated.

It is replied: It has already been stated [in the previous verse], namely, "fat, semen... (MDh 5.133). Furthermore, the mention of "man" (*nṛ*) there is for the purpose of illustration, based on the observation of other Smṛtis. [The list includes] dogs, cats, donkeys, camels, monkeys, crows, village pigs, domestic cocks, rats, jackals, carnivorous animals, wild beasts, birds, clawed animals, and mongooses. And the mention of "fat and so forth" (*vasādi*) includes hair and flesh.

Furthermore, because of the mention of "purity," this refinement (*saṃskāra*) must be performed for impure things such as those defiled by urine and the like, but not for those being employed [as materials] in their natural state. For substances such as gold are not impure in their own nature, such that they would require purification at the time of use.

Alternatively, if it is argued that a refinement is prescribed for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), based upon a visible application—just as eating while facing east [is prescribed for merit despite the food being edible anyway]—then the mention of "purity" would be contradicted.

As for the sweeping and washing of vessels at the commencement of a meal, these are matters of customary practice (*samācāra*), and not part of this *Smṛti* on purification. Furthermore, whatever else is untouchable for a person—such as outcasts (*patita*), *caṇḍālas*, and so forth, as well as garlic, onions, liquor, meat, and the like—that too is a defiler of substances. In that regard, which purification applies to which specific defilement must be sought from other *Smṛtis* and customary practice. And specific details have been stated by the sages Hārīta, Āpastamba, and Parāśara; however, we have not set down all those statements here, lest it lead to excessive prolixity, as in the case of the author of the *Tantra* by Candragomin. (5.110)
A gold vessel that is free from stains is purified by water alone;
so too are those made of lotus-fiber, stone, and unadorned silver. (5.111)

This rule applies to gold and silver, which are specific types of *taijasa* (metallic substances), when they are free from stains. For other materials, such as copper and the like, purification occurs through scrubbing with brick-powder (*iṣṭakā*) and so forth, as in the case of contact with food remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*). Where milk or water has been drunk, no stain remains. However, where parts [of the vessel] come into contact with remnants of meat, ghee, milk, and so forth, the author will state: "Therefore, for those two, by their own source alone" (MDh 5.112). Furthermore, because of the statement regarding the removal of stains and odors (GDh 1.42), whatever substance is capable of removing a particular stain should be employed there; it is not restricted solely to ash and water. Thus Hārīta recites: "With the powders of wheat, *kuṣṭhaka*, peas, barley, mung beans, and lentils," and so forth. Likewise, Hārīta states: "But upon contact with a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), and so on, even for those [objects] free from stains, there shall be wiping twenty-one times with ash. Śaṅkha, however, says: "For metallic objects defiled by a corpse, blood, semen, urine, or feces, there is either recasting (*āvartana*), scraping (*ullekhana*), or wiping twenty-one times with ash. In that context, "recasting" refers to melting down those items that have been permeated by urine and so forth over a long period; it is the re-formation of the desired shape after destroying the previous name and form. "Scraping" is the rubbing with a sharp weapon or a stone.

In another *Smṛti*, however, mining (*ākara*), heating (*dāha*), and hammering (*avacūlana*) are prescribed. Among these, *ākara* is the purification of gold that has been made into a color by goldsmiths. *Dāha* is the finalizing of the gold by goldsmiths in fire. *Avacūlana* is the striking on all sides with a solid golden vessel by the goldsmiths when it has been raised up by heating, within that colored mine. And so it is said: "All mines are pure" (BDh 1.9.3).

The "lotus-born" refers to the conch, crystal, and so forth. Regarding the conch, however, if it is stained with impurities, it should be cleaned with a paste of white mustard seeds, cow's urine, water, and milk. For it is stated in another Smṛti: "The conch is purified by water," and "That which is defiled by food remnants or oily substances is purified by milk, water, and a paste of white mustard seeds. "Unadorned" means not filled by digging, or otherwise entirely unimpaired. This applies as a general rule for all such items; therefore, even when touched by dry impure things, Cāṇḍālas, and the like, if there is no visible stain, the purification prescribed in other Vedic branches (śākhās) as previously shown is to be applied. 5.111.
From the conjunction of water and fire, gold and silver emerged; therefore, their purification by means of their own source is more effective. (5.112)

This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Starting from "Agni [desired] the wives of Varuṇa," and continuing through the explanatory passages beginning with "He desired," the origin of gold (*suvarṇa*) and silver is heard in the scripture. Through the male faculty, Agni desired the waters, the wives of Varuṇa; he united with them through the act of sexual intercourse, and from that these two were produced and emerged. Therefore, their extreme defilement is caused by fire—their own source and cause of origin—and by water. In the reading *sayonyā*, it should be explained as meaning "by ash," which shares a common origin. And because of that observation, even clods of earth are sometimes permitted for purification. Cleansing (*nirṇeka*) is the means of purification that is more effective. (5.112)
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin, and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water.

"According to what is appropriate" (*yathārham*) means that for whatever [substance] a certain [means] is suitable, or by which the impurity of a certain [substance] can be removed; this is the meaning. For this very reason, what is stated in another *Smṛti* is also applicable: "Objects made of tin or lead are to be carried away [to be purified] with cow-dung and chaff. As it is said:
"Brass vessels smelled by cows, those defiled by the remnants of a Śūdra, and those contaminated by a dog-cooker (*śvapaca*), are purified by ten applications of alkaline substances (*kṣāra*)."
For this very reason, various types of alkaline preparations combined with sour gruel, pomegranate, and so forth, become effective. || 5.113 ||
The purification of all liquid substances is traditionally held to be straining;
for solid objects it is sprinkling, and for wooden items it is planing.

Substances subject to flowing out are liquids such as clarified butter, oil, milk-whey, and so forth. Regarding those that have been defiled by the remnants of crows and other such creatures, *utpavana*—the removal of a certain portion—is the taking away of what remains in the front part [of the vessel]. However, another Smṛti text prescribes this with the mantra: "The purifying, gold-born [wind] with the tips of Kuśa grass" (MS 3.11.10).
Others, however, say that *utpavana* is *plāvana* (overflowing): namely, pouring in another substance of the same kind until, the vessel being full, some small amount overflows.

This constitutes direct defilement; there is simply the discarding of small quantities. However, in the case of the defilement of a vessel, one should transfer the contents to another vessel. Regarding contact with food remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*), it is stated that one should pour oil or clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into water and recite mantras over them. In that context, by implication, the vessel itself must be lifted out [and discarded], for it is not possible to utilize oil that has been cast into water without its container. By association, the same applies to clarified butter as well. And this purification by straining (*utpavana*) pertains to liquids where the odor and color caused by contact with intoxicants or impure substances are no longer perceived; however, if those two are present, there is simply discarding. All of this is adopted from the *Baudhāyana-smṛti* (BDh 1.8.32–53). Furthermore, Śaṅkha has prescribed re-cooking for cooked substances. This same method of purification applies even to all those things such as intoxicants and impurities when they concern Śūdras and others; in these cases, however, "straining" means merely immersing [the substance] in water, as Vasiṣṭha has stated: "For those situated on the ground, it is like [the rule for] water."

Compounded hard substances include cold ghee, *āmikṣā*, molasses, *parpaṭaka*, and so forth. Of these, that portion which has been defiled should be removed, and the remainder is purified. And it was stated by Śaṅkha: "Of dry things from which the defect has been extracted. Alternatively, "compounded" refers to composite wholes (*avayavin*) such as beds, seats, and vehicles, which consist of an aggregate of homogeneous and heterogeneous substances. The phrase "from which the defect has been extracted" is to be understood in all cases. In the case of contact with a corpse, dried excrement, or impure substances, that part where the contact occurred must be washed, while the remainder is to be sprinkled with water.

Regarding objects made of wood—such as mats (*bṛsī*), wooden planks, and the like—which are fashioned entirely from wood: if they come into contact with a corpse, a *caṇḍāla*, or excrement, they must be planed. Others, however, maintain that this applies only in the case of contact with excrement. By planing, the odor and the coating [of impurity] are to be removed; what remains is then to be washed with earth and water or sprinkled. But in the case of defilement by a dog or similar animals, there is simply washing, just as in the case of excrement. As for beds, couches, and the like, which are constructed of wood, leather, and cords, their purification is achieved through scrubbing because they are composite objects. (5.114)
In the sacrificial rite, the purification of the sacrificial vessels is by wiping with the hand;
however, the cleansing of the *camasa* and *graha* cups is by washing.

The purification of the *caru* vessels, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as the wooden sword (*sphya*), the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the cart (*śakaṭa*), and the pestle and mortar (*musala-ulkhala*), is by means of hot water. (5.116)

These two verses are to be understood as illustrations by way of restating a matter established in the Śruti. Regarding the sacrificial vessels such as the *graha* and *camasa*, when they are being used for another performance, one must remove the remnants of clarified butter (*ājya*), oblation (*havis*), and so forth that adhered during the previous performance by means of hot water. Thereafter, according to the scriptural injunctions, the wiping (*saṃmārga*) should be performed with the hand in some cases, with *darbha* grass in others, and with the *daśāpavitra* strainer in yet others. This is the purification pertaining to ritual usage (*prāyogikī śuddhi*). However, in the event of defilement by food-leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*) and the like, it is like ordinary worldly vessels; from the specific scriptural statement, "They do not become defiled by Soma" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.6.3), it is known that in cases of other types of defilement, the general rules of purification apply. The *graha*, *camasa*, and *sphya* are to be identified among the sacrificial implements by their specific shapes. (5.115–116)
The purification of large quantities of grain and clothing is by sprinkling with water;
however, for small quantities, purification is ordained by washing them with water. (5.117)

The abundance of grain is traditionally recorded as being when it exceeds one *droṇa*. Others, however, describe it in relation to the person and in relation to place and time. For a certain impoverished person, even half a *kuḍava* may be considered much; likewise, in a certain state of affairs, a treasury that has increased becomes "much. Thus Baudhāyana says:
"Having understood the place, the time, as well as oneself, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the circumstances, and the state, one should apply the purification. (BDh 1.8.53)

Similarly, regarding garments as well, some say: "more than three, i.e., many. Although the term "plurality" (*bahutva*) applies to three or more, since the plural form "of the few" (*alpanām*) is heard in the text, therefore those ending with three are considered "few. The mention of "with water" (*adbhiḥ*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); by this, whatever garment is purified from a defect by whatever means—that too should be understood. And that has been shown previously. The connection with sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is for the purpose of restricting the use of water; the sprinkling must be performed with water alone. It is for this very distinction that there is a double recitation [of the rule].

And this [purification] applies in the case of a great injury, such as contact with a corpse, excrement, or a *caṇḍāla*; otherwise, however, for small amounts, only sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is prescribed.
If, even after washing, a stain or the like does not leave the garment, then the cutting off of that portion alone is required, as stated by Gautama: "Or its discarding" (GDh 1.34). || 5.117 ||
The purification of skins is like that of clothes, and the same applies to articles made of split cane;
however, the purification of vegetables, roots, and fruits is held to be like that of grain. (5.118)

[This rule applies] to hides and leather straps that are fit to be touched, but not to those naturally impure by nature, such as those belonging to dogs, jackals, and the like. This same rule applies to sandals, armor, and other products made from them; for in this context, the derivative is understood through the primary material, and the primary material is understood through the derivative. Thus, in the case of the phrase "of wooden [objects]," this same purification applies to wood as well. For Vasiṣṭha, after stating the purification of wooden objects, says: "Wood, bone, and earth... (VaDh 3.52). If the primary material were not included by means of the derivative, how could there be an extension (*atideśa*) of the rule for wood through a purification procedure not explicitly mentioned? However, the inclusion of the derivative within the primary material is entirely logical, since the cognition of the primary material does not cease.

*Vaidala* refers to items such as tree bark and the like. In another *Smṛti*, this same purification is prescribed for feathers, *pavitra* grass, skins, chowries, grasses, cane, hair, and bark. Among these, "feathers" includes those of peacocks and others, as well as objects made from them, such as umbrellas and fly-whisks. "*Pavitra*" refers to *darbha* grass and to garments made of *darbha*. By the word "grass" (*tṛṇa*), palm leaves are meant; it is recorded in tradition that "the palm is known as the king of grasses. In this context, the term for the whole is understood from a part of it, as in the case of the word "Datta" referring to Devadatta. "Hair" (*bāla*) refers to that of cows, horses, and goats, not that of humans, because human hair, once fallen, is considered untouchable.

All this purification is said to occur upon the destruction of a different substance (*dravyāntara*), not upon the destruction of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) [of the object], because cloth and grain share the same status regarding purification. The mention of vegetables and the like is similar to that of grain; just as for grains, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and washing (*prakṣālana*) are the causes of purification when they remain in the state of grain without undergoing other preparatory rites such as threshing, so it is with vegetables and the like. Therefore, this rule applies to those that are uncooked. However, for cooked items, even though they are denoted by the term "vegetables" and so forth, another method of purification must be sought, as it has been stated: "with gold, water, and the flame of fire," and so on. But for vegetables and the like brought from a mine, as well as for curds, whey, milk, and so forth, sprinkling and carrying fire around them (*paryagnikaraṇa*) are specifically prescribed by Hārīta. Likewise, for leguminous grains, there is rubbing, splitting, and grinding, and so on. And this is for the purpose of removing suspicion regarding contact with the feet. Thus it is said: "All mines are pure" (BDh 1.9.3). || 5.118 ||
Silk and woolen cloths [are purified] with salts; blankets of *kutapa* wool with *ariṣṭaka* fruits; fine cotton fabrics with *bilva* fruits; and linen cloths with white mustard seeds. (5.119)

*Ūṣāḥ* are golden clays; *ariṣṭaka* and others are well known. When there is a coating of oil or similar substances, one should perform the removal of that coating by means of water mixed with the powder of those substances. *Kauśeya* is a specific kind of silk cloth. Similarly, *aṃśupaṭṭa* (linen) and *āvikam* (woolen), which consists of wool—regarding these, Hārīta has stated: "For those made of wool, [purification is] by the sun. This should be understood to apply to items that are constantly worn and come into contact with the bodies of many people, and not in the case of other types of damage. Since sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and washing (*prakṣālana*) would otherwise apply to these alone, the rules for removing coatings of oil and the like are extended to them. The mention of *kṣauma* (linen) is intended to indicate *śāṇa* (hemp) and other such materials as well. (5.119)
For objects made of conch, horn, bone, or ivory, as well as for linen, purification should be performed by one who knows the rules using either cow’s urine or water. (5.120)

The bones, horns, and teeth of animals such as cows, sheep, and elephants—those that are fit to be touched—are [the materials for purification], but not those of dogs, donkeys, and the like. There is an option between cow’s urine and water; however, a paste of white mustard seeds is to be used in combination with both. (5.120)
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by being fired again. (5.121)
The stalks of rice and other grains used for making mats and the like are *palāla*. "Grasses" refers to *kuśa*, *śādvala*, and so forth.

Now, one might object: since it was stated that in the case of the term "of wooden things" (*dāravāṇām*), the modification includes the original material, why is "wood" (*kāṣṭha*) mentioned separately?
