This is for the purpose of restriction, namely, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) alone. Therefore, as long as there is no great damage, the wooden pieces are not to be carved. However, in the event of contact with a *caṇḍāla* or similar persons, purification is achieved by the rule itself: "By the rays of the moon and sun, and by the wind" (YDh 1.193). But in the case of slight damage to their derivatives, such as ladles and the like, washing and carving must be performed for those items used for food and other purposes.

*Sammārjana* (sweeping) is the cleansing of the house, which consists of removing smoke, darkness, and the like. *Upāñjana* (smearing) is the plastering of the floor with lime, cow dung, and so forth. This [requirement] should be understood to apply when there is pervasive contact with a corpse, a *caṇḍāla*, a woman in her courses (*udakyā*), or similar impurities; however, if the contact is not pervasive, it applies only to that specific area. Furthermore, in the case of defilement by a corpse, [the requirements are] scraping the wall, allowing the rays of the sun to enter, touching it with the flame of fire, and in some cases, as recorded in other texts, renovating it; this constitutes *saṃmārjana*.

For earthenware vessels, there is re-firing. The rite of circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) should be understood to apply to contact with a person who has not washed after eating (*ucchiṣṭa-puruṣa*) and similar cases; however, re-firing should be understood to apply to contact with a vessel that held liquor and the like. In the case of direct contact [with such substances], there is simply abandonment. As it has been said:
"Earthenware that has come into contact with liquors, urine, feces, spittle, pus, or blood is not purified even by re-firing. (VaDh 3.59)
The ground is purified by these five means: by sweeping, by smearing with cow dung, by sprinkling, by scraping, and by the dwelling of cows. (5.122)

Sprinkling (*seka*) is performed with cow urine or water; in some cases, it is said to be done even with milk. Scraping (*ullekhana*) is the making of furrows with a weapon or similar tool, as well as sowing (*āvāpana*). This is because of Gautama’s specific instruction: "And [the sprinkling] of the ground" (GDh 1.32). The repetition of the word "by five" is intended to show that these may be employed either individually or collectively, depending on the nature of the impact. Among these, purification devoid of sweeping is *upāñjana* (smearing with cow-dung), which is used alone for ground free of refuse. Scrapping and sweeping are required when there is a coating of urine, feces, and so forth. Sprinkling is appropriate for riverbanks, forests, and the like. "Habituation by cows" (*gavāṃ parivāsaḥ*) means keeping the ground as a cow-pen for just one day. All of this must be performed for ground belonging to a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). However, "sowing" (*āvāpana*) refers to removing bones, potsherds, and the like that were previously present and then adding other earth; it also applies to places where [remains] are hidden and their existence might be suspected after some time has passed, and so forth. (5.122)
Food that has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, sneezed at, or defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth over it. (5.123)
Here, from the indicative mark of the word "jagdhi" (eating), it is understood that this verse has food as its subject matter.

However, regarding food made impure by birds such as parrots and other edible species—but not by crows, *kaṅkas*, vultures, and the like—there is a heavy penance prescribed for that case: "That which has been licked by a bird" (MDh 4.209). This refers to the penance for eating [food] that has become pure according to the present context. And thus, there is no purification at all for food smelled by a cow, as it would entail a penance equal to that. Such may be the logical principle; nevertheless, the practices of other *smṛtis* must be investigated. For in this way, the learned, having removed only that portion of food exceeding ten *śarāvas* which has been defiled by carnivorous birds such as crows, purify the remainder and consume it; but if it is less than that, they discard it. Even here, specific circumstances must be taken into account. In another *smṛti*, however, even food defiled by a black bird is prohibited.

*Avadhūtam* is that which has been shaken by the breath from the mouth, or over which an action such as tossing [the cloth] upward from the air is performed for the purpose of removing dust from a garment. *Avakṣutam* is that very thing over which someone has sneezed. *Keśāḥ* are the hairs fallen from humans. *Kīṭāḥ* are small creatures, worms. Some of these—those born from the sweat or food in a house—do not cause defilement while alive, just like flies. This purification applies when they touch food after they have died. However, those born from contact with impure substances and those that eat excrement cause defilement even while they are alive. Regarding this, Gautama states: "That which is constantly contaminated by hair or insects is unfit to be eaten" (GDh 17.8–9). When there is extensive contamination, there is discarding of the whole; however, when it is a large heap and there is contact with impure insects, one should merely remove that specific portion, and the remainder is purified. According to another Smṛti, touching gold, silver, Darbha grass, or gems together with water is prescribed when they are contaminated by hair and the like. In some cases, flaming [with fire] is also prescribed.
But those who claim that this purification of the ground is sufficient have abandoned both the traditional practice of other Smṛtis and the true meaning of the scriptural statement. 5.123.
As long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impurity do not depart from an object smeared with it, so long must earth and water be applied in all purifications of substances. 5.124.

"Unclean" (*amedhya*) means "untouchable. Furthermore, whatever is inedible for a particular person is the cause of impurity for that person; for example, *surā* liquor and intoxicants are [impure] for a Brāhmaṇa, but not for a Śūdra. That is incorrect. Before the *homa*, the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are inedible, yet they are not untouchable. However, *surā* liquor, intoxicants, and the like are forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa even by touch. Therefore, it is only for that person whose touch is forbidden that contact with the substance brings about impurity. Consequently, this rule does not hold: "whatever is inedible is untouchable, and whatever is untouchable is inedible."

*Āktam*, *liptam*, and *upadigdham* mean smeared or anointed. The word *tāvat* (so much) prescribes the extent of the application. *Mṛdvāri* means earth and water; this is required when there is a purpose. And the purpose is the removal of odor and stain. In the case of contact with dry impurities (*amedhya*) or contact that has occurred long ago, even over time, the cleansing of those odors and stains is accomplished by wiping once with earth and water alone. Now, one might object: the taking up of earth, water, and so forth for the sake of purification serves a visible purpose; since the object becomes pure as soon as the stain has vanished, what is the point of this rule, "as long as [the stain] does not depart"?

It is said: [The rule] beginning with "one on the penis" (MDh 5.134) is for the purpose of exceeding the stated number. When the removal of smears of feces and the like cannot be accomplished by the stated number, one should disregard that scriptural number and resort to even a greater amount. However, the mention of a specific number is intended to mean that even if the smears are removed with fewer than that number, the count must still be fulfilled.

They explain that the mention of "water" is intended as an illustration for any means of purification. Therefore, even if water—which is the cause of impurity—has been used to wash something, it must still be scrubbed with alkaline substances and the like; otherwise, the stain would not be seen. "It departs" (*apaiti*) means it goes away or ceases to exist. "Caused by that" (*tatkṛtaḥ*) means produced by that impure substance. Consequently, the fragrance of musk and similar scents on a garment does not depart, nor is it considered defiled. However, if a portion of a body smeared with saffron or other pigments comes into contact with an impure substance, even the saffron and such must be wiped away, because that area is indeed in contact with the impure matter; this is because the text specifies the removal of both odor and smear. If, however, the color of saffron adhering to the body cannot be removed by rubbing, then purity is indeed attained. (5.124)
The gods have ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is commended by word. (5.125)

"Purified" means pure. The mention of "gods" is for the sake of praise. The mention of "Brāhmaṇas" also, according to established custom, is intended for all castes. "Unseen" refers to an object situated in an unprotected place that has not been seen to come into contact with dogs, crows, and the like. One should not, merely on the basis of its existence, entertain a groundless suspicion of its defilement. Thus, food items prepared in a kitchen by cooks and others who have not performed purification do not become tainted when consumed, provided they remain unseen [by such impurities].

Furthermore, one should not entertain this doubt: that there is no fault if a prior defilement was unknown at a later time. For if that were so, it would contradict such rules as, "and these [things] unintentionally" (MDh 5.20). Thus, first of all, that which is not perceived by any means of knowledge to be connected with a fault is pure. However, where, even in the absence of a definitive means of knowledge, a fault is suspected through fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*), there it must be cleansed with water. For example, when vessels, cooking pots, and the like situated in the same place are seen to be defiled by dogs, crows, and so forth, other items—though not seen to be defiled—must likewise be cleansed with water.

In the same way, one who is praiseworthy by word of mouth should be made to recite by the learned, saying, "May this be pure. They say that purity comes from the word of a Brāhmaṇa. The present tense (*laṭ*) in the word *praśasyate* (is praised) is to be understood here as having the sense of an injunction. As for those who say that when there is a visible defilement, and while purification is being performed by the transactor directly, if the learned say, "His purification has been accomplished," even though it is not visibly apparent—then it is to be accepted; such is the meaning of "one praised by word."

That is incorrect; since the lack of authority for the word of a trustworthy person (*āpta-vacana*) has not been accepted in all cases, there would be the consequence of tautology. Others, however, explain "cleansed with water" as an illustration: two things are prescribed that are unseen yet praised by speech—just as what is cleansed with water is pure, so too is what is unseen but praised by speech prescribed.
But if something is pure because its defects are unseen according to perception, inference, and scripture, then how [can one say], "even one day of the year"? (MDh 5.21).

That [rule] pertains to the subject of food; this purification pertains to the subject of touchables. The distinction is established either by the gravity or lightness of the offense, or by the difference between times of distress and non-distress. 5.125.
Water on the ground is pure if it quenches the thirst of a cow, provided it has not been contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural fragrance, color, and taste. (5.126)

The mention of "ground" (*bhūmi*) is intended as an illustration; by this, even water that has entered through conduits is indeed pure. For water is pure by its very nature whether it is on the ground or in the sky. However, because of contact with impure substances, the earth acquires some degree of impurity. Regarding those waters that have reached it, since they might acquire impurity by virtue of that contact, this rule—"that much [water] in which a cow would lose her thirst"—is stated for the purpose of determining their purification. "Loss of thirst" (*vaitṛṣṇya*) means the cessation of the desire to drink. This is also intended to indicate a specific measure. In this regard, the ancient commentators have explained it by citing an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "Just as the dewlap of a cow, having been immersed in the water... That is, the amount of water in which the cow's dewlap and so forth sink and her thirst is quenched is what is meant. But those waters situated on pure ground are pure even in small quantities. How, then, is the pervasion by impurity to be determined? By the phrase "endowed with the smell, color, and taste of the impure. The word ending in the instrumental case (*amedhyena*), "by the impure," is to be understood as being changed to the genitive. If they are endowed—that is, joined—with the smell and other qualities belonging to the impure substance, then they are said to be "pervaded" by it. And this being the case, if in a pond or similar body of water impurity is seen in one spot, yet another part is devoid of such smell and other qualities, that [other part] shall indeed be pure. (5.126)
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise spread out for sale;
almsfood received by a student of sacred knowledge is always pure—this is the settled rule. (5.127)

Artisans—such as craftsmen, leather-workers, dyers, weavers, and so forth—their hands are always pure. Consequently, they may be touched during the periods of impurity caused by birth or death. However, their purity is not to be understood as remaining even when visible smears of excrement or other filth are present. That which was stated, "they are proclaimed to be immediately pure," refers precisely to this. There is no redundancy here, as this has not been taught in the *Manusmṛti*. Furthermore, there is another scope for this rule: "Weavers weave without having sipped water. The flour-paste and such substances that are applied to separate the fibers from the stalks, as well as the vessel used for them, are placed anywhere on the ground; whatever impurity arises from that is removed by this [rule]. Yet, one should not understand their purity to result from touching those things that are inherently impure, for such contact is not prescribed for their craft.

And thus, this very same reasoning applies so that even those things mixed with the products of barbarians (mleccha) are not impure; in that regard, sprinkling and washing are prescribed according to the words of Śaṅkha. For it is stated therein: "The hand of an artisan is pure, as are raw materials."

*Paṇya* (merchandise) is that substance which is sold for money or measured by another substance for the purpose of trade; that is *paṇya*, and it is pure when displayed on the floor of a marketplace. Because it comes into contact with many buyers and is placed upon a ground devoid of plastering and the like, it suffers defilement; therefore, it is not impure even though it is repeatedly seen to be subject to such defilement. By the inclusion of the term "displayed," there is no purity for merchandise remaining in the house, even if it is present in one's mind. However, regarding prepared foods such as barley-meal (*saktu*) and cakes (*apūpa*), although they may be pure, their inedibility follows precisely from the statement of Śaṅkha: "Goods from a marketplace are inedible."

Because of this very association, the previously mentioned purification for one who has become a *brahmacārin* is understood to apply in the event of such an impairment. For one who is begging, impairments such as walking along a street, seeing impure things, sneezing, spitting, or the contact of many hands with the alms-food are possible; [the text] states that [these] constitute impurity despite [the food's] natural purity. (5.127)
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall; a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game. (5.128)

"The mouth of all women is pure for the purpose of kissing and the like. Another Smṛti states: "And women [are pure] in connection with sexual union" (VaDh 28.8). This refers only to those connected with sexual union, not to one's mother, sister, and so forth. In this context, it should not be thought that this prohibition regarding *ucchiṣṭa* (remnants of food) applies to women; for even though they are connected with sexual union, it is established in the fourth chapter that one should not eat together with one's wife, based on the statement: "One should not eat together with one's wife" (MDh 4.43). Because of the use of the word "always" (*nitya*), it does not apply only at the time of sexual union, but rather when she is engaged in activities intended for that purpose. If she does not engage in such activity, [the rule does not apply].

The term *śakuni* refers to the falling of fruit. Although the word *śakuni* denotes birds in general, based on established usage (*samācāra*), it is not intended here for crows, herons, and other scavengers. Because of the mention of "falling," this rule applies specifically to fruit situated upon a tree.

When a cow is being milked, the calf clings to her udders for the purpose of causing the milk to flow. Now, since it is said, "Cows are pure except for their mouths," impurity might otherwise be presumed; therefore, this statement is made to preclude that [impurity] regarding contact with her mouth. However, a dog is not pure. But a deer is pure when it seizes [its prey] in hunting and the like in order to kill it. (5.128)
Manu has declared that the flesh of an animal killed by dogs is pure, as is the flesh of one killed by other carnivorous beasts, or by outcasts and other predatory robbers. (5.129)

Previously, in the verse "A dog [is pure] when seizing game" (MDh 5.128), the intention was merely that a dog is pure when it kills wild animals. Here, however, the distinction is that the animal has been seized by it or by others through the striking of sticks and so forth.

The meaning of the second half of the verse is now prescribed: "by carnivorous beasts such as hawks, jackals, and the like; by Caṇḍālas and others"—the inclusion of the word "others" is for the purpose of not excluding wild beasts and similar creatures; and "by robbers," namely Niṣādas, hunters, and others whose livelihood consists of killing living beings. (5.129)
Those apertures which are above the navel are entirely pure;
those which are below are impure, as are the excretions that fall from the body. (5.130)

This word *kha* denotes the sense organs (*indriya*). Therefore, when referring to the two feet, there is a plural form [in the phrase] "the organs of action (*karmendriya*) which are below are impure. This is incorrect, because it contradicts the statement that [the body] "above the navel" is pure; for in that context, it is stated that the area above the navel is more pure (*medhyatara*), implying a degree of excellence. If there were impurity below, then this would be logical; for one does not say, "white, yet blacker."

And this term *indriya* does not refer to the sense organs; rather, it has the meaning of "aperture. As it is said: "There are seven vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) in the head" (ŚB 13.1.7.2). There are two apertures below. The plural number is used due to the distinction between the female and male generative organs. This being so, even when there is contact with the interior of the mouth, the hands and other limbs remain pure provided there is no connection with the phlegm located therein. Likewise, one must avoid touching [the hands] again if they have been defiled by rheum of the eyes (*dūṣikā*). 5.130.
One should specify that flies, droplets, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun, dust, earth, wind, and fire are pure to the touch. 5.131.

The mention of flies [266] refers to those born from sweat. The mention of cows refers to goats and sheep. The mention of horses refers to elephants and mules. The mention of the sun refers to luminaries. "Drops" are water droplets which, through the mere experience of touch, do not possess any visible specific form. "Shadow" refers to that of outcastes (caṇḍāla) and others. "Earth" is pure when touched by outcastes and others, provided it is stepped upon with the feet; for other types of ground, however, sweeping and so forth are prescribed. These [creatures], such as flies and the rest, do not cause defilement even when touching excrement and the like.
Goats and horses are pure from their mouths; cows are pure except for their mouths.
The cat and the mongoose may be touched, as well as auspicious beasts and birds.
Thus, in another Smṛti. 5.131.
Earth and water should be taken as required for the purpose of purification after voiding feces or urine, and likewise for the twelve types of bodily impurities. (5.132)

Regarding the impurity expressed in the verse, “And from the body, impurities fall” (MDh 5.130), this is stated: for the purpose of purifying that which is the passage for the discharge of feces and urine—the anus and so forth—one should take earth and water as required. Disregarding any fixed number, one should take as much water and earth as will remove the odor and the smear. The bodily impurities (*daihika-mala*) are those residing in the body that cause a state of impurity. For the purification intended for those [impurities] as well, both earth and water are to be taken as required. This is recited in another Smṛti:
One should take earth and water for purification during the first six [actions];
however, during the latter six, one is purified by water alone.

Regarding the purification of phlegm and the other [impurities], another Smṛti text states: "The nasal [cleansing] removes the discharge of oiliness; it destroys phlegm. Even though these belong to the latter group of six, earth must certainly not be used for them. (5.132)
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nasal mucus, phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat—these twelve are the impurities of human beings. (5.133)

Regarding these twelve impurities that have been shown: the mention of "man" is for the purpose of illustrating [the rule for] five-toed animals; as for dogs, jackals, and the like, their status is established by the very fact of their being untouchable. However, in the case of feces and urine, this applies to everyone except goats, sheep, cows, and horses. (5.133)
One application of clay should be made on the penis, three on the anus, ten on one hand, and seven on both hands by one who desires purification. (5.134)

After the voiding of feces and urine, one application of clay with water should be made to the left hand for the purification of the penis. According to the prescription for purification in another Smṛti, as much clay as fits into that hand should be taken along with water. However, I say that the measure is indeed stated by the rule, "as much as is necessary" (MDh 5.132). Some read: "The first [application] should be known as a handful (prasṛti); the second is half of that;
the third application of clay should be known as filling a third part of the hand."

And this measurement applies only to the *pāda*s; elsewhere, however, it is governed by the rule "that which possesses meaning. Even when there is a single elision (*utsarga*), the number remains exactly as it was. This is a prescription for repetition (*āvṛtti*), just like the division of clay [into lumps] such as cows and so forth. And thus it is said here: "other than from an anthill, from a very distant place, or from a horse-stable," and so on. Likewise, in this context, [distinctions such as] "white, black, red," and so forth, are not to be taken into account. [The term] *abhīpsatā* means "by one who desires. 5.134.
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics. (5.135)

The rule for purification varies according to the specific stage of life (*āśrama*). For those who do not belong to a stage of life, however, the rule is simply this: earth and water should be used as much as necessary. A Śūdra also certainly has the right to the householder’s stage; such is the enumeration. (5.135)
Having voided urine or feces, one who has sipped water should touch the cavities of the head;
so too when about to study the Veda, and always before eating food. (5.136)

Having relieved himself in a place suitable for urination and having purified it according to the prescribed rule, he should sip water (*ācānta*) and touch the *khāni*, that is, the sense organs. Furthermore, when about to study the Veda, as stated in the second rule regarding Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), the verb *kṛ* is used in its primary sense; thus, the sequence "having performed [the evacuation], he should void [it]" is understood. Having wiped away urine and feces and washed the anus and the generative organ, he should sip water. And one who is about to study the Veda must do so because it is declared as a duty within the rules for Vedic recitation: "But one who is about to study, having sipped water... (MDh 2.70). This applies to either the teacher who is teaching or the student who is about to study. Otherwise, those who are merely reciting the Veda are addressed. After performing other worldly activities, one should not utter the syllables of the Veda without having sipped water, nor while eating food. (5.136)
One who desires bodily purity should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice; however, a woman or a Śūdra should do so only once each. (5.137)
This restatement is for the sake of women and Śūdras. Although this has already been stated, it is repeated for the sake of women and Śūdras.

Some explain that according to the rule "a Śūdra [is purified] by water touched" (MDh 2.62), a Śūdra need only perform the mere touching of water; therefore, this [rule regarding] wiping or touching the ears and so forth is prescribed as applicable specifically to virtuous Śūdras. As for women, since the rule "a Brāhmaṇa is purified by water reaching the heart" (MDh 2.62) specifies the caste [only], they would—like men—be subject to the same [general rule]; thus, this [present rule] is stated.

By the force of the statement, "seeking bodily purity," if one were to engage in study or eating while already pure, then the triple repetition would not be necessary, nor would there be wiping. What then? There is merely the sipping of as much water as required and the touching of the sense organs; no other rule for sipping (ācamana) is prescribed here than that which has been stated among the duties of the student (brahmacārin). (5.137)
Śūdras who follow the right path must have their hair shaved every month;
their rules for purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of the food of the twice-born. (5.138)

This duty, which was mentioned generally for *śūdras*, is now stated in detail as an incidental topic. Those who follow the right path, serve the twice-born (*dvija*), and perform the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) must have their hair shaved every month; here the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental. Alternatively, they are those dependent on and subservient to Brāhmaṇas; the action is to be performed by the Brāhmaṇas. Since the root *kṛ* has multiple meanings, the understanding is that they are to be instructed [in this matter]. Their specific rules for purification, such as during periods of birth or death (*sūtaka*) and regarding ritual sipping (*ācamana*), are like those of the Vaiśyas. And eating the remnants of the twice-born has been explained previously. (5.138)
The primary [limbs] do not become defiled by food remnants, nor do droplets that fall upon the body;
nor do the hairs of the beard that enter the mouth, nor what remains stuck between the teeth. (5.139)

Regarding the rule, "Having spat or spoken untruths" (MDh 5.143), since the injunction for sipping water (*ācamana*) is prescribed after spitting, it is made known that one who has not sipped water is impure. Since even droplets (*vipruṣaḥ*) are indeed spit from the mouth, the question arises as to why the rule for sipping water does not apply to them, given that spitting consists of the expulsion of phlegm; therefore, he says this: "Principal" (*mukhya*) means those which exist in the mouth or have emerged from the mouth. Droplets do not cause one to become ritually impure (*anucchiṣṭa*) provided they do not fall upon a limb, according to the rule: "If they do not fall on a limb" (GDh 1.41).

But has it not been stated that "drops are pure" in the passage concerning "drops from the mouth"? [This applies] elsewhere, excluding bodily excrement; this itself is the indicator. Not every subject has been shown.

*Śmaśrūṇi* refers to the hairs of the beard; *āsyagatāni* means those that have entered the mouth. The phrase "they do not make one impure" (*nocchiṣṭaṃ kurvanti*) is to be supplied [to this]. Therefore, other things such as betel nut (*pūgaphala*) certainly do produce impurity. Likewise, what remains stuck between the teeth (*dantāntaradhiṣṭhitaṃ lagnam*). There is a specific rule in another Smṛti: "Regarding what is stuck to the teeth, it is like the teeth themselves, except when touched by the tongue. Some say [this applies] until it falls out. When they have fallen out, one should know it is like saliva; he becomes pure simply by swallowing it" (GDh 1.38–40). One should understand "when they have fallen out" to mean "without the tongue," because purity is prohibited if there is contact with the tongue. 5.139.
The drops that touch the feet of one who is rinsing the mouth for others are to be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them. 5.140

"Causing others to sip water" means giving water for sipping to others. This is what is intended: when one gives water for sipping to another, if the feet of the giver of the water are touched by drops of water falling from the fingers of the hand of the person making him sip—drops which arise from the impact with the ground as they fall through the spaces between the fingers—then he does not become impure because of them. Just as certain quantities of water remaining on the earth are pure when they stand on ground that has not been defiled, so too are those drops of water falling from the hand, even though they are "leftovers" (ucchiṣṭa). One who is touched by them is not *aprayata* (unfit) or impure. Because of the mention of "others," both the one who is sipping and any other person standing nearby must avoid contact with that [water]. And because of the mention of "feet," contact with the shanks or other parts of the leg is indeed defective. (5.140)
If one who holds a substance in his hand is somehow touched by something defiled, he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that substance down. 5.141

A person who is subject to an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) involving sipping water (*ācamana*) is said to be "impure" (*ucchiṣṭa*). For example: a person who has discharged urine or other excrement but has not yet performed purification and sipping of water; or one who is defiled by contact with impure substances (*amedhya*) and the like; or if a person has an object in hand—meaning he holds in his hand foodstuffs such as edible or chewable items, or objects such as clothing—and he is thus called "one with an object in hand. The usage of the term is established according to its application, as in the case of "one with a thunderbolt in hand" (*vajrahasta*). If he becomes touched [by something impure], then without setting that object down—that is, without removing it—he should sip water while still holding the object in his hand.
But how can sipping water be possible when the substance is held in the hand? Regarding this, the rule is: "One should wash the hands up to the wrist" (GDh 1.36).

Some say: what is intended by "contact with a substance" is merely contact with the body, not specifically with the hand. Thus, even in the case of impurity, when a substance is placed upon the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth, the impurity belongs to the one who has left food remnants; likewise, purification occurs through sipping water (ācamana). Therefore, having taken a substance from a place other than the hand—such as the forearm or the lap—one may sip water. The intention is that just as [the person] is indeed impure due to connection with human impurity, so too is there purification through its cleansing.

Gautama, however, has stated: "One who is impure with something in hand, having set it down, should perform ācamana" (GDh 1.28). Regarding this, they explain: although the state of being accompanied by the object is equal [to other cases], in this instance only the setting down of the object is intended. Otherwise, when purification must be performed for both [the person and the object] by one holding an object in hand, what occasion would there be for the setting down of the object? Therefore, since setting it down would not otherwise be established, this statement is solely for the purpose of prescribing the setting down. How, then, is the purification of the object achieved? It is through being grasped by a person who is purified, or by sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) as prescribed in another Smṛti.
"If, while moving among food and drink, one should touch something defiled, one should sip water after sprinkling the substance; thus one does not incur fault.

If the placement [of the vessel] were obtained here even without this statement, then the statement "even without placing it down" would be redundant. Since the Smṛtis form a single coherent whole, it is understood here according to the established rule; however, a difference of opinion is perceived now, and consequently, there is an option.

And its regulation is as follows: a more important substance is set aside, while another, being placed on a limb, is understood [to be touched]. Even when one eats food oneself, or touches a large amount of leavings, or is touched by one who ought to rinse but has not rinsed, all such contact with the leavings of a substance constitutes impurity. (5.141)
One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then consume clarified butter;
one who has eaten food should simply sip water, while bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.

Vomiting (*vamana*) and purging (*virecana*) are well known. A man who has vomited up food that he had eaten through his mouth is one who has "vomited" (*vānta*). One for whom the urges to defecate have occurred more than eight times—either by the consumption of *harītakī* and similar substances or due to disease—is one who has been "purged" (*virikta*). These two should first perform a bath. Then, at the end, having consumed clarified butter (*ghṛta*), they may eat this other food. This consumption of clarified butter does not exclude further meals; rather, among expiations, this consumption of clarified butter is a purification of the substance, like cleansing with ashes or water. One should indeed sip water (*ācamet*) after eating food. If vomiting or purging should occur on the very same day after eating food, then there is only the sipping of water, and neither the bath nor the consumption of clarified butter.
Others, however, explain it independently: "Having eaten, one should indeed sip water. This is an exception to the rule that sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed immediately after eating.
Regarding "one who has engaged in sexual intercourse": one who has discharged semen with a woman becomes pure by bathing. (5.142)
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, and having spoken untruths;
and after drinking water, one who is about to study should sip water (ācamana), even if he is already pure. (5.143)

The sound that arises from the nostrils of one who has sneezed—even if unwillingly and impelled by the wind—is *kṣavathu*; having produced that [sound], even though he is already pure (*prayata*), he must act. This is connected specifically with the word "about to study" (*adhyeṣyamāṇa*). The meaning is: even if he is already pure, when about to study, he should sip water (*ācamya*) and then study; that is, he should perform the sipping of water as an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the rule for studying. However, after bathing and other such acts, he does so only once. Furthermore, it has been said:
"Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, and likewise having drunk water, the sage [should sip water]."
"Having sipped water, one should sip again after spitting or speaking an untruth.

This is how the connection should be made here: "Having sipped water after eating, one should sip again. However, where it is recited that "one should sip twice," there the repetition of the single action follows immediately. (5.143)
This entire rule for purification, as well as the cleansing of objects, has been declared to you for all social classes; now learn the duties of women. (5.144)

With the first three words, there is a conclusion of the section on purification; with the fourth, there is a brief statement of what is about to be said. Although the term *śaucavidhi* (rules of purification) is a general term, because of its proximity to the purification of substances (*dravyaśuddhi*), it becomes restricted to the other specific [types of] purification, like the expression "cattle and bulls" (*gobalīvarda*). The duties of women refer only to those whose performance is unique to women; that which is common [to both sexes], such as sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, is not mentioned here. (5.144)
Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an old woman, a female must not perform any action independently, even within her own home. (5.145)

The purpose of the instruction is that independence for women does not exist in any state whatsoever. However, the statement regarding the divisions of age is intended merely to demonstrate the circumstances under which her dependence exists; its specific nature is not what is intended to be emphasized. (5.145) In childhood she shall remain under the control of her father, in youth under the control of her husband, and when her husband has died, under the control of her sons; a woman must never enjoy independence. (5.146)
And so it has been said:
"While there are sapinda relatives on the father's side, the husband is the master of the woman;
but when both sides have come to an end, the king is considered the husband of the woman."
And by the words "among his sapindas," etc., [it is indicated that] the rite should be performed even when the owner is absent. 5.146.
A woman should not desire separation from her father, her husband, or her sons; for by being separated from them, she brings reproach upon both families. (5.147)

"Indecision is said to be the cause for being censured; one should act [only] when there is blame. For, in the absence of these [conditions], she might live or go to another village—this is to be supplied [to the verse]. 5.147.
She should always remain cheerful, be skillful in household duties, keep the utensils well-maintained, and be not wasteful in expenditure. (5.148)

The word *sadā* (always) expresses frequency, just like the word *nitya*. Regarding the phrase “with one who is constantly smiling”: even when there is an intensity of anger or grief elsewhere, upon seeing her husband, she should display joy through a brightening of the face, a smile, playful words, and so forth. This instruction applies to both a maiden and a married woman. Regarding the phrase “and being skillful in household duties”: household duties have been described [in MDh 9.11] with the words, “In the accumulation of wealth, and in this...,” and so on. In that regard, she must be *dakṣā*—that is, clever. Here, tasks such as purification must be performed quickly. “With well-kept utensils” (*susaṃskṛtopaskarā*): *upaskara* refers to household implements such as bowls, jars, and the like; these must be kept well-maintained, well-cleaned, and beautiful. And regarding expenditure: in matters of wealth intended for feeding friends, relatives, and guests, she must not be *amuktahastā*—that is, she must not be extravagant. The meaning is that she should not spend excessively. The analysis of the compound *susaṃskṛtopaskarā* is a *bahuvrīhi*: “she whose utensils (*upaskara*) are well-maintained. Similarly, the analysis of *amuktahastā* is: “she whose hand (*hasta*) is not loose (*mukta*). Subsequently, there is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). By conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the word *muktahasta* signifies one who is generous or extravagant. (5.148)
To whomsoever her father or her brother—by the father’s consent—may give her, she shall serve him while he lives, and once he has passed away, she must not disregard him. 5.149.

Or, with the father’s permission, by the brother. Just as a brother has the authority to give when permitted by the father, so too, although there is scriptural evidence for the father’s independent authority to give, it should be understood that the giving occurs when the wife’s consent is obtained, because they have joint authority in all matters and both possess ownership over the daughter. It was shown in the ninth [book] that even in the absence of the father, she may be given away by the mother; thus, since the child belongs to both the mother and the father, and their ownership is based on that [child], mutual dependence is logical. She should serve—that is, she should propitiate him. And when he has passed away—that is, when he is dead—she must not transgress [his will]. Transgression means overstepping. The meaning is that she should not live independently. Just as while the husband is alive she is subject to his control, so even after he is dead she must remain dependent on him at that very time. For it says: “Giving effects ownership” (MDh 5.150). At the very moment she is given by the father, the father’s ownership ceases, and ownership arises in him to whom she is given. Therefore, the giving does not occur only at the time of marriage; the giving exists even before the marriage, at the time of the formal selection (*varaṇa*). 5.149.
What, then, is the purpose of marriage?
For their sake, rites for prosperity, auspicious blessings, and sacrifices to Prajāpati are performed;
however, in marriage, the formal giving away of the bride is the cause of [the husband's] ownership. (5.150)

The accomplishment of a desired object is *maṅgala* (auspiciousness); that which brings about its realization is employed for that purpose. In this context, the word *yajñaḥ* (sacrifice) is neuter because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) of the act of Prajāpati. *Svastyayanam* is that by which *svasti* (well-being) is attained or reached; the meaning is that whatever dear object belongs to him does not perish. [This refers to] these women, in those marriages. A sacrifice is performed for the deity Prajāpati; for some, *ājya-homas* (libations of clarified butter) are prescribed for the marriage ceremony with the mantra: "O Prajāpati, none other than you... (RV 10.121.10). This is an illustration, and it includes other deities as well, such as Pūṣan, Varuṇa, and Aryaman. For instance, there are Vedic verses (*mantravarṇas*) therein: "To the god Pūṣan," "To the god Varuṇa," etc., which are intended to manifest other deities. By the very act of giving, ownership (*svāmya*) arises even in the absence of a formal marriage; this is what is made known here. The statement that the marriage-sacrifice is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is not intended to be emphasized. It is recorded in the Smṛtis that "marriage is the making of a wife. Even though ownership exists, one does not become a wife without a marriage ceremony. (5.150)

A husband who has performed the sacramental rite with mantras, whether out of season or during the fertile period, is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife both in this world and in the next. (5.151)

"Everywhere, except when it is prohibited" (GDh 5.2); thus, he is the giver of pleasure even outside the fertile season (*anṛtu*). He is the performer of the *mantra-saṃskāra*, which is the marriage rite; hence he is called the "performer of the *mantra* sacrament. Furthermore, because she has the right to perform religious duties (*dharma*) together with her husband in the next world, and because she attains the fruits thereof, he is said to be the giver of happiness in the next world. (5.151)
Whether he is lacking in virtue, given over to lust, or devoid of good qualities, a husband must always be attended upon by a virtuous wife like a god. (5.152)

Excessively addicted to gambling and lacking in moral conduct; one whose behavior is dominated by desire is called *kāmavṛtta*. Alternatively, he is devoid of virtues, being destitute of qualities such as sacred learning (*śruta*) and wealth (*dhana*). He is to be attended upon—that is, to be propitiated. (5.152)
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by that service which she renders to her husband, she is glorified in heaven. (5.153)

It has been established more than once that those who have been separated from their husband have no entitlement to perform sacrifices. Therefore, even when performing vows (*vrata*) or fasts (*upavāsa*), she must obtain his permission. A *vrata* is a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to abstain from liquor, meat, and so forth, but it does not include the *kṛcchra* penances. This is because *japa* (recitation) and *homa* (fire-offering) are constituent parts (*aṅga*) of those [sacrifices], and these are absent for a woman. Nor is it proper to say, "Her performance of the *kṛcchra* will be deficient in *japa* and *homa*. For it is not proper to omit constituent parts at one's own discretion; since a ritual action is understood to be a means to prosperity (*abhyudaya*) only when endowed with all its constituent parts, and constituent parts do not undergo increase or decrease based on the difference in a person's capacity. Furthermore, members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) of the same class (*savarṇa*) are capable of performing the ritual application by incorporating all the constituent parts. Consequently, a woman or a *śūdra* who desires prosperity has no entitlement to the *kṛcchra* penances. We shall explain the specific rules regarding expiations (*prāyaścitta*) later. A fast (*upoṣita*) is a fasting (*upavāsa*), which is the cessation of food for one night, two nights, and so forth. She "serves" (*śuśrūṣate*) means she attends upon him. (5.153)
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, should never do anything displeasing to him who took her hand, whether he be living or dead. (5.154)

The "world of the husband" (patiloka) is that world of heaven and so forth which is earned through the performance of dharma together with her husband. Desiring—that is, wishing to attain—that world, she should not perform anything unpleasant, such as association with other men, which is forbidden by the scriptures. For it is impossible to determine what is pleasant or unpleasant for one who is dead; nor is that which is pleasant while living necessarily pleasant for the dead, because the nature of pleasure differs for those who have entered another state of existence. Therefore, that very independence which is forbidden is what is unpleasant; she should not practice that. (5.154)
She may indeed sustain her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits; but she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died. (5.155)

He demonstrates that very point with its specific details: suicide is forbidden for women just as it is for men. As for what is stated in the *Āṅgirasa*—"they should follow their husband in death"—that too is not something that must necessarily be performed as an obligatory duty (*nitya*). There is praise of the fruit [of such an act] there; and when one who desires a fruit is qualified [for the act], it is similar to the *Śyena* sacrifice. Just so, in the case of the qualification "one should destroy beings by means of the *Śyena*," even though there is engagement [in the act] due to being blinded by an exceedingly intense hatred, there is no quality of *dharma*. Likewise here, even though there is a prohibition, because engagement in dying by transgressing it is possible for a woman whose desire for the fruit is exceedingly great, it lacks scriptural authority (*śāstrīyatva*). Therefore, the prohibition against a woman following her husband in death certainly exists. Furthermore, this Smṛti rule can be interpreted as being in contradiction with the direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "Therefore, indeed, one should not depart before the end of one's lifespan" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 10.2.6.7). It is like the Smṛti rule "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe" (*Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra* 2.5.6), which prescribes bathing immediately after study for one who has not yet realized the meaning of the texts. Therefore, in the case of a woman whose husband is dead and who is childless, and who has no husband’s wealth or other heirs, she should live by some means such as spinning, for life is extremely dear to her. Since disregarding life is unscriptural and prohibited, and since all forms of sexual misconduct (*vyabhicāra*) are permitted in times of distress by such rules as "the thigh of Viśvāmitra" (*Viśvāmitrajāghanī*), and thus the possibility of living through misconduct arises, this is said: "In this state, she may at will emaciate her body, bring it to exhaustion, and provide her livelihood with flowers, roots, and fruits as they happen to be available. But she must not even mention the name of another man, saying, "You alone are my husband today. As for that which... [text ends].

"When the husband has disappeared, died, renounced the world, become impotent, or fallen [from caste]—in these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women. (NSm 12.97) In that context, because of the duty of protection (*pālana*), she may resort to another husband for the sake of her own livelihood through work such as that of a *sairandhrī*. This will be determined precisely in the ninth chapter. And this same rule applies to a woman whose husband is away on a journey. The use of the word "if she desires" (*kāma*) is intended to indicate a lack of approval. Even the emaciation of the body is an improper act; but this other act—sexual union with another man—is even more improper. (5.155)
Until death she remained patient, self-restrained, and chaste, longing for that supreme dharma which belongs to women who have but one husband. 5.156

This very point is made clear: she should remain a celibate student until death. In this calamity, she must not sustain herself through unchastity. "Patient" means disregarding the suffering caused by that [famine]. She should not let her celibacy be broken by hunger, which might shatter her mind like a wave. Those who have one husband are *ekapatnyaḥ*—or those who are the wives of one man; of such women as Sāvitrī and others, there is a certain dharma and its fruit, namely the power to bestow boons or utter curses. Desiring—that is, longing for—that [dharma], she should not abandon her celibacy. In this state, if death occurs while she is subsisting on roots and fruits, there is no fault. (5.156)
Many thousands of brahmins who practiced celibacy from their youth have gone to heaven without having produced offspring to continue their lineage. (5.157)

In the preceding verse, intercourse with another man for the sake of livelihood was forbidden; by this [verse], however, the undertaking [of intercourse] for the sake of a son is prohibited. For it is indeed heard [in scripture]: "There is no world for one who has no son" (AitB 33.1). Furthermore, the gender [of the subject in that passage] is not intended to be significant; therefore, this is stated in response to the objection regarding the pursuit of a son. Many thousands of youths alone—celibate students (*brahmacārin*) who have not taken wives and are lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika*)—have gone to heaven; they attain the celestial realm. As for *niyoga* (authorization for procreation), it is ordained in the ninth chapter (MDh 9.59) by the will of the teacher's wife, and not by her own independent authority when she herself desires a son. "Without having established the lineage" means without having produced offspring for the sake of increasing the family line—that is, without having begotten sons. Regarding the word *anekāni* ("many"), the use of the plural is to be considered since, in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the meaning of the final member is predominant. Even though there is a negation of oneness, the expression of numbers such as two and so forth is difficult to obtain. Nevertheless, this [word], while its own form is obscured by being absorbed into its own specific duty (*svadharma*) and thus having its own nature concealed, expresses very long specific numbers, just as one says "Moda is a village. And it has been said by the author of the *Cūrṇikā*: "The form *anekasmāt* is established. He has thus shown the establishment of the rule for using the singular number. Alternatively, this word *aneka* signifies "without a companion. "They have gone without companions" means that these [students] had no wife to serve as a companion. (5.157)
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who are lifelong celibates. (5.158)
This very same point is stated again for the sake of strengthening one's practice. 5.158
But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband, incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world. (5.159)

"The desire 'May a son be born to me' is the longing for offspring; because of that [desire], she who acts transgressing her husband and would unite with another incurs censure and reproach in this world and does not attain heaven. (5.159)
No offspring born here belongs to anyone else, nor does it fall under the guardianship of another; for virtuous women, a second husband is nowhere prescribed. (5.160)
The offspring produced by one through another man is not his offspring at all; and that which is produced by a man upon the wife of another does not belong to him either. (5.160)
She who, having abandoned her own inferior husband, serves one who is superior, becomes contemptible in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband. (5.161)
Not only does she incur reproach for this, but when there is infidelity toward her husband, a woman incurs contempt in the world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases. (5.162)
Therefore, out of desire for rewards both seen and unseen, she should not transgress against her husband.
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, attains the world of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous. (5.162–163)
By this conduct, a woman who is restrained in mind, speech, and body attains supreme fame in this world and the world of her husband in the next. (5.164)

The verses summarizing the duties of women are straightforward; therefore, I have not bestowed much effort upon their explanation here. This much is the purpose of the instruction therein: just as for a man, the act of resuming sexual union with another woman is not permitted here by the principle of the rule "and she should not transgress what is established" (MDh 5.149), meaning there is no further joint engagement; likewise, by the rule "she goes to heaven even if childless" (MDh 5.158), the procreation of offspring is prohibited in times of distress—though that same act will be permitted again by the Smṛti on *niyoga*—thus this procreation of offspring is subject to option because it is both enjoined and prohibited. Regarding these two Smṛtis, it is impossible to determine which is superior such that in one case there is offspring and in the other her self-restraint (*saṃyama*). Both cases, however, fulfill the reality of the matter. (5.163–164)

A twice-born man who knows the law should cause his wife—who has behaved accordingly, is of the same caste, and dies before him—to be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire and the sacrificial implements. (5.165)

The verse is a restatement of what is established by logic: thus, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the fire-maintainer (*agnihotrin*) has already been stated here in the passage beginning with "she is a virtuous wife" (*evaṃ tasyāḥ sādhvī*). [This is supported by the text: "Indeed, these fires are not maintained when the wife has died. (5.165)
Having given the sacred fires to his wife who dies first during the funeral rites, he may again perform the marriage ceremony and likewise the re-establishment of the fires. (5.166)

This is cited again for the sake of further qualification. This too is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding eligibility (*adhikāra*) along with another [case]. However, when it concerns wealth, a purpose, or the performance of religious duties (*dharmakarma*), then even due to the absence of assistance, there is no prohibition of eligibility for the forest-dweller’s stage (*vānaprastha*) or the wandering mendicant’s stage (*pārivrājya*). And so says the Śruti: "One is indeed released from this by old age. Or, it may be due to the loss of the purpose. Others, however, say: the word "when" (*yadā*) will be supplied here; by this, the non-contradiction of the Śruti concerning the lifelong fire-oblation (*yāvajjīvahomīya*) will be established. (5.166)
By this rule, he should never neglect the five sacrifices;
having taken a wife, he should dwell in his house during the second stage of life. (5.167)
The concluding verse: "And the mention of the five sacrifices is for the sake of establishing everything. (5.167)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi Svāmin, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
